"One person saved is great. Fifteen percent, and the 40 people we've saved, is tremendous," he said.

Bass will face off against progressive city councilwoman Nithya Raman, who has her own ties to the homeless crisis as chair of the Los Angeles City Council's Housing and Homelessness Committee, in her bid to win another term as mayor in November.

World.title: Washington mother pulls children from school after Pride lesson shown in music class without notice
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A Washington mother says she is withdrawing her children from an elementary school after learning a Pride-themed lesson had been presented during music class without advance notice to parents or an opportunity to opt out, raising questions about district policies governing classroom instruction.

"I assumed I had probably missed an email asking for consent, but there was nothing," Maria Varchetto said in communications with school administrators, which she shared with Fox News Digital on Monday. "No advanced notice, no opportunity to review the lesson, no information letting parents know this topic would be discussed. No option to request that our kids be allowed to opt out and participate in an alternative activity. There was nothing."

Varchetto alleged the lesson was presented to elementary school students, including her daughter, on June 15 at Martha Lake Elementary School in the Edmonds School District as part of a music class and that parents were not informed beforehand.

TRUMP ADMIN TARGETS WOKE SCHOOLS ACCUSED OF HIDING STUDENTS' GENDER TRANSITIONS FROM PARENTS

Varchetto said that a video entitled, "Why is Pride in June," from the YouTube account, "Queer Kid Stuff," which, according to the account, "imagines a kinder and more equal future through highly-accessible education and entertainment for kids ages 3+," was shown to her fourth-grade daughter.

The YouTube channel describes itself as an "LGBTQ+ educational webseries for children ages 3+ hosted by a tie-wearing queer lady, Lindsay, and her non-binary best-stuffed friend, Teddy. Gender Studies 101 meets Mr. Rodgers’ Neighborhood!"

Varchetto said the incident prompted her to remove her children from the school.

VIRGINIA SCHOOL DISTRICT SUED OVER ALLEGED POLICY OF KEEPING STUDENTS' GENDER TRANSITIONS HIDDEN FROM PARENTS

"We are 100% removing our kids from this school as I have no trust in the leadership," Varchetto said.

Other materials Varchetto said were included were a list of videos from musicians in the LGBTQ+ community such as Freddie Mercury of Queen, Lil Nas X, and Billy Porter dancing in a ballgown on Sesame Street.

Varchetto told school officials that her daughter recalled hearing during the lesson that students could identify as gay, lesbian, transgender, asexual, nonbinary or Two-Spirit.

She said an administrator told her she had not been aware those topics were part of the classroom discussion, leaving Varchetto wondering whether the lesson included more than the materials she had been shown.

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION OPENS FOUR TITLE IX INVESTIGATIONS INTO MICHIGAN AND NORTH CAROLINA SCHOOL DISTRICTS

"No handouts were sent home (which is typical for music class)," Varchetto told Fox News Digital in a statement.

Varchetto said she asked the school for a copy of the lesson materials but was told they could only be reviewed in person rather than sent electronically. She also said parents were not notified beforehand that the lesson would be taught, were not given an opportunity to opt their children out, and received no advance communication about its content.

She said that cultural lessons were taught every month for the theme of that month, but that Pride month was left off of the list of lessons.

"I feel mad they did this, mad they hid it," Varchetto said. "I feel insulted, offended, angry, and sad that my kids are now being taken out of a lifestyle they've grown to love, away from the friendships they've built, all because this one teacher didn't care to ask permission and a principal lied and hid it."

In a statement to Fox News Digital, a spokesperson for Edmonds School District said, "The lesson was not part of a districtwide Pride curriculum. It was a music lesson developed by the school’s music teacher that highlighted the contributions of influential musicians, including some who identify as LGBTQ+."

The spokesperson continued, "The purpose of the lesson was to teach music and music history through the lives and contributions of notable artists. Discussions about an artist’s background or identity were included as relevant biographical context, similar to how students may learn about other aspects of historical figures’ lives that helped shape their experiences and contributions."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The spokesperson added, "We expect instructional materials to be age-appropriate and aligned with district expectations and state standards. As with any concern raised about classroom instruction, we will work with the school administrator to determine whether they met those expectations."

World.title: Man sentenced to 6 months in jail for ramming car into Jewish group's world headquarters in New York
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A man was sentenced on Wednesday to six months and a week behind bars for ramming his car into the Chabad Lubavitch World Headquarters in January, damaging some of the a side-entrance door.

Dan Sohail, 36, of New Jersey, was sentenced in Brooklyn federal court, where he was also ordered to pay $20,000 in restitution. The sentence will allow Sohail, who has already spent six months in custody, to be released in about a week.

Sohail was charged with intentionally damaging religious property, and he pleaded guilty in May.

Prosecutors recommended a 14-month sentence, which would have kept Sohail behind bars for roughly another eight months, but the judge declined the request. Prosecutors sought the longer sentence as a deterrent to future attacks on Jewish institutions amid a rise in antisemitic hate crimes.

DRIVER RAMS CAR REPEATEDLY INTO DOORS OF NYC JEWISH SITE, SUSPECT DETAINED

On Jan. 28, Sohail repeatedly rammed his vehicle into the Chabad Lubavitch World Headquarters. He moved protective barriers, gestured for congregants to get out of the way and drove his car into the building’s side entrance five times, knocking the door off its hinges and destroying his car's front bumper.

While the doors were damaged, no injuries were reported.

Judge Eric N. Vitaliano said he was "somewhat saddened" that the Justice Department wanted him to be influenced at sentencing by the public’s mistaken initial impression that the attack was a hate crime.

Prosecutors said ahead of sentencing that 80 of 146 hate crime incidents across New York City since the start of the year were based on crimes targeting Jewish people and institutions.

NY ASSEMBLYMAN CALLS FOR DOJ TO INVESTIGATE MAMDANI, PROTECT JEWISH NEW YORKERS AFTER STABBING ATTACKS

But Vitaliano said the government's push for a stricter sentence as a deterrent to future attacks was in part based on the incident initially being labeled as an "I-hate-the-Jews crime, or, worse, an act-of-terrorism crime."

The judge cited a psychiatric report and said Sohail's mental health challenges "played an important role" in his sentencing.

"This is a sad tale," Vitaliano said.

Sohail's lawyer, Mia Eisner-Grynberg, said he had been trying to win acceptance at the Jewish institution as he struggled with psychological issues.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Eisner-Grynberg told the judge in court papers before sentencing that Sohail was battling depression and post-traumatic stress disorder after a traumatic childhood when he carried out the attack, even as he "desperately sought belonging and understanding through his exploration of Judaism."

She said Sohail attended the Chabad he later attacked, finding rabbinical students there "warm and welcoming."

Sohail "danced with them" and followed their recommendation to visit Israel, but he became erratic and extremely anxious after returning to the U.S., "begging" members of Chabad to help him, Eisner-Grynberg said.

Ramming the car into the building was "an irrational cry for help," she said.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

World.title: George and Amal Clooney evacuate France home as wildfires spread across Europe
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A representative for George Clooney confirmed the evacuation to People and shared a letter the couple sent to Brignoles Mayor Didier Brémond

The couple and their 9-year-old twins left their home in Brignoles, in France's Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur region, as fires threatened large swaths of the Mediterranean, the outlet reported. A representative for George Clooney confirmed to People that the couple sent a letter to Brignoles Mayor Didier Brémond before leaving.

"Dear Didier, At this point we have no idea whether our beautiful home makes it through this terrible moment," the letter began.

DEADLY FRENCH WILDFIRES THREATEN MISSILE PLANTS, NUCLEAR SITES AS FOURTH HEATWAVE LOOMS

"As we evacuate Brignoles we want to emphasise 2 things, first we hope you and the people of our city are safe and second that Amal and i are committed to making sure that whatever happens to our village, we are part of this community and we’ll be part of making it whole," the letter continued. "We love Brignoles and our friends who live there."

Fox News Digital has reached out to Clooney's representatives for additional comment, including whether the family has safely evacuated and if there is any update on the condition of their home.

The evacuation comes as wildfires continue to scorch southern Europe.

EUROPE'S FIRES REVEAL DEADLY MIX OF RECORD HEAT, HUMAN ERROR, ARSON AND LAND MISMANAGEMENT

As of Wednesday, an uncontained wildfire roughly four times the size of Paris was burning across southwestern France. The blaze was separate from the fire threatening the Brignoles area, where about 3,000 people were evacuated. Fires also continued to threaten parts of southern Europe, and three firefighters died in Greece as crews battled extreme heat, drought and strong winds, according to The Associated Press.

More than 300,000 people have been forced to evacuate in France and Spain, including residents and tourists.

Temperatures climbed to nearly 104 degrees Wednesday in France's Gironde region, where the country's largest wildfire prompted the evacuation of roughly 220,000 residents and vacationers at its peak. While many have since returned, tens of thousands remain displaced.

HEATHER LOCKLEAR SAYS SHE LIVES 'FAR AWAY' FROM HOLLYWOOD AND STAYS OUT OF THE SOCIAL SCENE

In an October 2025 interview with Esquire , Clooney said he and Amal chose to raise their family on a farm in France to give their children a quieter upbringing away from Hollywood.

"A good portion of my life growing up was on a farm, and as a kid, I hated the whole idea of it," he said. "But now, for them, it’s like—they’re not on their iPads, you know? They have dinner with grown-ups and have to take their dishes in. They have a much better life."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Clooney also said he was "worried about raising our kids in L.A., in the culture of Hollywood."

"I felt like they were never going to get a fair shake at life," he said. "France — they kind of don’t give a s--- about fame. I don’t want them to be walking around worried about paparazzi. I don’t want them being compared to somebody else’s famous kids."

World.title: Storm co-owner suspended after incident with Sophie Cunningham fans as star breaks silence on controversy
World.content:
Seattle Storm co-owner Celeste Keaton has been fined and suspended from attending the team's next five home games, the WNBA confirmed to Fox News Digital.

The suspension and fine come after Keaton allegedly called a pair of teenage Sophie Cunningham fans "f—ing insane" during a game on Tuesday, independent Seattle-based journalist Brandi Kruse told Fox News Digital. Kruse was in the arena and accompanied the girls, who were there to watch Cunningham and the Indianaa Fever take on the Storm.

Cunningham addressed the incident involving Keaton in an X repost of Fox News Digital's report late Wednesday night.

WHITE HOUSE DEFENDS WNBA STAR SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM AFTER SHE SPEAKS OUT IN SUPPORT OF PROTECTING WOMEN'S SPORTS

"I truly believe there is a safe space and love for EVERYBODY. Biological girls, biological boys, trans women, and trans men. Everyone is welcome at my table! You can disagree and still be kind. Bravo to those girls for standing up for what they believe. You’ll be hearing from me soon yay for gifts. Truly embarrassing of the co-owner. Unfortunately shows the type of leader she is," Cunningham wrote.

Storm majority owner Ginny Gilder issued a statement Wednesday apologizing for the co-owner’s comments during the game.

"We are aware one of our co-owners made comments to two fans in attendance at last night's game. We apologize that this happened. Everyone who attends a Storm game deserves to feel welcome, and we remain committed to creating an inclusive environment where every fan is treated with respect," the statement read.

SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM RALLY ROCKS WNBA GAME AS 'SAVE WOMEN'S SPORTS' ACTIVISTS FACE COUNTERPROTEST

Two girls went to the game wearing XX-XY Athletics gear to celebrate Cunningham coming out in support of saving women's sports, and even got to sit court-side. But the night took a dark turn, and now they are viral martyrs. The Storm put out an apology after a team co-owner allegedly shouted insults at the girls during the game. Additional footage, distributed by Fox News Digital, of them in a confrontation with another fan at the game has ignited further outrage.

The incident drew so much attention that famed "Harry Potter" author J.K. Rowling even cast judgment on the night that is bound to live in WNBA infamy.

Rowling and other prominent social media users amplified the girls’ account of the incident.

The night began with a rally outside Climate Pledge Arena in Seattle to celebrate Cunningham's recent public stance.

A small group of counterprotesters supporting transgender inclusion also gathered outside the arena.

Kruse, who helped organize the event and went into the game to accompany the girls during portions of the night, said she saw Storm players make mocking gestures toward them. Separately, the girls alleged that Keaton approached them and used profane language.

"They were giving them thumbs down — like, to their faces," Kruse said.

Kruse said the girls then told her that an older woman associated with the Storm had approached them, yelled at them and called them "f---ing insane."

The girls later pointed out the woman sitting directly across from them beside Storm legend and team co-owner Sue Bird, according to Kruse. When Kruse alerted an arena security guard, she said the guard identified the woman as "one of the owners of the team."

Kruse later identified the woman as Keaton, who has previously been publicly identified as a member of the Storm’s ownership group.

Kruse said she pressed security to confront the woman, arguing that the alleged conduct violated the arena’s code of conduct. Climate Pledge Arena prohibits abusive or obscene language and says violators may be ejected.

"Had this been any other fan under any other circumstances who swore at and called some teenage girls ‘f---ing insane’ until they cried, they would’ve been ejected," Kruse said.

Kruse said one of the girls broke down in tears during the game after the alleged exchange.

"I look over at halftime, and she’s sobbing," Kruse said. "They were so excited for those seats, like a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to see some of their favorite players. They stayed up the night before making signs."

Kruse also claimed that the girls were not forced to put down their signs in support of Cunningham, despite online rumors, but that they chose to put them down after the alleged harassment.

"The report that they told the girls to put those signs away is not true," Kruse said. "The girls put their signs away because of what happened with Celeste, and they just felt so scared and uncomfortable, they decided not to hold them anymore."

Before the game, the Storm said it was aware of the planned demonstration and was "tracking it closely." The team said it remained committed to providing a safe and inclusive environment for all guests.

Storm head coach Sonia Raman addressed the rally after the game but did not discuss the allegations involving the girls.

"We always want to be an area where people feel welcome coming into this building," Raman said, adding that the organization coordinated with arena security. "From what I understand, that was successful."

The comments came before Kruse publicly detailed the allegations involving the teenagers.

The Fever, meanwhile, distanced the organization and Cunningham from the rally. A team public relations representative interrupted when head coach Stephanie White was asked about the gathering during her postgame press conference.

"Neither our organization nor Sophie had any knowledge of this demonstration and no contact with its organizers," the representative said.

The representative added that the Fever remained united around winning games and building its fan base before directing reporters back to basketball questions.

Neither Cunningham nor Clark was made available to reporters after the game. Mitchell and Monique Billings appeared beside White instead. When White was asked about the rally, she also said the team and its players were not aware of it and had not been in touch with the organizers.

World.title: Senate committee postpones vote on Todd Blanche’s nomination over disagreements with GOP senators
World.content:
WASHINGTON — The Senate Judiciary Committee postponed its vote on whether to advance Todd Blanche’s nomination to be attorney general after two Republican senators said they did not receive written assurances they were seeking from the Justice Department surrounding a settlement between President Donald Trump and the IRS.

The GOP-led committee was scheduled to vote Thursday morning on sending Blanche’s nomination to the full Senate, but Republican Sens. John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, both of whom have clashed with Trump and neither of whom faces re-election in November, have complicated Blanche’s path to confirmation with their demands from the Justice Department.

Cornyn and Tillis met with Judiciary Committee Chair Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, on Wednesday afternoon as they said they were continuing to negotiate with the Justice Department.

A spokesperson for the committee said Wednesday evening that the vote would not happen Thursday.

“Chairman Grassley works to set President Trump’s nominees up for success in committee, not failure,” the spokesperson said in a statement. “Senators Cornyn and Tillis want written assurances from the Department of Justice regarding the Trump-IRS settlement. Tomorrow’s markup is postponed as work continues to secure sufficient support in committee to favorably report Attorney General-nominee Todd Blanche, who is highly qualified for the job.”

A Justice Department official said Wednesday night that the Justice Department has transmitted new language to Cornyn and Tillis and that conversations to resolve their concerns continue.

Much of Cornyn and Tillis’ negotiations with the Justice Department has been around the “anti-weaponization” fund that was established under a purported settlement between Trump and the executive branch, which he controls, over a lawsuit he filed over the disclosure of his tax records. The suit led to a five-year prison sentence for a former IRS contractor.

A federal judge in Virginia indefinitely blocked the fund after a former Jan. 6 prosecutor sued. A federal judge in Florida found that Trump’s IRS lawsuit was brought in “bad faith” for an “improper purpose” and ordered sanctions against several people involved, including Blanche.

But the settlement agreement also had provisions that offered Trump — along with his family members and companies — some protection from IRS audits.

Tillis said Wednesday that his demands to the Justice Department have been consistent: kill the anti-weaponization fund and narrow the settlement with Trump involving IRS audits.

“Get whoever the president’s lawyers are the parties to the agreement to sign off on that, we’re good to go,” Tillis said before the vote was postponed.

He said he has been in “constant daily contact with the DOJ” and that it was “working on a draft right now.” After the meeting with Grassley and Cornyn, Tillis said that it appeared the Justice Department has agreed to his terms on the anti-weaponization fund but that he still needed clarification on who is protected against IRS audits through the settlement.

Cornyn, who lost his primary race to Trump-endorsed Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, said Wednesday that it is Grassley’s decision when the vote is held.

It was not immediately clear Wednesday evening when the vote would take place.

Cornyn told reporters that Blanche’s team had failed to provide written proposals to modify the document release that was signed in the tax dispute with Trump and his organization.

“I haven’t seen a single piece of writing that is responsive to what I’ve requested,” Cornyn said.

He later said Trump’s claim that he is holding up the vote because Trump didn’t endorse him in the GOP primary is “a convenient excuse for not cooperating with the Judiciary Committee’s appropriate role in judicial confirmations.”

As the talks continued Wednesday night, the administration was pointing the finger at Cornyn, making some of the same accusations from earlier in the day.

According to a senior administration official, people familiar with the conversations described the senator as continually moving the goal posts, canceling meetings and refusing to communicate — no matter what the Justice Department offered.

Cornyn’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment Wednesday evening.

Blanche, who previously was Trump’s personal defense attorney, had served in the key No. 2 position at the Justice Department until Trump fired Pam Bondi as attorney general in April amid frustrations with her leadership.

After he took over as the acting attorney general, Blanche told NBC News in April that Americans should be “happy” that Trump was so involved in Justice Department matters. Less than two weeks later, the Trump administration brought a case against former FBI Director James Comey, a longtime Trump foe, over an Instagram photo of seashells.

Following the Comey indictment, Trump was said to be happy with Blanche’s performance and ultimately ended up nominating him for the job permanently. Comey’s legal team argued in a court filing this week that the seashells case came about because Blanche was seeking to “please President Trump” during his “audition” for the role.

During his confirmation hearing this month, Blanche said he was not a “yes man” for Trump.

World.title: City’s first female mayor investigated after police chief’s sexual harassment complaint
World.content:
The St. Paul, Minnesota, police chief has submitted a sexual harassment complaint against the city’s first female mayor, alleging she behaved inappropriately toward him and other members of his department, the local NBC affiliate reported Wednesday.

The city has hired an outside law firm to investigate the allegations against Mayor Kaohly Her, who has been in office for just seven months.

Chief Axel Henry, who has led the St. Paul Police Department since 2022, outlined the allegations in an April 1 letter his lawyer sent to the St. Paul city attorney.

“The City is on notice that Mayor Her has engaged in illegal conduct towards City employees,” attorney Christopher Madel wrote in the letter, which was obtained by the NBC affiliate, KARE.

Henry sent the letter of complaint after having become “aware that the Mayor’s conduct has extended beyond isolated incidents and has included sexual harassment of subordinate City employees, including members of the Saint Paul Police Department,” Madel wrote.

“Chief Henry is not only seeking to address the wrongdoing but also create a measure of protection for his team, signaling that such conduct will not be tolerated,” Madel wrote.

Included with the letter is a screenshot of an alleged text message from Her to an unnamed city employee that reads “Happy Weiner Wednesday! Wish I was having a (hot dog emoji) with you all on 6 today!”

Below the text message is an internet meme showing a swaddled baby with an adult’s head, which has been redacted, The Minnesota Star Tribune reported.

“When she wraps you up in her blanket after you gave her a good weinering,” reads the caption.

“Wienering” is an internet slang term for sexual intercourse and is frequently misspelled as “weinering.”

The letter alleges that “Her has used one or more mobile phones to communicate inappropriate, and, indeed, unlawful text messages.”

But it does not spell out any other specific allegations of inappropriate communications.

Madel wrote that future litigation is “reasonably foreseeable” and demanded that the city “immediately take all steps necessary to perform a full filesystem extraction of each of Mayor Her’s mobile phones.”

In a written statement Wednesday, Her said she has cooperated with the investigation and believes the “full facts will come to light.”

“As Mayor, I take my responsibility to treat every employee with professionalism and respect very seriously. I recognize that some of my attempts at humor fell short of the standard I expect of myself,” she said.

Police spokesperson Nikki Muehlhausen said, “Chief Henry and the department has no comment at this time.”

The Star Tribune reported that Resolute Law, based in St. Cloud and described on its website as a “women-owned firm,” has been hired to investigate the allegations.

The law firm did not respond to a request for comment on the status of the investigation.

Her, 53, was born in Laos and spent part of her childhood in a refugee camp. She was 3 when she arrived in the U.S., and she grew up in Illinois and Wisconsin, according to her campaign biography.

The Star Tribune reported that she had faced an accusation of inappropriate behavior before.

Her was hit with a restraining order petition last year by a former friend who claimed she had sent her “inappropriate or sexualized questions” and had gotten her removed from the National Kidney Foundation Board.

The petition was denied by Ramsey County District Court Referee Elizabeth Clysdale, who wrote that the text messages filed showed that Her had not threatened her former friend and that Her’s husband had tried to help resolve the issue.

Clysdale also wrote there was no proof that Her had played a role in the woman’s removal from the National Kidney Foundation Board, the newspaper reported.

World.title: Todd Blanche’s rocky road: From the Politics Desk
World.content:
Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.

In today’s edition, we dig into the uncertain paths forward for Todd Blanche’s attorney general nomination and the Iran war.

Sign up to receive this newsletter in your inbox every weekday here.

— Adam Wollner

Trump’s IRS carveout threatens to hold up Todd Blanche’s AG nomination

Todd Blanche’s bid to be the next attorney general faced a setback today as two key Republicans pressed the Justice Department to commit in writing to kill an “anti-weaponization” fund that could give money to President Donald Trump’s allies and restrict the scope of the tax audit immunity given to him and his family members.

The Senate Judiciary Committee is set to hold a hearing to advance Blanche’s nomination tomorrow morning. But GOP Sens. John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, who have clashed with Trump and are not facing re-election in November, have emerged as potential roadblocks on Blanche’s path to the full Senate.

Much of the discussion has been around the “anti-weaponization fund” that was established under a purported settlement between Trump and the executive branch he controls over a lawsuit the president filed over the disclosure of his tax records, which led to a five-year prison sentence for a former IRS contractor.

A federal judge in Virginia indefinitely blocked the fund after a former Jan. 6 prosecutor sued. A federal judge in Florida found that Trump’s IRS lawsuit was brought in “bad faith” for an “improper purpose,” and ordered sanctions against several people involved, including Blanche.

But the settlement agreement also had provisions that offered Trump — along with his family members and companies — some protection from IRS audits.

Cornyn, who lost his GOP primary earlier this year to Trump-backed Ken Paxton, told reporters that Blanche’s team had failed to provide written proposals to modify the release that was signed in the tax dispute with Trump and his organization.

“I haven’t seen a single piece of writing that is responsive to what I’ve requested,” Cornyn said.

Tillis, who is retiring at the end of his term, said he was in active discussions with the Justice Department.

“They’re working on a draft right now,” Tillis said this afternoon. “We’ve been in constant daily contact with DOJ, and to their credit, they’re engaging.”

Read more →

After Trump and Netanyahu meet, the Iran war’s future remains hazy

Analysis by Andrea Mitchell

As the United States enters its sixth month of a war with Iran that Israeli and U.S. leaders both said would last only four to six weeks, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu met with President Donald Trump Tuesday and other top national security officials for the first time since the conflict started.

In Washington for the funeral of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, a key Netanyahu ally, a senior Israeli official told NBC News and other reporters that they discussed three major options: a good deal to eliminate Iran having a nuclear weapon; no deal, but a sustained blockade and economic pressure; and military action.

Without saying what Israel’s preference is, a senior Israeli official said there was broad agreement — as Trump repeatedly affirms — that Iran cannot be allowed to have a nuclear weapon. But Trump told my colleague Kristen Welker last month that the U.S. has eyes on the nuclear facilities the U.S. and Israel bombed last June, and that nothing can move in or out of those two sites without the U.S. seeing it.

Today, the Israeli official demurred from saying his country disagrees with Trump’s assessments. In particular, he wouldn’t say whether Netanyahu is urging the U.S. to bomb another suspected nuclear site — Pickaxe Mountain. It has been widely reported that U.S. intelligence assesses that site would be impossible to eliminate even with the most devastating U.S. bunker-buster bombs, but it could be effectively closed and made unreachable by Iran.

At the behest of the administration, Israel has not re-engaged in the recurring U.S. strikes against Iran that have taken place since a 60-day ceasefire was officially agreed to in mid-June. At the time, Israel strongly criticized the memorandum of understanding as being far too generous to Iran because it approved the release of billions of dollars in frozen Iranian assets. None of that was turned over because of the collapse of diplomacy and reignition of airstrikes by both sides, and more recently, strikes by Iran against U.S. and Arab allied assets in the region.

During his three days in Washington, Netanyahu also met separately with Vice President JD Vance, who was initially skeptical of the Iran war, and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and other Pentagon officials. Still at issue: Will economic pressure alone get the Iranian regime to permit open access to the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow international waterway critical to the global economy?

The Israeli official who briefed reporters today acknowledged that sustained economic pressure — if it cut off all supplies to Iran — could be a solution, although it would hurt Iranian civilians. But a second Israeli official said money is still flowing from Iran’s regime through Turkey to Hezbollah, its proxy that Israel is fighting in southern Lebanon.

Both Trump and Netanyahu are facing elections this fall. The big difference is that Netanyahu, despite growing opposition at home, has strong popular support for resuming attacks against Iran.

Trump’s political reality is exactly opposite: The war has depleted the supply of U.S. missiles and interceptors for Patriot air defense systems and is damaging his popularity, even with his own base. It has caused gas and diesel fuel prices to spike and contributed to inflation.

While the Israeli briefer said today that Trump has been an “amazing ally” for Israel in the war, he acknowledged the U.S. president is the senior partner and Netanyahu the junior — making it more imperative for Trump’s political standing to find some diplomatic way out of the current standoff.

World.title: Deodorant for kids: Derms talk the right age for deodorant and the best ones for young skin
World.content:
We don’t always have the answers, but we have some people on speed dial who do — which is why we present to you our series FYI where we have experts explain if lip balm is actually bad, how often you should wash your hair and more.

It used to be that as kids approached their teen years, they’d start incorporating deodorant into their routine. But these days, lots of kids are reaching for it before they’ve even turned 10 years old. Because of this, brands have poured into the kids’ deodorant space in recent years, with gentler formulas aimed at tweens and even younger children.

Dermatologists say the shift tracks a real biological change. “This reflects the fact that many children are entering puberty earlier than previous generations,” says Dr. Kristina Collins, a board-certified dermatologist specializing in Mohs micrographic surgery, as well as surgical and cosmetic dermatology in Texas. “Body odor is often one of the first signs that the apocrine sweat glands are becoming active. If a child is experiencing body odor that affects their comfort or confidence, using a gentle deodorant can be appropriate.”

But is it safe for kids to wear deodorant? And if they’re going to, what should you look for in a formula? To get the answers to these questions, I spoke with Collins and another board-certified dermatologist.

Is deodorant safe for kids?

Deodorant is generally safe for kids to use, including during those early tween years when body odor first shows up. That said, kids’ skin tends to be more sensitive than adult skin, so the formula matters more than it might for a grown-up reaching for whatever’s under the sink.

“Heavy fragrances may trigger irritation or allergic reactions and alcohol-heavy formulas can sting or dry out the skin,” says Collins. “If your child has sensitive skin, even ingredients that are ‘natural’ can trigger allergic reactions.”

Translation: It’s worth paying closer attention to labels and doing a bit of trial and error to find something that works for your child’s skin, rather than assuming any deodorant will do.

At what age should a kid start wearing deodorant?

There’s no universal starting line for deodorant use and it really comes down to your child’s own body, not a birthday on the calendar. “It is based on when the sweat glands become active, which is different in everybody,” says Dr. Debra Jaliman, a board-certified dermatologist in New York City. “Most kids can start once body odor becomes noticeable, typically between the ages of 8 and 10.”

The easiest way to know it’s time is if you or your child start noticing a change in smell, especially after gym class, recess, or a hot day; that’s usually the signal that their apocrine sweat glands (ones located in your armpit that secrete oily sweat) have kicked in. At that point, introducing a gentle, kids’ deodorant can help with odor, comfort and confidence.

The best deodorants for kids

To come up with a list of the best deodorants for kids, I used expert guidance (find it below) to select options safe for younger skin. I also focused on trusted brands or products with at least a four-star average rating from hundreds of shoppers.

I regularly use Tubby Todd products and love how gentle they are, so their Deo Stick is an easy pick for sensitive skin. It’s aluminum- and baking soda-free, using tapioca starch and magnesium hydroxide (ingredients our experts say are gentle enough for kid skin) to absorb wetness and fight odor-causing bacteria. According to the brand, it is gentle enough for kids ages 6 and up.

Level Up Boys Deodorant is made specifically for young, sensitive skin. It has an Ocean Fresh scent and is free of aluminum, alcohol and parabens. Similar to the Tubby Todd option, it uses natural tapioca starch to absorb wetness. Reviewers note that the scent is pleasant without being overpowering, and say that it’s effective for 24 hours.

Evereden’s deodorant has an aluminum-free formula that’s made without baking soda or silicones. It contains vitaminsE and B5 to nourish skin and it is dermatologist-tested, according to the brand. It also has a sweet scent of rose, strawberry, and vanilla.

This deodorant is free of aluminum, parabens, phthalates, dyes and baking soda and contains shea butter to keep underarms soft and hydrated. It’s dermatologically tested and vegan, with a sweet watermelon and peach scent. The bright packaging is also appealing for younger kids.

This deodorant delivers 24-hour odor protection without aluminum, parabens or phthalates, according to the brand. It’s hypoallergenic and dermatologist-tested for sensitive skin, glides on clear without white marks, according to parents who’ve bought it, and it comes in a playful gummy burst scent. Parents also say it helps kids who get sweaty and stinky in gym class or on the playground, and that they like that it isn’t irritating.

Want more from NBC Select? 

How to shop for deodorant for kids

Both Collins and Jaliman recommend starting kids with deodorant rather than antiperspirant, since most children simply need help with odor rather than sweat reduction (which is what antiperspirant does — more on that below). Beyond that, they suggest looking for gentle formulas with minimal, recognizable ingredients rather than long lists of additives.

For kids with sensitive skin in particular, both dermatologists recommend opting for fragrance-free options or those with only light fragrance, since heavier scents and unnecessary extras are more likely to cause irritation on young, developing skin.

Do kids need antiperspirant?

Deodorant and antiperspirant often get lumped together, but they do different jobs. Deodorant works by masking and reducing odor, while antiperspirant actually blocks sweat production, typically using aluminum-based compounds.

“For most children, deodorant alone is sufficient because it helps reduce odor without affecting the body’s natural sweating process,” says Collins. “Antiperspirants contain aluminum salts that temporarily reduce sweating and are typically only necessary if a child has excessive sweating that interferes with daily life. If excessive sweating is present, it’s worth discussing with a pediatrician or dermatologist to determine the best treatment.”

In other words, reach for deodorant first, and don’t feel pressure to introduce antiperspirant unless your child is dealing with sweating that goes beyond the normal, everyday kind. And even then, talk to a doctor before you add aluminum and other ingredients to their body care routine.

Frequently asked questions Is there a difference between kid and adult deodorant? Not as much as the packaging might suggest. “The biggest differences are usually in the fragrance and marketing,” says Collins. “Children’s deodorants often use milder fragrances and are more likely to be formulated for sensitive skin. But from an ingredient standpoint, many are very similar to adult deodorants.” In many cases, the kid-focused branding is less about a fundamentally different product and more about making an everyday routine feel approachable for a first-time user. Is there anything else you can do to help prevent body odor in kids? Deodorant alone isn’t the whole equation. Both Collins and Jaliman emphasize that good hygiene habits are just as important, if not more so, in keeping body odor in check. That means taking daily showers or baths, especially after sports or physical activity, and wearing clean clothes and breathable fabrics that don’t trap sweat and bacteria against the skin. Building these habits alongside deodorant use can go a long way in helping kids feel fresh and confident as their bodies go through changes.

Meet our skin care experts

At NBC Selected, we work with experts with specialized knowledge and authority based on relevant training and/or experience. We also ensure all expert advice and recommendations are made independently and without undisclosed financial conflicts of interest.

Dr. Kristina Collins is a board-certified dermatologist specializing in Mohs micrographic surgery, as well as surgical and cosmetic dermatology in Texas.

Dr. Debra Jaliman, is a board-certified dermatologist in New York City and author of “Skin Rules.”

Why trust NBC Selected?

I am a commerce editor at NBC Selected and a journalist who regularly covers wellness, beauty, home and lifestyle. I have written about whether deodorant concealer really works, if beauty pillows actually ward off wrinkles, the benefits of tranexamic acid and more. I’m also a mom of two who is studying up for the days when my kids hit puberty. For this story, I spoke with two board-certified dermatologists on what you should know about kids’ deodorant.

World.title: Several dead as Russian attacks on Ukraine prompt new Zelenskyy call for help
World.content:
Kyiv, Ukraine — Russian attacks across Ukraine overnight into Thursday killed at least eight people and wounded dozens of others, officials said, with the heaviest casualties reported in the eastern Dnipropetrovsk and western Lviv regions.

The attacks were the latest in a series of large-scale Russian strikes on Ukrainian cities that Russia has intensified over the summer, now occurring on a nearly weekly basis.

Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv and the surrounding region, along with the Dnipro, Lviv, Poltava, Kharkiv, Mykolaiv, Sumy, Vinnytsia, Cherkasy and Ivano-Frankivsk regions, were attacked overnight, with dozens of homes, businesses and infrastructure facilities destroyed or damaged.

He said Russia used more than 70 missiles in the strikes, a significant number of them ballistic, along with more than 280 attack drones, of which more than 260 were intercepted.

"Given the critical shortage of air defense missiles from our partners, our warriors are accomplishing truly incredible things, demonstrating a very high level of professionalism," he said. "This Russian terror once again proves that protection against the Russian missile threat is the most important task when it comes to saving the lives of our people."

Zelensky again called for allies to send Ukraine more anti-ballistic missiles.

Local residents react outside a residential building partially destroyed as a result of Russian missile strikes in the western Ukrainian city of Lviv on July 30, 2026. YURIY DYACHYSHYN / AFP via Getty Images

Poland scrambled fighter jets as the Russian attacks were being carried out, the Reuters news serviced reported, adding that Polish police found a crater and debris in a field after an unidentified object vanished from army radar tracking it in Polish airspace during the Russian attacks.

In the Dnipropetrovsk region, Russian forces carried out a mass attack that killed six people and wounded 10 and damaged or destroyed civilian infrastructure, said Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the regional military administration.

Children were among the dead, he said on Telegram - a 6-year-old girl and boys aged 11 and 17.

Zelenskyy specified in his post on X that their parents were killed as well in the same attack, but two more children were pulled alive from under the rubble.

"It was an ordinary home, blown into smithereens by a ballistic missile," he said. Delays in the delivery of anti-ballistic missiles lead to the kind of destruction and casualties seen in the attack, he continued.

In the Poltava region, next to Dnipropetrovsk region in the west, a drone strike hit warehouses at a private enterprise, killing one person, said regional head Vitalii Diakivnych. He said a delivery hub also was attacked, sparking a fire at warehouses that was quickly extinguished by State Emergency Service units, with no injuries reported there.

In Lviv, the number of people injured in a Russian missile attack rose to 30 as a rescue operation continued, said Maksym Kozytskyi, head of the Lviv regional military administration.

The city was struck at about 4:45 a.m., with the worst damage to two residential buildings, Lviv Mayor Andrii Sadovyi said. More than 20 residential buildings were damaged, along with a school and two kindergartens, he said, adding that children were among those injured, including one who was hospitalized.

Russian forces struck the capital of Kyiv with ballistic missiles, killing a 31-year-old man and wounding two others, the National Police press service said. Residential buildings, a market, a garage cooperative, storage facilities and vehicles were damaged in the city, police said.

In the Kyiv region, five people were wounded in the Brovary district, including a minor and two women, acting regional administration head Ruslan Oliinyk said on Facebook.

In Moscow, the Defense Ministry said the Russian armed forces overnight launched a massive strike on air bases, arms factories and military telecommunications and logistics facilities in Kyiv, Lviv and in the Ivano-Frankivsk, Zhytomyr, Rivne, Vinnytsia and Dnipropetrovsk regions.

It said the military also hit a ship in the Pivdennyi port and two ships east and south of Odesa.

Meanwhile, Russia's Defense Ministry said air defenses downed 258 Ukrainian drones overnight. Penza Gov. Oleg Melnichenko said a depot belonging to Wildberries online retailer was set ablaze. He said one person was injured and 200 workers were evacuated.

Wildberries also reported that its warehouse in Sarapul in the region of Udmurtia was struck by a Ukrainian drone and set ablaze. It said the workers had been safely evacuated. The attacks were the latest in a series of Ukrainian strikes that hit depots belonging to Wildberries, the country's largest online retailer, causing massive damage.

World.title: DOJ asking secretive court to remove Afghan woman allegedly tied to terror plot
World.content:
The Justice Department is seeking to convince a federal judge to deport a Texas-based Afghan woman who prosecutors allege is an "alien terrorist," it revealed Wednesday, in the first-ever test case before a secretive court that has never convened since it was created three decades ago.

Nazira Haji Zada, 47, of Fort Worth, Texas, will appear Thursday morning in the Alien Terrorist Removal Court in Washington, D.C., where a judge will hear evidence from the Justice Department over whether she should be removed from the United States, according to the Justice Department and court filings. The government is accusing her of links to a foiled Islamic State-inspired terrorist plot to carry out a mass shooting on Election Day in 2024.

"The allegations in this case show the matriarch of an ISIS-sympathizing family aiding in a plot to launch a mass casualty attack on American voters on Election Day," Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement.

Zada has never been publicly charged by the government with any crimes of terrorism, and has no known criminal history, according to the government.

Last year, her son Abdullah Haji Zada and son-in-law Nasir Ahmad Tawhedi each pleaded guilty in a federal court in Oklahoma to purchasing two AK-47 style rifles and 500 rounds of ammunition from an undercover FBI agent as part of an alleged plot targeting the 2024 election in support of the Islamic State.

At the time of his arrest in 2024, Zada's son was only 17. He was charged as an adult and pleaded guilty to gun crimes when he was 18. Tawhedi pleaded guilty to terrorism and gun offenses.

In an unclassified FBI summary filed in the Alien Terrorist Removal Court, the government alleged that Zada "supported" her son and son-in-law's conspiracy. The FBI also alleged she "pledged loyalty to ISIS" and "worked to indoctrinate her children with ISIS ideology," citing information from a "reliable source."

"Nazira worked with Tawhedi to radicalize the family and to conceal their pro-ISIS teaching and planned family relocation to ISIS-controlled territory from her unsuspecting husband," the FBI wrote.

The Alien Terrorist Removal Court was created by Congress in 1996 and signed into law by President Bill Clinton. It was set up to deport noncitizens who could not be removed by the traditional legal process because the information about their cases was classified and could not be made public for national security reasons.

The targets of noncitizen terrorist removal proceedings — including legal permanent residents — are not permitted to review the classified evidence against them, and unlike in criminal proceedings, they are barred from legally challenging how the evidence was collected by the government.

Applications for removal must be certified by the attorney general and are reviewed by the court ex parte and in camera — meaning the target of the deportation proceeding is not a party to the hearing.

If the application is accepted, it moves to the removal stage and a public hearing is conducted. As part of that, the Justice Department also releases an unclassified summary of the case, as it did in a newly created website for the court that was only launched on July 17.

Until July 15, when the Justice Department first filed its removal application against Zada, the Alien Terrorist Removal Court had been a "zombie" court that existed only on paper. It had never been used before, and prior efforts by the Justice Department earlier on after its creation to find a test case failed.

The court is structured similarly to the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court, another secret court that reviews sensitive requests for surveillance warrants. All five of its judges also sit on the FISC and are appointed by the chief justice of the Supreme Court.

U.S. District Judge Joan Ericksen, who sits on the federal bench in Minnesota, is the chief judge of the Alien Terrorist Removal Court, and will preside over Zada's public removal hearing at the federal courthouse in Washington, D.C., at 11 a.m. ET Thursday.

Zada has a green card, according to publicly unsealed court records. Under the rules of the court, lawful permanent residents are afforded the right to government-appointed counsel — though that attorney may not share classified evidence with the defendant.

According to court filings, her spouse was employed at the Bagram Air Base in Afghanistan from 2009 to 2016, and was granted a green card under a program for Afghans who assisted U.S. forces during the war in Afghanistan.

CBS News could not immediately determine who may represent Zada at her removal hearing on Thursday.

CBS News has reached out to the defense attorney who represented her son in his criminal case in the Western District of Oklahoma, where the original case was brought.

Tawhedi and Abdullah Haji Zada were arrested on Oct. 7, 2024, after purchasing the firearms and ammunition from the undercover agent.

Abdullah Haji Zada, who was also a green card-holder like his mother, was sentenced to 15 years in prison. In his plea deal, he consented to being deported to Afghanistan after serving his sentence and acknowledged his lawful permanent resident status would be revoked.

Tawhedi, 28, pleaded guilty on June 13, 2025, to conspiring and attempting to provide material support and resources to the Islamic State.

Both were accused of conspiring to relocate their female and juvenile male family members, including Nazira Zada, to Islamic State-controlled territory in Afghanistan while their alleged Election Day plot was carried out.

World.title: Husband of North Carolina woman missing in Grenada doesn't suspect foul play
World.content:
The husband of a North Carolina woman who went missing last week while visiting the Caribbean island of Grenada said Wednesday he believes "there was no foul play" in her disappearance.

Cailen Waddell, the husband of Elizabeth Waddell, said in a statement that the ongoing investigation will focus on tracing his wife's movements in the hours before she disappeared, adding that "no detail is too small."

Waddell was last seen on security video at around noon on July 22 swimming off Grand Anse Beach, the Royal Grenada Police Force previously reported. According to Cailen Waddell, eyewitnesses later reported interacting with her at about 5:30 p.m. further from shore that same evening.

"After careful and thoughtful consultation with family, local authorities, the U.S. Embassy, and others here in Grenada, I join authorities in believing there was no foul play," Cailen Waddell said in Wednesday's statement. "Liz was last seen swimming in the ocean near Grand Anse, around 5:30 PM, far from shore. She communicated her confidence in her swimming and location, as well as the beauty of the island."

Grenada Police/Cailen Waddell

The 44-year-old North Carolina mother was on a three-week vacation with her close friend, Heather, at the time of her disappearance. According to her family, Waddell left the Airbnb she was sharing with Heather, and when she didn't return for hours, Heather went looking for her and found just her towel, but no other sign of her.

A friend of Waddell said this week that surveillance video of her last known movements on the day of her disappearance showed her "floating" and "swimming around."

"But then she, you know, she floats out of the camera view and so that's the last footage of Liz," her friend Amanda Romano-Harmon said.

Surveillance video showed Elizabeth Waddell walking toward a beachside pier around 11:30 a.m. before entering the water and swimming beneath the pier shortly after noon, Royal Grenada Police Acting Police Commissioner Randy Connaught said Tuesday. About 45 minutes later, her friend was seen heading toward the pier before returning alone.

Cailen Waddell described his wife as "a loving free-spirit person," telling Grenadian media last week that his wife "could make friends with anyone and she often did."

Police have asked anyone with information on Waddell's whereabouts to contact authorities immediately. The U.S. State Department has said it is aware of the disappearance.

World.title: Blanche's nomination for AG on hold over fate of DOJ's "anti-weaponization fund"
World.content:
Washington — Todd Blanche's confirmation as attorney general is on hold as Republican Sen. John Cornyn of Texas leverages his vote in exchange for an agreement in writing to formally kill the Justice Department's "anti-weaponization fund."

The Senate Judiciary Committee was set to vote on advancing Blanche's nomination, but Cornyn, a pivotal vote on the panel, told reporters, "I'm not prepared to vote yes" without an agreement.

Late Wednesday, the committee announced it had delayed a Thursday morning hearing to consider Blanche's nomination. A committee spokesperson said the hearing was "postponed as work continues to secure sufficient support in committee to favorably report Attorney General-nominee Todd Blanche, who is highly qualified for the job."

In a statement Wednesday night, a Justice Department spokesperson told CBS News that it "has been in regular communication with Committee members for weeks, and we look forward to continuing to work productively with Senators to address any concerns."

Opposition from Cornyn could sink the nomination of Blanche, who currently serves as acting attorney general.

GOP Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina, another member of the committee, said he shared Cornyn's concerns, but appeared more hopeful about a resolution. The two met with Senate Judiciary Chairman Chuck Grassley, an Iowa Republican, hours before Thursday's vote was canceled.

Cornyn has also demanded modifications to restrict the scope of the Justice Department agreement with President Trump that granted tax audit immunity to the president and his family for prior tax returns.

The audit protection and the nearly $1.8 billion fund to pay people who claim they were politically persecuted were part of a settlement to resolve Mr. Trump's lawsuit against the IRS and Treasury Department.

"All I want them to do is to confirm what he said in his sworn testimony before the Judiciary Committee, with regard not only to the weaponization fund, but also who is protected from future audits and what agencies of the federal government are bound by the release," Cornyn said Wednesday afternoon. "It's pretty simple, and we've actually sent them a redline strikeout."

Earlier in the day, Cornyn said he hadn't seen "a single piece of writing that is responsive to what I've requested."

A Justice Department official said the department provided a "written proposal" to Cornyn's staff Tuesday.

"We look forward to further discussion around any outstanding concerns," the official said.

But Cornyn said the Justice Department's proposal was "not responsive" to some of his concerns.

The Justice Department transmitted a new response to Cornyn and Tillis that "addresses their concerns," a source familiar with the matter said later Wednesday.

The "anti-weaponization" fund was met with fierce resistance from members on both sides of the aisle after its unveiling in May, leading the Justice Department to back away from it.

At his confirmation hearing earlier this month, Blanche reiterated that the fund was "dead." Cornyn noted that the settlement states that any changes to it must be agreed upon in writing by all parties involved.

"Has there been a written agreement of the parties to modify the settlement fund?" he asked.

"No, the settlement fund is just not moving forward," Blanche responded. "There's no modification. It never started. No money went from the Treasury to any other account."

Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office, Mr. Trump suggested Cornyn's opposition stemmed from his endorsement of his primary opponent, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. Paxton defeated Cornyn in the May primary.

"Maybe John Cornyn is upset with me because I didn't endorse him," Mr. Trump said.

In response to Mr. Trump, Cornyn said: "That's a convenient excuse, and it happens to be untrue."

World.title: Acting CDC director says Fauci "abused the place of power" during pandemic
World.content:
One of the Trump administration's top health officials, Dr. Jay Bhattacharya, is accusing Dr. Anthony Fauci, the longtime former director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, of an abuse of power during the COVID-19 pandemic.

"He frankly abused the place of power that he had been given both by the media and by powerful politicians," Bhattacharya told CBS News chief correspondent Matt Gutman in an interview Wednesday. Bhattacharya currently serves as both director of the National Institutes of Health and acting director of the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Bhattacharya alleged that Fauci's "primary abuse" during the pandemic was that he "shut down scientific debate" and "denigrated scientists that disagreed with him, including myself and many, many others, simply for the sin of disagreeing with him."

During the pandemic, Bhattacharya, then a professor at the Stanford University School of Medicine, was publicly critical of the federal government's response and was vocal in his opposition to lockdowns and mask mandates.

In the interview, Bhattacharya took issue with Fauci's leading role during the pandemic. "You know, he was the head of a research institute, he wasn't the head of public health, yet he acted as if he were the head of public health in this country," he said.

When it was noted the first Trump administration had informally elevated Fauci into that role at the pandemic's onset, Bhattacharya countered that it was "absolutely imperative" that Fauci "convey clearly what is known and what is not known, that you don't step beyond the role that you actually have based on the expertise that you have."

The accusations Wednesday came hours after Fauci's appearance before the Senate Homeland Security Committee under subpoena.

After reading an opening statement, Fauci invoked his Fifth Amendment rights on all questions, saying he did so because the chairman, Republican Sen. Rand Paul, was attempting "to get me to say something, anything, that could vindicate his repeated public pledges that I end up, in his words, quote, 'behind bars,' unquote."

Over the weekend, Paul, a longtime Fauci critic, released a trove of more than 1,000 pages of diary entries that Fauci wrote during his time as NIAID director during the pandemic. After nearly four decades in the post, Fauci retired in 2022.

Bhattacharya said he supported the release of Fauci's journal entries and noted they had been "kept on government servers."

"They reflect somebody who had a tremendous impact on the lives of every single person in the country, and in fact in the world," the acting CDC director said. "I think it's in the public interest for those notes to be released."

Bhattacharya argued there was a contradiction between Fauci's public statements during the pandemic and his journal entries.

"The way he was thinking in private regarding all of the advice he was giving to tremendously powerful people, and what he showed in public, were very different," Bhattacharya said.

As an example, Bhattacharya pointed to Fauci's recommendation in early 2020 that schools be closed.

"He was making decisions about closing schools, in my view, against what the actual evidence was saying at the time," Bhattacharya said. "... He conveyed a certainty that it turns out in his diary he didn't even feel himself."

As the federal government's top infectious disease expert, Fauci didn't have any direct power to impose restrictions or close schools, but his words carried weight with federal, state and local officials.

In a June 2024 interview with "CBS Mornings," Fauci said he believed the initial school closures were "the right thing," but agreed that keeping schools shuttered "for a year was not a good idea."

"If you go back and look at the YouTube, I kept on saying, 'Close the bars, open the schools. Open the schools as quickly and as safely as you possibly can,'" he said.

COVID origins controversy

Regarding the debate over COVID's possible origins, Bhattacharya said he believes it likely originated in a lab in Wuhan, China. It is an issue that has been studied extensively with no clear consensus, and many scientists believe the evidence suggests a natural spillover of the virus from animals to humans is more likely.

"We don't know for certain, but it seems really quite likely, given the evidence that I've seen, that it originated in a Chinese lab," Bhattacharya said.

Asked whether he thought Fauci lied to the American people about COVID and its origins, Bhattacharya said, "I think that Dr. Fauci's role in the COVID origins is much more complicated than he led on in his public statements earlier. Lie, I'll leave for other people to say one way or the other."

Fauci has long insisted he kept an open mind on research into the virus' origins and denied downplaying it or misleading the public.

World.title: Latest on Iran war after Saudi forces join U.S. strikes
World.content: Latest on Iran war after Saudi forces join U.S. strikes Iran on Wednesday launched a barrage of missiles at American forces in the Middle East. This comes as the U.S. and Saudi Arabia strike Tehran-backed militias in Iraq. Ret. U.S. Navy Vice Adm. Robert Murrett joins with analysis.

World.title: Congress hasn't passed AI rules for schools. So these 98 teens did it themselves
World.content:
Congress hasn't passed AI rules for schools. So these 98 teens did it themselves

toggle caption Kieran Kesner for NPR

BOSTON — Over the course of one frantic, late-July weekend, 98 teens representing all 50 states put their busy lives on hold to try to do something remarkable.

The students, most of them high school juniors and seniors, gathered in a precise replica of the U.S. Senate chamber and attempted what the real, adult Congress has largely failed to do: draft and pass "legislation" to help the nation's K-12 schools navigate the questions and chaos created by artificial intelligence.

Should students be allowed to use AI on assignments? What about on tests? Is it schools' job to teach the nation's children what AI is and how to use it? There is no national policy for AI use in schools, meaning states and school districts have had to scramble to craft their own.

Sponsor Message

"This is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity for us to actually help and try to change the country for the better," said student Gabriel Sutphin, representing South Carolina, speaking from the chamber floor at the Edward M. Kennedy Institute for the United States Senate.

To these teens, the stakes for getting ahead of AI are clear. They pointed out how adult leaders were slow to protect students from the risks of other tech developments.

"We missed the mark with social media and phones," said Hunter Wurzel, a high school senior representing Ohio. "That's been a huge talking point already [this weekend], is how we failed to implement those things into education and teach the youth how to use them."

Wurzel and his 97 colleagues were handpicked by their school leaders and hosted by a handful of education- and tech-focused groups, including the Edward M. Kennedy Institute, AASA (The School Superintendents Association), and Day of AI, a nonprofit launched out of MIT's RAISE AI literacy initiative.

At times during the weekend, where NPR was able to watch the events unfold, the bill seemed doomed, only to be revived by a flurry of student-led negotiation, old-fashioned compromises and some spirited speeches.

"[This bill] is about who gets a seat at the table. Today, students have that seat," Bena Mejia Romero of Connecticut told her fellow senators before the final vote.

Sponsor Message

Ultimately, their Students First Act passed overwhelmingly, 82-16.

Among the bill's requirements: States should provide AI literacy as soon as students get access to classroom devices; AI use should be banned on all graded tests; and teachers can require an oral defense of any project from a student suspected of using AI inappropriately. (You can read the full bill at the end of this article.)

"The adults themselves haven't been able to come to consensus on this, right? And so now it falls to the kids. Let them lead the way," said Jeffrey Riley, the executive director of Day of AI and former education commissioner of Massachusetts.

While the Students First Act isn't actually law, any more than the teens are actually senators, AASA plans to send the text to its members: 10,000 school leaders across the country, many of whom are right now crafting their own AI rules in the absence of regulation.

Rules for students

When students arrived at the start of the weekend, they were presented with a stew of policies that they had suggested in the run-up to the event. Then they were divided into subcommittees — focused on students, educators, administrators and families — to debate the dozens of proposals and create a coherent bill they could all support.

The student-focused section of the final bill includes 15 provisions, several focused on a concern many of the senators shared: that teens are using AI to do their thinking for them.

Without guidance and guardrails, "[AI use] is just gonna go unhinged," said Campbell McHenry, a high school junior from Mississippi. "Everyone's gonna stop learning and start relying on AI. Instead of using it as a tool, they're gonna use it as a brain."

toggle caption Kieran Kesner for NPR

Among the bill's student-focused proposals:

Approved uses: Students should not be allowed to use AI for writing, "though editing, brainstorming and studying" with AI should be allowed after eighth grade.

Prove mastery: Students permitted to use AI should have to cite how they used it and demonstrate their grasp of a subject through discussions, handwritten tests or oral defenses.

Plagiarism review: Any student suspected of using AI inappropriately should have their work reviewed not just by AI checker software, which can be unreliable, but also two school officials.



Sponsor Message

One of the most contentious issues was deciding when students should first be exposed to AI in the classroom: High school? Middle school? Earlier?

Lucia Herrera, a Missouri high schooler, took issue with an early draft of the bill.

"There's nothing that says students need to be proficient before using it," Herrera told her subcommittee colleagues. "It's basically saying they can use it whenever. Which I think is a misuse of it."

Her subcommittee's proposed solution: require schools to teach AI literacy as soon as devices are introduced in the classroom, including misinformation, plagiarism, bias in AI design, student privacy, appropriate academic use and AI's environmental impact.

toggle caption Kieran Kesner for NPR

When the provision came up later that day, before the full Senate, Connecticut's Bena Mejia Romero told her fellow student lawmakers they should support the new requirement. "If we're going to be using devices, we should know the dangers and the benefits that they have."

But one of the senators from California, Om Lala, argued that requiring schools to begin teaching AI literacy would be a heavy lift. "Teachers already are pretty under-resourced."

Tristan Tjetjep of Tennessee added that he worried how "underprivileged schools" would pay for this new instruction.

Suddenly, the students had run headlong into U.S. schools' funding inequities — a problem they attempted to resolve with a requirement that the federal government chip in funding.

Rules for educators, parents and caregivers

The Students First Act not only covers students' use of AI but also insists on rules for educators:

Approved teacher use of AI: Allowed for tasks including lesson planning, making practice materials, providing feedback and improving instruction.

Must have a clear AI policy: Each semester, teachers need to post "a clear, written AI usage policy," explaining when AI is allowed and when it's not.



What's more, if an AI detector flags potential inappropriate AI use in a student paper, the bill says "teachers must personally investigate the issue before reporting the student to admin."

Sponsor Message

The student senators struggled with the 10 provisions in the bill's parents/guardians section because, as Isabella Stringer of New Hampshire said on the Senate floor, "We cannot legislate parenthood. Schools cannot tell parents what or how to teach your children."

As such, some of the provisions here suggest rather than tell. For instance, one says simply that parents should encourage balanced technology habits and emphasize the importance of ethical academic behavior at home.

toggle caption Kieran Kesner for NPR

The early version of the bill also gave parents a full veto over their students' AI access, but many of the senators argued that AI is here to stay and students must be taught how to use it.

"Giving [parents] the complete say, especially in middle to high school, in what their child can and can't do with AI is gonna limit [students] because a lot of [adults] don't even know what AI is themselves," said junior Tatiyana Reaves of North Carolina.

In one of the weekend's more passionate exchanges, senators debated what should happen if a student attempts to use a school-based AI tool, like a chatbot, "for emotional support."

Several teens worried that if a student confided sensitive information about, say, their sexuality or a mental health crisis, they should be able to trust that it would be kept private.

But Dylan Dornack of Iowa argued on the Senate floor that, for students in crisis or experiencing suicidal thoughts, the technology must alert a human.

"This could be lifesaving," Dornack told his colleagues, "whether or not that student is fearful that they might get outed. This is just one of those things that has to be taken to trusted adults."

toggle caption Kieran Kesner for NPR

Ultimately, the students agreed: When a school chatbot detects a student in need of emotional support, it should not fulfill the student's request but instead alert school officials.

Sponsor Message

The rush to passage

At the end of the whirlwind weekend, the student senators gathered in the replica chamber and more than half volunteered to address their colleagues for one minute each.

Dornack was the first to speak and called the bill an important, if imperfect, foundation for schools' AI policies. "You have to lay the blocks before you can have the building. So here I say, let's lay the blocks and let's pass this."

toggle caption Kieran Kesner for NPR

But Jadelynn Petitjean of Alabama called the bill an "unstable foundation" and opposed it.

Earlier in the day, West Virginia's Ethan Liu had also opposed it, highlighting several contradictions in the bill, including amendments that both restricted students' AI access while appearing to give teachers wide discretion over when and how AI is used.

"I thought it reflected really badly on us. I had a whole different speech planned out against this bill, actually. It was really good," Liu told the Senate chamber before the final vote.

But at the last minute, the event's organizers allowed the students to iron out a few of the bill's inconsistencies, and, as a result, Liu changed his vote, saying "this bill is in much better shape."

Student after student walked to the microphone at the front of the chamber, and most endorsed the bill, including Kendall Terao-Toma of Hawaii:

"This is for our future — not just for education but for the workforce we will join, the economy that we will build and the communities we will lead."

Edited by: Nirvi Shah and Nicole Cohen; audio story produced by: Lauren Migaki

Visual design and development by: LA Johnson
