World.title: Watch out Brussels and Kyiv, Poland’s conservatives are veering right
World.content:
Allies of pro-EU Prime Minister Donald Tusk read it as good news. When Kaczyński stepped to the microphone to kick out Morawiecki, two lawmakers from Tusk’s governing coalition filmed themselves watching the speech, eating popcorn.

You can see why they might be happy. Before the split, POLITICO’s Poll of Polls put Tusk’s Civic Coalition at 32 percent support and PiS at 26 percent. PiS has now slumped to 22 percent.

But that is hardly the whole story. The combined forces of right-wing parties are still in a strong position if they team up for the 2027 election. And Friday’s split means that PiS is more likely to veer right in its alliances, choosing ideological consolidation over an attempt to win back the center.

The wing of PiS led by Morawiecki had argued the party needed to broaden its appeal and adopt a less combative approach toward Brussels. Kaczyński instead appears determined to recapture voters who have defected further right.

It is far from certain, however, how successfully Poland’s far-right parties can agree on a common agenda with PiS.

Among the potential beneficiaries of Friday’s split are parties that oppose Ukraine joining the European Union — and, in the case of Grzegorz Braun’s Federation of the Polish Crown movement, advocate taking Poland out of the bloc altogether.

World.title: The first election of the Andy Burnham era is already here
World.content:
“Let’s go in and have a look. Let’s open it up,” she said at a food market in Altrincham, a town in the south-west of Greater Manchester. Astley said Labour has had “an absolute stronghold of a vice-like grip” across the region for too long. “This is really the first time this level of political choice has been available to the voters,” she said.

Geraldine Coggins is the Green Party pick. She has stood in seven elections, and been elected as a councilor in Trafford three times.

Having joined the party in 2010, she is now relishing the growth in campaign resources after recent electoral successes, and said at a community garden cafe in Manchester that activists had come from as far away as Aberdeen and Cornwall to help out on the doorsteps.

Coggins’ pitch is that Greater Manchester needs a mayor to stand up to government — rather than a “Labour apologist,” a term she used to describe Craig. She also wants more devolution — including for mayors to be given the power to impose rent caps — and has her own bus pledge: to make them free for anyone under 22.

How will the vote be decided?

The mayoralty will once again be decided using the supplementary vote system — and that’s caused a little disquiet from Labour’s opponents on the right.

Voters will be asked to pick a first and second preference. If no candidate gets 50 percent or more of first preference votes, all but the top two candidates will be eliminated. The second preferences of voters who initially backed those losing candidates are then redistributed.

World.title: Spain inflation rises to 3.5% in July on fuel and electricity prices
World.content:
Inflation picked up again in Spain in July and reached 3.5% year on year, three tenths of a point higher than in June, driven by the rise in fuel prices and electricity, according to the flash estimate published on Thursday by the National Statistics Institute (INE).

 

The statistics office attributes the rebound to the fact that both fuels and lubricants for private vehicles and electricity rose more sharply than in the same month last year. With this increase, inflation has reached its highest level since May 2024 and has now been above 3% for five consecutive months.

Underlying inflation, which excludes unprocessed food and energy products because of their greater volatility, also rose by a tenth of a point in July, to 3%, suggesting that price pressures continue beyond the impact of energy.

Meanwhile, the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP), used to compare price developments between European Union countries, put the annual rate at 3.8%, two tenths higher than in June.

Despite the rise in prices, Spain's Ministry of Economy argued that the measures adopted to address the economic consequences of the conflict with Iran remain in force and are helping to contain the impact of higher energy costs on inflation and households' purchasing power.

The figures come against a backdrop of more expensive energy caused by geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, which have pushed up international oil and gas prices in recent weeks.

World.title: Microsoft posts record profit as shares surge 10%, while Meta disappoints
World.content:
Microsoft shares surged by as much as 10% in pre-market trading on Thursday after the technology giant forecast stronger-than-expected revenue and accelerating growth at its Azure cloud business, offering fresh evidence that its vast investment in artificial intelligence is paying off.

 

The company expects revenue of between $89.85bn (€78.5bn) and $90.95bn (€79.5bn) in the July-September quarter, representing growth of 16% to 17%. It also forecast that Azure revenue would grow by approximately 45% in constant currency, up from 43% in the quarter just ended.

The upbeat outlook followed better-than-expected fiscal fourth-quarter results. Revenue rose 18% year-on-year to $90bn (€78.7bn) in the April-June period, beating the $87.6bn (€76.6bn) forecast by analysts surveyed by FactSet.

Net profit climbed 31% to a record $35.8bn (€31.3bn), although the figure was boosted by a $3.2bn (€2.8bn) unrealised gain on Microsoft’s investment in artificial intelligence company Anthropic. Diluted earnings per share reached $4.81 (€4.20), above analysts’ forecast of $4.24 (€3.71).

Microsoft Cloud revenue was $59.3bn (€51.9bn) in the quarter, up 27% year-on-year. The strong growth reflects higher demand across Microsoft’s cloud computing platform, Azure, as well as its first-party AI applications and services. Azure and other cloud services revenue increased by 43%.

Microsoft said demand for Azure continued to exceed available capacity, despite bringing additional computing infrastructure online during the quarter.

For the full fiscal year ended in June, the company reported $331.8bn (€289.9bn) in revenue.

“This year, Azure revenue surpassed $100bn (€87.4bn) for the first time, and Microsoft 365 Copilot reached over 30 million paid seats, reflecting the confidence customers are placing in us to power their AI transformation,” Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said in a statement on Wednesday.

The concurrent Azure and Copilot growth indicates that Microsoft is “winning on both fronts,” Michael J. Wolf, founder and CEO of Activate Consulting, said in a statement. Microsoft is doing so by “supplying the cloud infrastructure for enterprise AI while monetising the AI tools embedded in the products workers use every day.”

Investors had been looking for evidence that Azure and Copilot, Microsoft’s flagship AI assistant, could eventually produce returns as concerns about high AI spending have steadily grown across the industry.

Chief financial officer Amy Hood told investors on a call that the company’s capital expenditure plans for the 2026 calendar year remain unchanged.

An accounting change will bring that guidance closer to approximately $175bn (€152.9bn), Hood said, but in practice, the expectations remain “unchanged.” This move marks a break from competitors that have been steadily increasing their spending forecasts.

Hood said earlier this year that the company expects to invest $190bn (€165.9bn) in capital expenditures in 2026.

Bryan Hayes, an investment strategist at Zacks Investment Research, said in a statement that “for the first time in three quarters, the market appears willing to grant that the spending is buying something real.”

“We remain very confident in the long-term return on these investments, given these strong demand signals, the increasing product usage we’ve seen and the efficiencies that we’re driving across the platform,” said Danielle Criste, Microsoft’s director of investor relations, in an interview.

Meta profit misses expectations

Meta Platforms said Wednesday its second-quarter profit declined even as revenue beat Wall Street’s expectations, as legal expenses and severance costs weighed on its results.

The Facebook and Instagram parent company earned $15.85bn (€13.8bn) in the April-June period. That’s down 14% from $18.34bn (€16bn) in the same period a year earlier.

Revenue grew 28% to $60.8bn (€53.1bn) from $47.52bn (€41.5bn).

Meta earned $6.18 (€5.40) per share, below the $7.19 (€6.30) expected by analysts surveyed by FactSet. Analysts had forecast revenue of $60.22bn (€52.6bn).

Total costs and expenses jumped 55% to $42.03bn (€36.7bn), including $2.4bn (€2.1bn) in charges related to legal proceedings and $1.18bn (€1.03bn) in severance expenses connected with Meta’s May workforce reduction. Its operating margin narrowed to 31% from 43% a year earlier.

“AI is accelerating our core business today, powering our next generation of products, and opening the door to entirely new enterprise opportunities,” said CEO Mark Zuckerberg in a statement. “The results are already showing, and I’m optimistic about the potential ahead.”

World.title: The world’s top 10 cities for street food have been revealed
World.content:
When you think about street food, you probably picture bánh mì in Vietnam, tacos in Mexico, or even pizza al taglio in Italy.

 

Certain countries and cities are well known for their offerings, with foodies heading specifically to a destination to grab miscellaneous meat on sticks on-the-go and the like.

But a new study has revealed the best street food city in the world, and it’s not where you would expect at all.

Paris in France came out on top in the research conducted by Radical Storage, which looked at 6,897 street food vendors in the 100 most-visited cities around the globe.

For the analysis, the team looked at the number of vendors with a star rating above four, the variety of cuisines on offer, the availability of vegetarian, vegan and gluten-free options, the proportion of budget-friendly eats, and the vendor density per square kilometre.

Street food was defined as food stalls and trucks, as well as sit-in restaurants that serve classic street food bites.

The vendor density had the highest impact on the score, with a weighting of 30%, followed by the budget-friendly proportion at 20%. The number of vendors over four stars, the average vendor rating, the cuisine varieties, the vegetarians and vegan options and the gluten-free options were all weighted 10% each.

The French capital came out with a score of 7.2 out of 10 – with 69.1% of the 401 eateries rated four stars or more. Paris has a density of 3.82 street food vendors per square kilometre, too.

Next up on the list are two Greek destinations: Athens and Thessaloniki. Athens scored 6.9 out of 10 thanks to the number of cuisines on offer (29), and the number of food vendors per square metre at 4.21.

Thessaloniki meanwhile scored 6.1, with 77.1% of street food options being budget-friendly.

Rhodes in Greece topped the list for the best-rated street food, with 82% of vendors rated four stars and up, while London won out for the best variety, with dishes from 39 distinct food types.

World.title: Hundreds evacuated as wildfires sweep Turkey's western and southern coasts
World.content:
Firefighters were still battling active blazes across several regions of Turkey on Thursday, with fires burning in parts of Antalya and across Muğla province — known for some of the country's most visited resorts — after breaking out on Wednesday during extreme summer heat.

 

Agriculture and Forestry Minister İbrahim Yumaklı said fires in Yalova's Armutlu, Kütahya's Domaniç and Altıntaş, and in Çanakkale had been fully brought under control. The regions of Antalya, Muğla and Balıkesir remained under threat.

The UK Foreign Office's standing travel advice notes that wildfires are a regular feature of Turkish summers — running roughly from June to October and peaking in July and August — without issuing a blanket warning against travel to Antalya, Muğla or İzmir.

As of Wednesday, Turkey had no active nationwide wildfire emergency, with recent fires, including those in Antalya's Kaş district, contained within hours of breaking out.

However, travellers heading to the region this week should be aware of specific disruptions.

The Fethiye–Antalya highway was temporarily closed due to smoke from the Seydikemer fire and later reopened under controlled conditions.

Access to the ancient ruins at Olympos in Antalya province was closed.

Kaş, a popular diving and boat-trip destination on the Lycian coast, has an active fire in the surrounding woodland.

Homes destroyed, farmland in peril

The most serious active fire is in Seydikemer, a district in the hills between Fethiye and Marmaris. The blaze started on farmland on Wednesday morning and spread into woodland.

Forty-five patients were evacuated from the local state hospital and transferred to nearby facilities.

Across six affected neighbourhoods, 408 homes were evacuated and 703 people along with around 100 animals were moved to safety. Fifty-five buildings were damaged, some completely destroyed.

More than 25 aircraft, 410 ground vehicles and over 1,100 personnel were deployed to the area.

In Kumluca, a district south of Antalya city on the road toward Kaş and the Lycian coast, a fire left 10 homes unusable. Crews brought the main blaze under control but were continuing cooling operations on Thursday.

Five separate fires broke out in Balıkesir province, which sits between İzmir and the Dardanelles coast, on Wednesday.

The most significant was in Altınoluk, a seaside town on the Aegean known for its olive groves, near the ancient site of Antandros. The fire grew rapidly in wind and threatened residential areas, prompting the evacuation of 210 homes.

The Gömeç fire, in the same province, was still active on Thursday evening. Six aircraft, five helicopters and dozens of fire trucks were deployed across the province.

Turkey's Aegean and Mediterranean coasts are vulnerable to wildfire each summer. A combination of prolonged drought, temperatures regularly exceeding 40C in July and August, low humidity and strong seasonal winds — particularly the dry, northerly Etesian winds known as the meltemi — creates conditions in which fires can spread rapidly through pine and scrub forests.

World.title: Wildfires near Bordeaux bring more troubles to France’s struggling wine industry
World.content:
Wildfires have already decimated 42,000 hectares in Bordeaux's Gironde region. Even though vineyards are still safe from the blaze, winegrowers fear the grapes might take on a 'smoke taint' if fumes from the fires get to the vines.

 

Grapes are still in their veraison period; from a small green marble, they are starting to grow into bigger burgundy or golden coloured fruit. It's a decisive phase of the grape's maturation when smoke can impact the wine's aroma.

Some wines naturally have ash scents from other sources, but if this flavour impedes the fruity aromas, winegrowers can decide to downgrade their harvest or sell it in bulk to distillers for the alcohol.

"If we’d been closer to the grape harvest, which is due to start in three weeks, it could have been far more serious," says to French Figaro newspaper Séverine Bonnie from château Malartic-Lagravière, just 20 kilometres away from the flames.

Grapes hang in a vineyard on the Grand Verdus wine estate in Sadirac, southwestern France's Bordeaux region. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

At that moment of the harvest, smoke can seriously impregnate the grapes, although not all vineyards exposed to the smoke are necessarily affected. Strong winds, time of exposure to smoke and weather conditions can change how the grapes taste.

"In Bordeaux, not only are we still at the veraison stage, but we can also hope for thunderstorms to wash away any berries that may have been affected," says to French Figaro newspaper Édouard Moueix, owner of multiple châteaux in the Bordeaux region.

A smell of "economic apocalypse"

Wildfires that have burned an area four times the size of Paris and driven 220,000 people from homes and some of the region’s tourist attractions promise to sting France’s already squeezed economy.

"It’s a physical apocalypse when you see all these sites where there’s nothing left aside from burnt homes and forests, and then there’s the economic apocalypse," said Patrick Seguin, president of the regional chamber of commerce, his voice choking with emotion.

It's going to be a stab in the back for what remains of our economy Patrick Seguin President of the regional chamber of commerce in the Bordeaux region

Edouard Le Grix de la Salle is among entrepreneurs bracing for pain. French government appeals for people to avoid the region are causing consternation.

"It’s incredible that they’ve said such a thing, especially when wine tourism is becoming more and more important," Le Grix de la Salle said.

Bordeaux’s legendary wine has seen consumption plunge as young people turn to other beverages and competition from vineyards abroad has grown. U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs have given winemakers — and much of the global economy — an added hangover.

An industry already in crisis

"The wine business has been in crisis for several years now, and it’s worsening with the geopolitical problems, the now widespread problems of inflation and the fact that wine is falling out of fashion among younger people," Le Grix de la Salle said.

"Tourism was really the only dynamic part of the business that was still growing, both for us and, more generally, for Bordeaux wines," he said. "And now this comes along as a brake."

His family’s Grand Verdus wine estate is roughly 35 kilometres from the fires that have raged since last week on the other side of the Garonne River that runs through Bordeaux. The fires have hit only a small percentage of the Gironde region, but the mark on its reputation is sizable.

"How did they not think about protecting that sector? And the cultural sector, too. There’s so much to visit in Bordeaux. There are so many museums, there are châteaux. It’s unbelievable," Le Grix de la Salle said.

The region in southwest France is replete with vacation spots for tourists lured by soft-sand beaches, winemaking châteaux, some of France’s largest pine forests and the historic city of Bordeaux, a UNESCO World Heritage site. The oyster-rich Arcachon Bay draws foodies. But the fire and evacuations have emptied some prime spots.

The chamber of commerce says 39,000 businesses have been affected in the region that’s a hub of defence and aerospace industries, including Airbus, Dassault and Thales.

Even before the fires, the chamber of commerce said rising energy costs were squeezing profits. Some 94% of businesses responding to a poll of regional enterprises in mid-July said they face difficulties.

World.title: K-pop giants BTS boycott 2027 Grammys after introduction of controversial new Asian pop prize
World.content:
K-pop superstars BTS will not submit their music for consideration for 2027 Grammy Awards.

 

Writing on Instagram, each member of the South Korean band said: "We have decided not to enter the Grammys this year." A translation of the message continued: "I hope that music can be heard and loved for what it is, rather than being divided by region or language."

That last segment of the posts seemingly refers to the addition of a new award for Best Asian Pop Music performance.

According to Academy president Harvey Mason Jr, the new category was added due to “our music community sharing with us that they felt they needed to have more opportunities to celebrate different and new genres of music.”

However, the decision to add this category, as well as the regionally specific Best Latin song award, has been met with backlash. Many see it as a way of sidelining acts from markets which are hardly "new" and distancing artists from territories like Asia from the top categories.

BTS has been nominated for a Grammy five times but never won, and Asian pop artists have traditionally been ignored by the US-centric awards show.

This year, 'Golden' from KPop Demon Hunters did win best song written for visual media, but stood out for being the first win for a K-pop act. Many fans felt that this win was long overdue, and that the new Grammy categories will only erect barriers and limit chances of winning in other categories.

The new Asian pop category requires “meaningful use” of an Asian language. BTS’ recent material on their hugely successful album 'Arirang' is predominantly sung in English, meaning that it may not have been eligible for the new category anyway, despite its traditional Korean title and themes.

Released in March, 'Arirang' debuted at No.1 in various territories, including the Billboard 200 in the US, South Korea’s Circle Chart, Japan’s Oricon Charts, and the UK Official Albums Chart.

BTS fans, known as ARMY, have taken to social media to share their reaction to the group not submitting their music for the 2027 Grammys, calling out the organisation but applauding their favourite band for doing the right thing.

One fan wrote: "The gag is BTS knew they would've had a near guaranteed Grammy win with this new Asian pop category but understand that cosigning this category wld mean that ultimately asian language acts would be gatekept out of the main/general categories."

"Watching BTS go from wanting a Grammy more than anything to realizing they’re bigger than the Grammys," one commented, while another said: "Some people spend their careers trying to get invited. BTS simply decided they don’t need an invitation anymore. Their music has already reached millions of people around the world. That’s worth more than a Grammy."

The 2027 Grammy ceremony will take place on 7 February in Los Angeles.

World.title: China lodges complaint after New Zealand foreign minister tells MP to ‘go back to your own country’
World.content:
China has lodged an official complaint after New Zealand's foreign minister Winston Peters told a Chinese-born MP to "go back to your own country" during a heated parliamentary exchange in Wellington.

 

Peters, the leader of the NZ First party, made the remarks on Wednesday after Green Party MP Lawrence Xu-Nan asked him, "Are you vaccinated?" during a debate over New Zealand's response to the Covid-19 pandemic.

Xu-Nan was born in Tianjin, China, but grew up in New Zealand.

Peters responded that the lawmaker had "come here five minutes ago" before telling him: "Go back to your own country."

"This is called a democracy, unlike what you're used to. Go back to where you've come from, you loudmouth," Peters added.

Speaking to the 1News channel on Thursday, Xu-nan said: "It's a little bit unbelievable to have a Minister for Foreign Affairs, I guess, scapegoating the migrant communities as a distraction to shift the blame away from all of the harm that this government is doing."

China lodges complaint

The remarks prompted a rare intervention from China's ambassador to New Zealand, Wang Xiaolong, who wrote on X that he normally avoided commenting on domestic politics but that "sometimes, a statement says more about the person that makes it than anything or anybody else".

The Chinese embassy in Wellington said on Thursday it had lodged a complaint with New Zealand's foreign ministry over what it described as "negative China-related remarks made by a certain politician".

Peters has refused to back down, arguing his comments were a defence of democratic freedoms.

"We live in a democracy that includes free speech and rights," he wrote on X, adding that he would "not resile from that point".

New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon, whose National Party governs in coalition with NZ First, condemned Peters' remarks as "inappropriate attention-seeking".

NZ First politicians have faced criticism over similar remarks before. Last year, Peters' deputy Shane Jones shouted "send the Mexicans home" at MP Francisco Hernandez, who was born in the Philippines.

Mexico's ambassador, Alfredo Pérez Bravo, subsequently issued an official diplomatic communication to New Zealand's Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade, opting to raise the issue through diplomatic channels rather than publicly.

Peters later withdrew his support for Jones' remarks, acknowledging that "in the heat of the moment" they "may have been expressed differently."

World.title: ‘Lost forever’: What does the future look like for a Mediterranean flooded with invasive species?
World.content:
The Mediterranean of our ancestors is no more.

 

Scientists say climate change, caused mainly by burning oil, coal and gas, is making the Mediterranean Sea hotter, bringing hundreds of new and invasive fish species that decimate indigenous populations.

As biodiversity diminishes, coastal communities will struggle to make ends meet in the ways they’ve known for generations.

“The Mediterranean of our grandfathers, of our elders, and of the Greeks, of ancient Greece is lost forever. So many of those changes are irreversible,” says Ernesto Azzuro, a marine biologist with the Italian National Research Council's Institute for Marine Biological Resources and Biotechnology.

Warmth can't dissipate in the Mediterranean's basin

Scientists have designated the Mediterranean as a climate change “hot spot”, with its waters expected to warm by 2 to 6 degrees Celsius by 2100. Heatwaves are likely to become more frequent and more extreme, according to the Mediterranean Experts on Climate and Environmental Change, an independent network of scientists.

Ronan McAdam, an oceanographer with the Euro-Mediterranean Center on Climate Change, says a key factor in the warming is that the sea is an enclosed basin and warmth can’t dissipate like in the vastness of the oceans.

The warming waters have made an inviting new home for invasive species like the spotted puffer fish, a voracious predator and the “worst invader”, Azzuro says.

These species are now heading toward France and Spain after entering the Mediterranean through the Suez Canal.

The UN food and agriculture body’s General Fisheries Commission for the Mediterranean says such invasive species have been present for decades, but their spread accelerated after the early 2000s, coinciding with rising sea temperatures. For example, the lionfish was first recorded in the eastern Mediterranean in 2012 and has expanded rapidly westward.

“The Mediterranean will be even poorer, even with less species, simply because climate changeis really making this part of the Mediterranean, especially the eastern part of the Mediterranean, really unsuitable for native species,” Azzuro says.

Cyprus, due to its proximity to the Suez Canal, was first to feel the impact of these invasive fish. Lionfish supplanted indigenous stocks like the red mullet to the dismay of fishers, who have seen local varieties popular with customers greatly diminish.

Then there are rabbitfish that can devour algae from the sea bottom, destroying the habitat for many indigenous species.

"We know what should be done. We should reduce the use of fossil [fuels]," says Piero Genovesi Papik, a zoologist with Italy’s Higher Institute for Environmental Protection and Research. “But that’s definitely an urgent matter for the humanity, and we all know the solutions, but of course they require a global and joint vision.”

Fisherman Photis Gaitanos catches a toadfish while fishing from his boat off the coast of Larnaca, Cyprus, in the eastern Mediterranean, early Saturday, Dec. 20, 2025. AP Photo/Petros Karadjias

About 1,000 invasive species have been identified

Azzuro says about 1,000 invasive species have been identified in the Mediterranean, with 800 of them firmly established.

The changes are stark. Azzuro says the shallows of the eastern Mediterranean have lost 93 per cent of their mollusk population. Along the Adriatic coast, once abundant with mussels, nearly all have died off because of the sea temperatures that at times have exceeded 30 degrees Celsius.

From Venice in the north to Bari in the south, “the die-off was spectacular,” he says. “Unless we… find populations able to survive through these different climates, the future of mussels is not a happy future, at least in the Adriatic Sea.”

Azzuro says his institute and its partner a few years ago launched a campaign, 'Beware of those four', to raise awareness about the dangers that invasive species pose to human health.

For instance, puffer fish is toxic and potentially lethal if consumed by humans. The lionfish's poisonous spikes can badly hurt anyone who’s stung.

A lionfish lies on a fishing boat off the coast of Larnaca, Cyprus, in the eastern Mediterranean, early Saturday, Dec. 20, 2025. AP Photo/Petros Karadjias

Experts say the spread of invasive species can't be reversed

Scientists are discussing how coastal communities can cope. One way is to commercialise invasive species that are edible. Another is to pay fishers to catch inedible ones like the puffer fish so they can be incinerated.

Some species, like the lionfish, have “clear economic benefits because it’s sold at very high prices, especially in some countries,” Azzuro says. But fishers haven’t taken advantage of the invasive dusky spinefoot, whose population has grown significantly in Italian waters.

Papik, the zoologist, says that while it’s “too late” to reverse the spread of invasive species in the Mediterranean, there are practical ways to mitigate the impact.

First is to prevent their further migration by enforcing an international treaty obliging national authorities to treat ballast waters inside incoming ships that may carry such species.

“This is something that is technically doable and that can reduce the number of... new alien species by 95 to 99 per cent,” he says. Another tactic is treating ship hulls with special paint that thwarts unwanted hitchhikers from latching on.

Papik also says fishing policies are being amended that would allow native species to reclaim some of their number, like growing mollusks that are less susceptible to the alien blue crab.

“In the coming years, I think that the challenge will be to find new ways to restore the environment,” Papik says.

World.title: Deaths in Ukraine after Zelenskyy warns of Russian strikes
World.content:
At least eight people have been killed in air strikes across Ukraine. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had warned of a "massive Russian attack" citing air force reports, as Kyiv in turn again bombed a logistics center.

At least eight people were killed in Ukraine overnight as Russia said it conducted airstrikes on targets across the country.

One person was killed in an airstrike on Kyiv, the capital of Ukraine, while other fatalities were reported as far west as Lviv.

Explosions were reported over Kyiv in the early hours of Thursday after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that Russia might conduct a "massive attack."

Zelenskyy later wrote that Russia had fired 70 rockets and 280 drones in the attack.

Both Reuters and AFP cited people on the ground as saying they had heard explosions.

"Sadly, one death has been confirmed," the Kyiv city military administration wrote on Telegram in the early hours of Thursday.

Russia struck Kyiv with ballistic missiles, the city's mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said, urging people to seek shelter. He added that several nonresidential sites in Kyiv caught fire.

"The enemy is attacking the capital with ballistic weapons. The threat of further attack remains present. Stay in shelters!" Klitschko said.

Zelenskyy said at least 10 Ukrainian regions were attacked Image: Sergei Supinsky/AFP

Several people killed in Kryvyi Rih

Russia also attacked other Ukrainian cities overnight. At least six people, including two girls, were killed in a Russian missile strike on the central Ukrainian city of Kryvyi Rih, according to the head of the local military administration.

"In a village on the outskirts of Kryvyi Rih, a direct strike by an Iskander-M ballistic missile, launched from Voronezh, hit a private house where a large family lived, killing girls aged five and 12 and four adults," Oleksandr Vilkul said.

He added that eight more people were wounded and that the death toll could rise..

Russian missiles also damaged two apartment buildings and injured six people in Lviv, a city in western Ukraine near the Polish border, according to local officials.

Meanwhile, the Polish Armed Forces announced on X that Poland had scrambled its fighter jets on Thursday to protect its airspace amid Russian airstrikes on Ukraine.

"Fighter aircraft and an early warning aircraft have begun operations while ground-based air defense systems and radar reconnaissance systems have reached a state of readiness," the post said, adding that the actions are preventive in nature.

What did Zelenskyy say ahead of the Kyiv explosions?

The strikes came after Zelenskyy warned of a "high probability that the strike will be carried out tonight."

"I received a report from Air Force Commander Anatolii Kryvonozhko. The Russians prepared a massive attack several days ago," Zelenskyy said on X.

The Ukrainian president stressed that Ukrainians' safety depended on the willingness of Kyiv's allies to provide anti-missile defenses. His statements came on the heels of a trip to the US, where he said President Donald Trump had agreed to give Ukraine licenses related to Patriot missile production.

Zelenskyy said Thursday: "It is important that our partners fully understand what's happening, and that the protection of lives directly depends on their readiness, or lack thereof, to help us with air defense missiles."

Ukraine renews attacks on Russian logistics centers

For its part, Ukraine continued its attacks on logistics centers inside Russia on Thursday.

In Penza, a warehouse belonging to online retailer Wildberries, often referred to as Russia's Amazon, caught fire after being struck by a Ukrainian drone, injuring one person and triggering the evacuation of 200 others.

Ukraine says Wildberries is providing logistical support for Russia's military.

Its attacks inside Russia also target the country's already anemic domestic economy and drive home to ordinary Russians the message that the war is not simply something that affects Ukrainians.

The strikes are being carried out in the hope of putting Russian President Vladimir Putin under pressure to end his more than four-year war of aggression.

Edited by: Rana Taha and Louis Oelofse

World.title: 'Rienzi': Why this Wagner opera is so relevant today
World.content:
Even before opening night, expectations of how the themes of Richard Wagner's "Rienzi" would be handled were running high — not least because the opera had never been staged at the Bayreuth Festival. Now it has opened the festival's 150th anniversary. One aspect that fueled the debate: The close relationship between Wagner's descendants and Adolf Hitler — "Rienzi" was one of Hitler's favorite operas.

"It's a piece that's highly contaminated," director Alexandra Szemerédy told DW. "When Katharina Wagner [the festival's director] first approached us, my initial excitement was definitely a bit dampened." Nonetheless, the production received enthusiastic applause at its premiere — conductor Nathalie Stutzmann and the Bayreuth Festival Orchestra were given standing ovations, and Hungarian directors Alexandra Szemerédy and Magdolna Parditka were warmly celebrated for their interpretation of the work.

The directors tell the tale of the rise and fall of the 14th-century Roman tribune Rienzi in the present day. Rienzi, who initially seeks to free the people of Rome from aristocratic rule, is ultimately consumed by power and becomes a dictator himself.

A glimpse of the surveillance state: Everyone knows everything about everyone else Image: Enrico Nawrath

The production opens with a stark landscape of identical concrete apartment blocks that later break off into individual units. Through the windows, neighbors watch each other's lives unfold. Every apartment contains screens broadcasting the same news. Whatever can't be seen through the windows is shared through smartphones, social media and omnipresent screens.

From utopia to dystopia

In this new production, Rienzi initially doesn't defeat the aristocracy with violence. He calls for democratic elections — and wins. Afterward, he lavishly celebrates with the elites. But that changes when the same aristocrats attempt to assassinate him. Rienzi survives, imposes a military dictatorship and begins executing his enemies in the streets. Increasingly consumed by paranoia and delusion, he loses his grip on power and ultimately dies.

The directors said they were particularly interested in how someone can inspire the masses and, fueled by populism, become an authoritarian ruler. "He's considered a reference figure in the study of populism because of this first major citizens' uprising in Rome," Szemerédy said. The charisma of the real historical figure Cola di Rienzo, who lived in the 14th century, had also fascinated Adolf Hitler.

A controversial choice

Musicologist and theater scholar Anno Mungen criticized the decision to stage "Rienzi" for the first time during the Bayreuth Festival's 150th anniversary, calling it "historically tone-deaf." Wagner himself chose not to include "Rienzi" in the repertoire of his new Festspielhaus in Bayreuth in the 1870s, citing musical considerations.

In his book on the intersections between the festival and the Holocaust, Mungen writes about the deportations from Bayreuth to Auschwitz, which included Jewish members of the Bayreuth Festival Orchestra. "When we look at 'Rienzi,' it would have been both meaningful and necessary to place the production within the context of a major academic conference," Mungen said. "The University of Bayreuth would have been very willing to participate."

The path to the Kingdom of Heaven: a favorite theme of Wagner's. But just before reaching his destination, Rienzi collapses Image: Enrico Nawrath

From 1940 to 1944, in what are now known as the "Wartime Festivals," Bayreuth kept running thanks to Hitler's financial support. Performances were held for selected audiences only, including wounded soldiers and workers from the arms industry. History students are currently exploring that period in an exhibition at the Steingraeber piano factory in Bayreuth. "These wartime festivals became a cultural showcase, intended to project the message that 'things aren't really so bad in Germany'," Mungen said. He chose not to attend the "Rienzi" premiere because the subject remains too personal.

The opera's dramaturge Markus Kiesel also believes it's essential to confront the controvery surrounding the piece. "Not performing the opera — or even banning it — would achieve nothing," Kiesel said. "On the contrary, we need to face these issues openly, creatively and honestly, and discuss them critically. If not in Bayreuth, then where?" Szemerédy added: "We have to build a bridge from the past to the future, especially at a time when right-wing populism is once again gaining strength and becoming a threat. That's exactly why this work needs to be performed today."

At the end of the opera, Rienzi dies, new elections are held, and two candidates emerge victorious.

AI images from decades of opera history form the concept for the production of this years Ring Cycle Image: Enrico Nawrath

Throughout Richard Wagner's operas, power, greed, cruelty, love until death and the destruction of the world are recurring themes. His 16-hour cycle "The Ring of the Nibelung," written for the Bayreuth Festspielhaus that he built specifically for it, explores these human impulses. The Rhine gold guarded by the Rhinemaidens becomes an object of universal desire — and ultimately brings catastrophe.

The piece has been reinterpreted in Bayreuth many times. Patrice Chéreau's landmark 1976 production presented "The Ring" as a parable about greed and the decline of capitalism. Frank Castorf later replaced the symbolism of gold with oil as the true source of capitalist power.

An AI reinvention

The festival's interpretation curated by Marcus Lobbes, has no stage director. Instead, Lobbes and his team developed a new AI-based imaging system in which the singers perform inside a holographic three-dimensional environment. "What appears on stage is a unified audiovisual image," Lobbes explained. "We create a visual landscape for both the singers and the orchestral performance." To generate the projections, the team trained the AI using archival material from previous Ring productions spanning from 1876 to 2024.

In "Das Rheingold," the first installment of the cycle, viewers see Rhinemaidens in bathtubs, lakes and streams, along with forests of trees, vines and vegetation alternating with wood and metal structures, creating shifting worlds between nature and industrial romanticism. Images crack apart, dissolve into one another and morph continuously. At times, the visuals are mesmerizing; at others, human faces become distorted beyond recognition.

'Das Rheingold' used a Neo-Romantic style generated by AI Image: Enrico Nawrath

Whether the technology can sustain audience interest over the entire 16-hour cycle remains to be seen. While the imagery is constantly in motion, the singers often stand almost motionless so as not to disrupt the projections. "The singers' positions are predetermined, but they can still interact with one another," Lobbes said. After the performance, one audience member joked that perhaps Siegfried and Sieglinde would eventually be blowing kisses at each other. Musically, however, the production boasts an outstanding cast, including Klaus Florian Vogt, Jochen Schmeckenbecher and Evelin Novak, with Christian Thielemann conducting. As one audience member put it: "If the AI becomes too much for me, I'll simply close my eyes and enjoy the music."

This article was originally written in German and edited by Tenzin Sekhon.

World.title: German lawsuit tests copyright limits for AI music training
World.content:
It's more than a copyright issue: The flood of AI-generated tracks is unfair competition for the original creators, says GEMA.

A landmark European case in AI music copyright law is set to reach a conclusion on July 31, when the Munich Regional Court is expected to deliver its verdict in the lawsuit brought by GEMA, Germany's music collecting society, against Suno AI, a US-based company that generates songs from text prompts.

In the case filed in January 2025, GEMA argues that Suno trained its AI models on copyrighted music without obtaining licences or compensating its rights holders.

The lawsuit is being closely watched, as it is one of the first major cases anywhere in the world to test how traditional copyright law applies to AI music training and AI-generated music outputs.

Paul McCartney & Rosalia: Strategies for surviving AI music To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The proceedings could help determine whether AI music companies must obtain licenses before training their models on copyrighted songs, and whether AI-generated music that closely resembles existing songs constitutes copyright infringement.

"Our goal is not to clear Suno from the face of the earth, but obviously to get into licensing negotiations on an eye-to-eye level, which was not possible with Suno so far," explains GEMA CEO Tobias Holzmüller, who describes the company as "by far the largest and commercially most successful of all AI music models." He believe Suno pursues a much more aggressive business strategy than its competitors.

Tobias Holzmüller, CEO of GEMA Image: Sebastian Linder

The outcome of the lawsuit is also linked to another central question: How should creators be compensated when their music is used to train generative AI systems?

At the forefront of the battle to protect artists' rights

Last year, GEMA won a related case against OpenAI before the same court. It found that OpenAI unlawfully trained its AI models on copyrighted song lyrics and reproduced them via ChatGPT without authorization.

OpenAI was ordered to cease and desist from reproducing the works in the model, to disclose information and pay damages. But as the company pursues an appeal, the ruling remains non-final.

In contrast to that decision, the current lawsuit does not focus on song lyrics, but on entire music pieces.

One of the aspects that makes this lawsuit important is that it has not been initiated by a private company or record label, but rather by a music collecting society, notes Martin Senftleben, professor of intellectual property law at the Amsterdam Law School.

Such initiatives "are particularly important because, by definition, you could say that they're more inclusive," Senftleben tells DW. "You can become a GEMA member even if you're not a very well-known high-profile artist or composer. And that means there's a chance of bringing remuneration for AI users to a much broader group of rights holders."

GEMA represents more than 95,000 composers, songwriters and music publishers in Germany, along with over 2 million rights holders worldwide.

How did GEMA present its case?

GEMA claims that Suno trained its AI on copyrighted music without permission or payment to songwriters, composers and publishers represented by the German music collecting society. GEMA also says that the US-based company is commercially benefiting from those works without compensating the artists.

Suno's music creation platform generates songs through simple text prompts. Users can describe the mood, style or genre they desire and the system synthesizes a structured track — complete with lyrics, vocals and instrumentation — in under a minute.

The songs that are produced by the AI system can be very similar to copyrighted songs.

During the court proceedings, GEMA demonstrated this by prompting Suno AI to create tracks with the original lyrics of different popular songs in its repertoire, including "Forever Young" by Alphaville, "Mambo No. 5" by Lou Bega, "Daddy Cool" by Boney M., "Cheri Cheri Lady" by Modern Talking and "Atemlos durch die Nacht," written by Kristina Bach and popularized by Helene Fischer.

Along with the lyrics, the plaintiffs prompted the desired musical style and the title of the work, without specifying any melody, rhythm, harmony or arrangement.

Yet the resulting AI songs are very similar to the original works.

German music: From 'Schlager' to 'Deutschrap' To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Suno admits that the original songs at the center of GEMA's lawsuit are among the numerous pieces that were used to train the AI model.

AI companies such as Suno claim that the ingestion of data for AI training can be done freely on the basis of what is known as "fair use" in the US and the "text and data mining exception" rule in the EU.

But whether such licence-free AI training is allowed under copyright law remains heavily contested globally. In different lawsuits around the world, courts are now examining whether such uses harm the economic market of the original creators through unfair competition.

"The novelty in the lawsuit is that GEMA does not focus on the AI training stage," explains Senftleben. By basing their claim on tests that demonstrate that these AI systems generate songs that have similarities with copyright-protected works from their repertoire, "they bridge this gap between relevant use now taking place in AI training, and the market harm done at AI output level," he adds.

Why AI shouldn't be compared to human brains

Anyone who wants to become a good musician needs to listen to and learn from existing music.

Similarly, the AI industry claims this analogy applies to how their models are trained — by absorbing countless creative works in order to generate new ones.

But from the rights holders' perspective, AI models are rather copying and commercially exploiting their works.

This argument that an AI learns from music and is inspired by it like a human being is "completely ridiculous," notes Tobias Holzmüller. "These are concepts that come from the human brain and have been designed for the human brain, and not for a machine that is able to digest millions of sound files in split seconds. I mean, just the amount of sheer data — they say it's data; for us, it's music — that these machines have swallowed up and then digested and are now spitting out, this is completely incomparable to what's happening in a human brain.

"To humanize these machines by using these concepts is not logical — and it's certainly not moral."

Suno users generate around 7 million tracks every day Image: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/picture alliance

Across Suno's platform globally, users collectively generate roughly 7 million songs per day. Around 75,000 of them end up on streaming services daily, adds Holzmüller. "This is definitely where it's not sustainable anymore, but really toxic for the music ecosystem."

"If you want to create a sustainable model where you accept that AI music is here to stay, but at the same time, that it shouldn't push human-created music out of the market, the only way to tackle this is to put a price tag on the output," says the CEO of GEMA. "Because otherwise you will have free-of-charge AI sounds that will outcompete human music in a lot of circumstances."

For example, music in movie scores or social media has until recently allowed various songwriters to make a living. For Holzmüller, if licences lead to an increase in costs in AI-created sounds to a point that they are as expensive as human-created songs, it could provide a level playing field. "Then — it's my firm belief — people will continue to use human music, because it has this additional element."

Edited by: Brenda Haas

World.title: Germany news: Deutsche Bahn reportedly returns to profit
World.content:
Skip next section Deutsche Bahn reportedly returns to profit in core business

07/30/2026 July 30, 2026 Deutsche Bahn reportedly returns to profit in core business

German rail operator Deutsche Bahn has reportedly returned to profit in its core business for the first time in seven years, marking a sharp turnaround for the crisis-hit rail operator.

The state-owned company recorded a profit in the hundreds of millions of euros between January and June, the Bild newspaper and Der Spiegel news magazine reported Wednesday night.

Deutsche Bahn had posted losses of around €760 million ($870 million) in the first half of 2025.

The reports said the railway carried around 960 million passengers during the first six months of 2026, a record, and 17 million more than in the same period last year. The company was initially unavailable for comment.

Deutsche Bahn reportedly attributed much of the rise in passenger numbers to rising fuel prices. Commuters in particular switched from cars to regional trains as petrol became more expensive while rail fares remained stable.

Demand for long-distance services has also risen significantly since April.

Discount offers are also likely to have contributed to the growth. Around 600,000 people used the last-minute ticket, while 200,000 traveled with the family ticket.

Deutsche Bahn CEO Evelyn Palla is due to present the company's first-half results on Thursday.

The operator has recently faced criticism over poor punctuality, deteriorating infrastructure, and heavy financial losses. It recorded a net loss of more than EUR1 billion in 2025.

World.title: India news: Assam flood toll rises to 78, more rain predicted
World.content:
07/30/2026 July 30, 2026 Opposition protest demands answers on alleged police brutality during 'Cockroach' demonstration

Parties from the INDIA bloc, the country's opposition coalition, on Thursday protested in the Parliament complex over the police action taken against the Cockroach movement youth protesters on July 20.

Opposition lawmakers were seen holding a banner with the text "Who gave the order?" as they demanded that Union Home Minister Shah answer questions in Parliament over the reported use of pellet guns on the protesters.

Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi railed against Shah for not addressing the alleged police excesses, which occurred on the first day of Parliament's second session of the year.

"Why is Amit Shah so scared of coming to Parliament and explaining the brutal violence against students?" Gandhi wrote on X.

"It reeks of guilt," the Congress leader said.

Gandhi called for the constitution of a Supreme Court-monitored high-powered committee to probe the allegations of police brutality against demonstrators.

"Students deserve justice," he said as he called for an independent committee and shared a video purportedly showing police baton-charging protesters and a man, not in uniform, throwing a protester carrying the Indian flag to the ground.

On Wednesday, Gandhi held a press conference calling for Shah's sacking as he accused the minister of ordering the police action on the youth protesters.

He alleged that Shah was either "culpable" if he gave the order or "incompetent" if he did not know what was happening as police clamped down on the protesters demanding the education minister's resignation over a major medical college entrance exam paper leak.

What has the government said on Gandhi's allegations against Amit Shah?

Union Minister Jitendra Singh on Wednesday dismissed Gandhi's claim that Shah ordered the police action.

Speaking in Parliament's lower house, the Lok Sabha, Singh questioned Gandhi's understanding of the administration, saying that orders to open fire "could only be given by a magistrate and not any minister."

Singh also said that no shots were fired at the protesters and only tear gas was used.

On Thursday, the opposition MPs also held demonstrations over an alleged donation theft linked to the Ram Temple in Ayodhya, a shrine key to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Hindu-first politics, officials said.

World.title: French student fined over Singapore straw licking prank
World.content:
A social media stunt involving a single straw has left a French student facing a hefty fine — and possible consequences for his right to remain in Singapore.

A French student has been fined 600 Singapore dollars (€400, $458) after licking a drinking straw and returning it to a dispenser in a prank filmed for social media.

The 19-year-old, Didier Gaspard Owen Maximilien, pleaded guilty to a public nuisance charge.

He avoided a possible prison sentence, but it remains unclear whether authorities will revoke his student pass. The French national studies at Singapore's ESSEC Business School.

What did the student do and why?

Maximilien removed a straw from a freshly squeezed orange juice vending machine in March, licked it and placed it back in the dispenser.

He filmed the stunt for an Instagram story, and the video later went viral.

An employee of the company operating the machine saw the footage and contacted police. As a result, all 500 straws in the dispenser had to be replaced.

The direct cost amounted to just 5 Singapore dollars, or around €3.30, according to court documents, but the case attracted nationwide attention.

Maximilien could have faced several months in prison, a fine, or both after being convicted of disturbing public order.

His lawyer told the court that he was remorseful and now understood that an apparently harmless prank could have far-reaching consequences.

Singapore's strict public-order laws

The wealthy city-state is known for its strict laws and rigorous enforcement, with cleanliness and tightly regulated public spaces forming part of its image for decades.

The import of chewing gum, for example, remains largely prohibited as part of efforts to prevent littering and vandalism.

Singapore also retains judicial caning for certain serious offenses, although the punishment was not applicable in the student's case.

World.title: Australia: Telegram faces legal action over failure to remove terrorist content
World.content:
Australia says videos of terrorist executions and mass shootings weren't removed from Telegram after they were reported. The move comes a day after Russia charged founder Pavel Durov with facilitating terrorist activity.

Telegram is facing a possible AU$54.6 million ($38 million, €33 million) fine in Australia as a regulator said on Thursday the messaging platform failed to remove terrorist content despite warnings.

What are the accusations against Telegram in Australia?

Australia's online safety regulator, the eSafety Commissioner, said it had begun action after videos of terrorist executions, mass shootings and other extremist material linked to attacks including the 2019 Christchurch mosque shootings and the 2022 Buffalo supermarket shooting continued to exist on Telegram.

"We allege ​that this content remained accessible on the service long after Telegram ​had been put on notice," eSafety Commissioner Julie Inman Grant said in a statement.

The regulator said Telegram failed to remove pro-terror content between July and October 2025 or suspend the accounts responsible, despite users reporting the content and its disseminators.

"This action comes at a time when Australia is experiencing a heightened security environment against the fresh backdrop of the Bondi tragedy," Grant said, a reference to an antisemitic mass shooting at a Sydney beach that killed 15 people last year.

Telegram denied the allegations and said it would contest the case in court, adding that it had blocked thousands of extremist communities in 2026.

Ukrainians turn to Telegram, social media for news To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Russia charges Telegram founder Durov with aiding terrorism

The court action comes a day after Russia charged Telegram's billionaire founder Pavel Durov with facilitating terrorist activity.

Russia's Federal Security Service issued an international warrant for his arrest, alleging the platform was used by Ukrainian operatives to organize attacks inside Russia.

Soon after the news of the warrant broke, Telegram's account on X posted a picture of Durov giving a middle finger to the camera.

The Russian-born billionaire Durov, now based in Dubai, built the Telegram messaging app with his brother Nikolai and launched it in 2013. The platform currently boasts over a billion monthly active users.

World.title: Spain: Hundreds of migrants attempt to swim toward Ceuta
World.content:
Spain's Civil Guard, maritime Rescue Services and the Red Cross said they rescued migrants from the water. The interior minister acknowledged the country was facing an "extraordinary, exceptional situation."

Spanish authorities said on Wednesday that hundreds of migrants swam from Morocco attempting to reach the territory of Ceuta.

Border security was overwhelmed by the action, as it did not expect the surge.

What do we know about the migrant attempts to reach Ceuta?

"In the last few days, more than 1,500 migrants, including adults and minors, have reached Ceuta by sea,” the leader of Ceuta's government, Juan Jesus Vivas, told journalists.

"The reception centers are collapsed and saturated," he added.

Spain's Civil Guard, maritime Rescue Services and the Red Cross reportedly rescued some 117 migrants from the water.

Moroccan authorities also reportedly grabbed dozens from the water on their way to Spanish waters.

Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska told Spanish television channel laSexta that authorities were facing "an extraordinary, exceptional situation."

Grande-Marlaska added that "we are dealing with it with the means that we already have deployed there permanently."

He praised Moroccan authorities for their involvement, saying they were cooperating and that the relationship with the kingdom was "close and based on loyalty."

Ceuta: Spain's North African exclave sees migration surge To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Mostly Moroccans seeking to swim across

The Spanish government did not confirm exactly how many migrants had reached the territory by swimming.

It also remains unclear why so many people sought to swim toward Spanish territory.

The swimmers were mostly Moroccans, along with a small number of Algerians who had been living in Morocco while trying to migrate to Europe, according to activists in Morocco and Ceuta.

The incident follows a Spanish Supreme Court ruling earlier this month which established that migrants arriving by sea cannot be immediately pushed back across the border without due process, unlike those crossing by land.

However, activists have discounted the probability that average Moroccans including those swimming toward Ceuta would be aware of such a ruling, dismissing a link between the ruling and the crossings.

Spain offers legal status to migrants To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Migrant arrivals in Spain through the Mediterranean enclaves Ceuta and Melilla, were lower this year compared to the same time last year, as many migrants have sought other routes like the Canary Islands.
