World.title: Poland asks US to extradite former minister Ziobro over criminal charges
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has formally asked the United States to detain and extradite former justice minister Zbigniew Ziobro, who is wanted on multiple criminal charges. Ziobro, a senior figure in the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, is accused of offences including leading an organised criminal group and abuse of office. Having previously fled Poland to Hungary, where Viktor Orbán’s government, an ally of PiS, granted him asylum, Ziobro arrived in the United States in May following a change of government in Budapest. Wniosek o ekstradycję podejrzanego Zbigniewa Ziobro: ⬇️https://t.co/YC7T3RrIEc — Prokuratura (@PK_GOV_PL) July 27, 2026 Ziobro served as justice minister in the PiS government from 2015 to 2023. Last year, prosecutors announced that they wanted to charge him with 26 crimes, including leading a criminal group and approving the unlawful purchase of Pegasus spyware. In October, parliament approved the lifting of Ziobro’s immunity from prosecution. By then, however, he had already travelled to Hungary, and in December he was granted political asylum by the Hungarian government. In February this year, Warsaw’s district court approved a request from prosecutors to place Ziobro in pretrial detention. That decision was needed in order for the authorities to issue domestic and European arrest warrants against the suspect. However, Ziobro’s lawyers appealed against the decision. While that appeal was waiting to be heard, Orbán lost power in Hungary and, as his successor Péter Magyar was being sworn in, Ziobro left the country and flew to the United States. In July, a Warsaw court rejected Ziobro’s appeal, opening the way for Poland to seek the politician’s extradition from the US. Ziobro has no valid travel documents after Poland cancelled his passports and Budapest revoked his refugee status. The extradition request covers 19 of the 26 offences listed in the indictment, the prosecutors said. The documents submitted include the final order for Ziobro’s detention, the indictment, a wanted notice and evidence supporting the case. The request will now be sent through diplomatic channels to the US Department of Justice, where it will be assessed to determine whether it meets the formal requirements of the Polish-US extradition treaty, prosecutor Anna Adamiak said. If the request satisfies those requirements, it will be referred to a US federal court, where a judge will decide on the legal admissibility of Ziobro’s extradition to Poland. A court has upheld a request by prosecutors to bring former justice minister Zbigniew Ziobro, who is wanted on 26 criminal charges, into detention. The decision paves the way for Poland to request Ziobro's extradition from the US, where he fled in May https://t.co/vIPRjvgQnA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 2, 2026 Asked how long the extradition process could take, Adamiak said previous cases suggested proceedings could last anywhere from a few months to several years, depending on their nature and complexity. Adamiak noted, however, that the extradition proceedings would not determine Ziobro’s guilt. “Its role is merely to assess whether the surrender of that person in extradition proceedings is legally permissible in light of treaty regulations and domestic law,” she told reporters, quoted by online news service Wirtualna Polska. “However, the decision on surrender is, of course, a decision made by the state, so other circumstances may also play a role,” she added. PiS, Poland’s largest opposition party, enjoys close ties with US President Donald Trump’s administration. Poland's conservative opposition enthusiastically welcomed Trump's return to the White House, but it is becoming increasingly difficult for them to maintain a tough anti-Russian line while also showing allegiance to the US president, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/4PW6H9nMEF — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 7, 2025 Asked at a news conference about the likelihood of Ziobro’s extradition and when it might take place, Poland’s Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the question should be directed at “the other Donald”, reported the Polish Press Agency (PAP). “We will, in accordance with the law, seek all available means to ensure that these politicians, against whom such serious charges have been brought, appear before a Polish court sooner or later,” he added. “We are waiting for positive signals from Washington. Will they come? I don’t know.” Ziobro has long denied all accusations, saying the case against him is an act of “political revenge” by Tusk’s government. Commenting on the extradition request on the conservative television channel Republika, Ziobro said he was pleased that the case would be heard “in the United States, on American soil, and before an American court”. He claimed that the proceedings would show that the Polish government “regularly breaks the law, ignores procedures, rejects democratic principles, has taken control of the prosecutor’s office unlawfully, and is trying to destroy the opposition”. World.title: Revolut Opens Private Market Funds to Czech Investors
World.content:
Revolut is expanding its investment services in the Czech Republic, giving retail customers access to funds focused on private equity, private credit and infrastructure.

The new products will become available in the Revolut app from July 31. The fintech has signed distribution agreements with four major asset managers — Apollo, Ares, Hamilton Lane and Partners Group — which collectively manage more than $2.8 trillion in assets.

The move gives Czech retail investors access to parts of the private markets that have traditionally been aimed largely at institutional investors.



Private market investments have often required substantial minimum commitments, frequently above €100,000, or around CZK 2.5 million. Revolut’s new offering is designed to lower that barrier and allow customers to add private assets to portfolios that may already include stocks, bonds and exchange-traded funds.

Investments will be available directly through the Revolut app.

The funds will be offered through the European Long-Term Investment Fund framework, known as ELTIF 2.0.

How ELTIF 2.0 works

The structure is intended to provide investors with greater flexibility than traditional private equity funds, where capital can remain committed for several years and withdrawals may not be possible during that period.

The products offered through Revolut use an “evergreen” structure. This allows investors to put money into funds with existing portfolios rather than waiting for a traditional investment cycle to begin.

ELTIF 2.0 also provides scheduled liquidity windows during which investors can request the redemption of their holdings, subject to the conditions of the individual fund.

That does not mean the investments are as liquid as publicly traded shares. Private market assets remain difficult to sell quickly, and investors should expect to hold their money for the long term.

Revolut already offers Czech customers access to a range of traditional investments, including US and European stocks, ETFs, bonds and commodities. The addition of private market funds expands the investment options available through the same app.

World.title: From Old Town to Main Station: Tourist Charged €150 for Short Taxi Ride
World.content:
A tourist has reported an alleged taxi scam in Prague, claiming that a journey from Old Town Square to Prague Main Railway Station ended with an unexpectedly high fare and a disputed payment.

The incident reportedly took place on July 25 at around 16:15. According to the complaint, the driver charged CZK 980 for the ride, an amount the passenger said was far higher than the expected price for such a short distance.

The tourist claims that the driver refused to accept payment by card and requested cash instead.



“I paid him 100 Euros for the fare. He just took the note, swapped it and lied to me saying what I gave was 100 in Czech currency, and demanded me to pay the remaining 50 euro taxi fare,” the tourist said in his complaint.

“So I paid the initial 100 euro that was swapped, plus the 50 euro taxi fare.”

According to the passenger, the total amount paid for the ride was therefore €150 (over 3,600 CZK). He said he was rushing to catch a train to Bratislava and was unable to resolve the dispute at the scene.

The tourist also claimed that no receipt was provided after the payment. According to his account, the driver said an invoice would be sent by email, but it was never received.

The case has been reported to the relevant authorities, while details of the incident have also been shared online to raise awareness among other visitors.

Travellers are also encouraged to use established taxi applications or services recommended by hotels, restaurants, and official tourist information centres. Paying by card and confirming the expected price in advance can help avoid disputes.

World.title: Babiš Warns Czechia Could Become Net EU Payer by 2029 as Contributions Surge
World.content:
The Czech prime minister also said Brussels is likely to permit a larger budget deficit as Prague seeks funding for hospitals, highways, and other domestic investment.

Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš has expressed alarm over the country’s rapidly increasing payments to the European Union, warning that the Czech Republic could become a net contributor to the bloc as early as 2029.

Following talks with Finance Minister Alena Schillerová, Babiš said Czech payments into the EU budget had risen by 22 billion crowns (€911 million) this year alone.

“I was shocked by how much we are paying into the European Union,” he said, as cited by Echo24. “If in one year we are told that we will pay 22 billion more, that is a lot.”



Officials currently expect the Czech Republic to become a net contributor to the EU budget for the first time in its history in either 2029 or 2030.

Babiš was also asked about next year’s state budget deficit. When asked whether it would exceed this year’s planned shortfall of 310 billion crowns (€12.8 billion), he replied, “Don’t test me. I don’t know what the deficit will be.”

Schillerová said a reliable estimate would only be possible after the Finance Ministry publishes its updated economic forecast next month.

The government has informed the European Commission that it expects next year’s structural deficit to reach as much as 2.9 percent of GDP, compared with 2.4 percent this year. According to Schillerová, Brussels has provisionally accepted the higher ceiling.

“We have to invest in hospitals, highways and bypasses,” he said, justifying the overspend but maintaining that the deficit should remain significantly below 400 billion crowns (€16.6 billion).

Planned spending includes psychiatric hospitals, surgical facilities, oncology centers, highways and city bypasses. The government also intends to maintain defense expenditure at 2 percent of GDP.

World.title: Hundreds of Czech Castles and Chateaus to Offer Free Entry on Two Special Days
World.content:
Visitors will be able to explore more than 100 state-managed castles, chateaus, monasteries, and other historic landmarks across Czechia free of charge on August 30 and September 27.

The initiative follows a spring pilot program that granted free admission to selected state museums and galleries. According to the Ministry, strong public interest in that campaign encouraged officials to extend the concept to historic monuments managed by the National Heritage Institute (NPÚ).

The free admission will apply to the standard sightseeing route at each participating site, along with selected additional visitor circuits where available.



Tours will operate under normal conditions, meaning visitor numbers will remain limited and capacity restrictions will continue to apply.

The National Heritage Institute is expected to publish a complete list of participating sites, opening hours, reservation requirements, and visitor information on its website in the coming days.

The latest initiative builds on an earlier trial introduced this spring.

Between April and June, visitors were granted free entry on selected Sundays to five of the country’s largest state museums: the National Museum in Prague, the Moravian Museum in Brno, the Silesian Museum in Opava, the National Technical Museum in Prague, and the Technical Museum in Brno.

According to the Ministry of Culture, attendance at those museums nearly doubled during the pilot period, with the Silesian Museum recording the largest increase in visitor numbers. Selected state galleries also participated in the program earlier this year while officials assessed the financial impact of waiving admission fees.

The ministry has said one of its long-term objectives is to help restore visitor numbers at cultural institutions to levels seen before the COVID-19 pandemic.

World.title: On this Day, in 1419: the First Defenestration of Prague
World.content:
Six hundred years ago, an angry crowd stormed Prague’s New Town Hall and threw several royal councillors from its windows.

The attack, known as the First Defenestration of Prague, took place on July 30, 1419, and is widely regarded as the event that ignited the Hussite Wars—a conflict that transformed medieval Bohemia and left a lasting mark on Czech history.

Yet the violence that unfolded that summer day had been years in the making.

Its roots lay in the teachings of Jan Hus, a Czech theologian, university lecturer, and religious reformer who became one of the most influential figures of the late Middle Ages. Hus openly criticized corruption within the Catholic Church, particularly the sale of indulgences and the growing power of the church hierarchy. Rather than viewing the Church as an institution led by the pope and bishops, he argued that the true Church was the community of faithful believers.

Summoned before the Council of Constance in 1415 to defend his beliefs, Hus was arrested despite receiving a promise of safe conduct. After refusing to renounce his teachings, he was convicted of heresy and burned at the stake.



His execution outraged many across Bohemia. While members of the nobility saw it as the unjust killing of one of the kingdom’s own, Hus’s followers spread his ideas far beyond Prague through a network of priests and former university students. The capital, home to Charles University and the Bethlehem Chapel where Hus had preached, became the center of a rapidly growing reform movement.

Bohemia’s political circumstances also allowed the movement to flourish. Neither King Wenceslas IV nor the Archbishop of Prague took decisive action to suppress it, allowing religious tensions to deepen over the following years.

By the summer of 1419, the situation had reached a breaking point.

On July 30, radical Hussite preacher Jan Želivský led a religious procession through Prague after delivering an impassioned sermon. Although the march may have appeared spontaneous, historians believe the confrontation had been carefully prepared. Some participants reportedly arrived carrying concealed weapons, expecting violence.

The procession made its way to Prague’s New Town Hall, demanding the release of Hussite supporters imprisoned there. When the councillors refused, the crowd forced its way inside.

The assault was led by Jan Žižka, a military commander who would later become one of medieval Europe’s greatest generals. Several councillors were seized and thrown from the building’s windows. Although the fall itself was not fatal for everyone, those who survived were beaten to death by the waiting crowd below.

For medieval society, the act carried a powerful symbolic meaning. Publicly casting powerful officials from an elevated position represented the dramatic downfall of those who had abused their authority.

The defenestration did not, by itself, begin the Hussite Wars, but it made peaceful reconciliation increasingly unlikely. Just weeks later, King Wenceslas IV died, leaving the throne to his brother Sigismund, whom many Bohemians blamed for failing to protect Jan Hus at Constance. Relations between the Hussites and the crown rapidly collapsed, and in 1420 the first crusade against Bohemia was launched.

The wars that followed lasted more than a decade. They devastated much of the kingdom but also produced extraordinary military victories under Jan Žižka and established the Hussites as one of medieval Europe’s most formidable fighting forces.

The First Defenestration of Prague remains one of the defining moments in Czech history—a single act of violence that turned years of religious unrest into a revolution whose legacy can still be seen throughout the country today.

World.title: Czech Company Enters Fortune Global 500 for the First Time
World.content:
A Czech company has entered the Fortune Global 500 ranking for the first time in history.

Energy and industrial group EP Group (EPG), controlled by Czech businessman Daniel Křetínský, placed 179th in the latest edition of the prestigious list of the world’s largest companies by revenue.

The ranking, published annually by the U.S. business magazine Fortune, evaluates companies based on their total sales. EP Group reported revenues of $75.387 billion, equivalent to around CZK 1.6 trillion.

To put the figure into perspective, the Czech state budget expects total revenues of CZK 2.118 trillion this year.



EP Group’s portfolio includes stakes in major companies across Europe, including British postal operator Royal Mail, Slovak energy producer Slovenské elektrárne, German retail chain Metro and French energy giant TotalEnergies.

With its debut in the ranking, EP Group has also placed Prague among the headquarters of the world’s largest corporations. The Czech capital is now one of 242 cities worldwide where at least one Fortune Global 500 company is based.

Only 14 other countries in the Fortune Global 500 ranking have a single representative, including Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Poland, Austria and Thailand.

EP Group is also among a very small number of newcomers. Only 13 companies worldwide entered the top 500 this year for the first time, while another 11 returned after previously dropping out of the ranking.

The company’s rise reflects the growing importance of energy, infrastructure and industrial businesses in the global economy.

US companies dominate the ranking

American companies continue to lead the Fortune Global 500, with 141 firms making the list — the highest number since the global financial crisis in 2008.

World.title: Inside IAM Prague: How a Travelling Exhibition Laid the Foundation for One of the City’s Top-Rated Museums
World.content:
Just off Old Town Square, past the cafes and the crowds waiting for the Astronomical Clock, sits a museum that started almost by accident.

Today, IAM Prague has welcomed well over 1 million visitors from around the world and has held TripAdvisor’s Travelers’ Choice Award for five straight years.

From Shopping Malls to Old Town Square

The museum wasn’t originally supposed to be a… museum. Co-founder Jakub Bechyně and his partner Patrik Proško had been running a traveling illusion exhibit that moved between shopping malls, renting space for a month at a time before packing up and relocating. It worked, but it wasn’t permanent.

Then, in 2017, the owner of a building on Old Town Square approached them with an idea: turn part of it into a museum. The catch was the timeline. They wanted it open in two months.

Rather than build something from scratch, the team pulled from what they already had on the shelf, opening with one floor and sixteen exhibits in 2018. The collection has grown to more than 60 pieces since.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Illusion Art Museum Prague (@iamprague)

The museum moved to its current location in 2022 after the original building was sold. The new space, ideally located between Old Town Square and Wenceslas Square, needed walls removed and floors rebuilt to accommodate the art. The costs were substantial, but it turned out to be a good problem to have as the location dramatically increased the exhibition’s visibility to passersby on one of Prague’s busiest tourist thoroughfares.

Choosing Technique Over Fame

IAM Prague doesn’t chase famous names. It chases techniques. The team looks for a specific kind of illusion craft, one with real artistic quality, a genuine optical trick, and ideally a story behind it worth telling.

That approach led them to reverse-perspective specialist Patrick Hughes, and to artists whose work they discovered secondhand and eventually acquired outright rather than simply displaying on loan. In several cases, the museum ended up owning the pieces after renting them for years and deciding they belonged permanently in the collection.

About 80 percent of the exhibition has changed since opening. Early pieces built quickly to fill the space have gradually been replaced as the museum brought in stronger, more polished work from local and international artists.

The exhibition’s evolution continues, with four new pieces from international artists like Jonty Hurwitz and Andrej Boleslavsky, ranging from traditional mirror anamorphoses to digital art, recently unveiled in June.

History Hidden in Plain Sight

Much of what makes IAM Prague distinct is how it uses illusion as a delivery method for history. A glass-art piece featuring four endangered animals turns out to double as an environmental message.

A defenestration scene lets visitors reenact one of Prague’s most repeated historical events, tied to the 1618 uprising that helped trigger the Thirty Years’ War. Even the museum’s own opening date, a century after Czechoslovak independence in 1918, was picked on purpose.

One exhibit nods to Karel Čapek, the Czech writer who coined the word “robot,” a term that entered global use even though it comes from a Slavic word for forced labor.

Another traces the story of Tomáš Baťa, the industrialist who pioneered mass shoe manufacturing and built factories across multiple continents, including a Pakistani city that still carries his name today.

AI’s Impact on Art & Travel

Though much has been made on artificial intelligence’s impact on the world of art, the team’s biggest current concern isn’t AI-generated art replacing the exhibition’s themselves. It’s the shift in how travelers plan their trips.

For years, visibility depended on traditional guidebooks, online travel agencies, physical advertising, and street presence. Increasingly, travelers are relying on AI chat tools to create itineraries, shifting the importance of more “traditional” visibility mechanisms, which is forcing venues like Illusion Art Museum Prague to adapt.

Despite the changing landscape, the plan going forward leans further into digital and kinetic art, including new motion-based installations recently brought in from Berlin by artists like Florian Goerlitz.

For a museum that started as a temporary mall exhibit, the goal has stayed consistent since day one: make people stop, look twice, and leave with a story they didn’t expect to learn.

World.title: Nearly One in Five Prague Farmers’ Market Vendors Fail Veterinary Inspections
World.content:
Nearly one in five vendors inspected at Prague’s farmers’ markets during the first half of 2026 were found to have breached food safety or labeling regulations, according to the State Veterinary Administration (SVS).

Between January and June, veterinary inspectors checked 53 vendors across Prague and identified violations in 10 cases, representing almost 19 percent of all inspections.

Nationwide, inspectors carried out 165 inspections, with irregularities detected in 27 cases, or roughly 16 percent.

Officials said the most common problems in Prague involved improper storage temperatures for food of animal origin, incorrect or incomplete product labeling, and inadequate protection of food from contamination during sale.

Inspectors also highlighted several cases they considered particularly serious. In one instance, a vendor was found producing meat products without the legally required authorization while packaging them with the identification mark of a production facility that no longer exists. Authorities said such practices can mislead consumers about where products originate.



The SVS warned that food safety risks increase during the summer months, especially at outdoor markets where high temperatures make it more difficult to maintain proper cooling conditions.

Across the Czech Republic, labeling violations were the most frequently recorded offense this year, accounting for 26 cases. Problems related to hygiene and production practices—including incorrect storage temperatures and insufficient protection against contamination—followed with 22 cases.

Inspectors also documented 18 violations involving improper handling of food products and 12 cases where the origin of goods was unclear or could not be verified.

The SVS noted that a single inspection may uncover multiple breaches. While inspectors found violations in 27 inspections nationwide, the total number of individual offenses reached 82.

Inspection results remained largely unchanged compared with the same period last year. During the first six months of 2025, inspectors also carried out 165 inspections, finding violations in 16 percent of them. The main difference was that hygiene-related shortcomings topped the list last year, while labeling issues have become the most common problem in 2026.

Looking at the full year, the SVS carried out 380 market inspections across the Czech Republic in 2025, compared with 372 inspections in 2024. The proportion of inspections uncovering violations rose slightly from 17 percent to 18 percent.

World.title: Hungarian agriculture, as we know it, is nearing the end – but researchers already have a plan
World.content:
We have already seen AI-generated visualisations of what Szeged might look like with a dried-up Tisza and a desertified landscape. The picture is not quite so bleak, but the fact remains that our lakes and rivers are facing record-low water levels, while vast swathes of the country are turning to desert. Hungary’s 19th-century water-management system, and the agricultural model built upon it, now require urgent and thorough overhaul. Hungarian agriculture as it is known today may disappear — but what comes next? A new study by Hungarian researchers offers some clues.

Wheat, maize and sunflower in the Great Plain desert?

There are many reasons for the drying of the Great Plain, above all ourselves: the descendants of those who, in the mid-19th century, decided that every last patch of land must be brought under cultivation. There was even an idea to drain Lake Balaton and farm that too. To this was added the torment of Hungary’s reduced status after Trianon, when successive governments sought to secure stable foreign currency earnings through the export of arable crops, chiefly cereals. The situation did not change under communism either: the fertile Hungarian soil was thus required to produce wheat, maize and sunflower rather than fruit and vegetables. That era, however, may now be drawing to a close.

Summer harvest in Hungary: lowering yields. Photo: Facebook/István Nagy, Hungary’s agriculture minister

We too have reported in numerous articles on the desertification of the Great Plain. The essence of these reports can perhaps be summed up as follows: without intervention, vast areas may become unfit for human habitation, and certainly for agriculture. The reasons are climate change, drought, low rainfall, and the lack of irrigation and water retention. The artificial water system of the Carpathian Basin — and within it Hungary — has, since the days of Széchenyi and Vasvári, been geared towards draining away as quickly as possible the precipitation arriving here as runoff or melting snow, and sending it beyond the country’s borders.

New 10,000 km² European sand desert forming in Hungary: Over 620,000 lives at risk

Shocking difference. Photo: Facebook/idokep

The soil-water table has paid the price. During extreme droughts, groundwater has sunk so low that it now lies beneath the root zone of plants. In other words, there may be arable land available, but if accessible water disappears from the soil, crops cannot survive.

What could replace it?

According to researchers, the answer lies in water retention and a wholesale rethinking of land use. In areas where cultivation is kept alive only by EU subsidies, arable farming should be abandoned and priority given instead to retaining water. One new study suggests that, in practice, this would mean flooding 1.5 million hectares of arable land — almost a third of the country’s total cultivated area.

The effect would be twofold: groundwater levels would rise, the root zone would once again reach the water table, and maize yields could increase by 20 to 28 per cent, while today’s droughts effectively wipe out everything in their path.

On poorer land, too, it may make more sense to switch back to the once-familiar practice of pasture-based farming, or to higher-value vegetable and fruit production. Naturally, this would need to be done using the most advanced drip-irrigation technology and other water-saving methods. That, too, may be in farmers’ interests: the study argues that on many marginal sites, conventional arable farming can now be sustained only with subsidies, while loss-making farming makes little sense either for farmers or for the Hungarian economy.

Bombs emerge from the Danube: record-low water levels expose suspected WWII explosives near Budapest

Change is coming

The key to change is therefore not irrigation alone. Water must be retained, farming adapted to the landscape, and intensive production concentrated where the conditions genuinely allow it.

The study, published in the journal Geography and Sustainability, was carried out by 15 Hungarian researchers and was supplemented in the article by Zsolt Pinke, a researcher at the Institute of Soil Sciences of the HUN-REN Centre for Agricultural Research, as reported by Válasz Online.

Perhaps the study’s most important message is this: the question is not whether Hungarian agriculture will change, but whether we adapt deliberately to a drying Great Plain — or wait until drought forces the issue.

World.title: Third-degree heat alert from today in Hungary – what it means
World.content:
A third-degree heat alert has come into force, ordered by the chief medical officer from 12 midnight on Thursday until midnight on Tuesday. According to HungaroMet’s Thursday morning bulletin, the average temperature in a further three counties may exceed 27C.

Third-degree heat alert in Hungary again

HungaroMet’s warning shows that on Thursday the average temperature will climb above 27C in Győr-Moson-Sopron, Komárom-Esztergom, Veszprém, Fejér, Bács-Kiskun and Csongrád-Csanád counties, while elsewhere — except in Nógrád, Heves, Borsod-Abaúj-Zemplén and Szabolcs-Szatmár-Bereg — it is expected to top 25C, the Hungarian news agency wrote.

On Thursday, the average temperature will also exceed 27C in Vas, Tolna and Pest counties, HungaroMet said.

On Friday, the average is forecast to rise above 29C in Komárom-Esztergom, Fejér and Bács-Kiskun counties. In Nógrád, Borsod-Abaúj-Zemplén and Szabolcs-Szatmár-Bereg counties it will be above 25C, and elsewhere above 27C.

Hot weather remains

Prolonged high temperatures reduce both physical and mental performance, increase fatigue and the risk of accidents, and have an adverse effect on the course of cardiovascular, respiratory and kidney diseases. The most serious consequence of heat stress is heatstroke, a life-threatening condition; if someone feels unwell, they should be taken to a cool place immediately, their body should be cooled, and an ambulance called if necessary.

World.title: Toxic metal levels found in wells near Semcorp plant in Hungary, Greenpeace calls for investigation
World.content:
Tests carried out on private wells near the Chinese-owned Semcorp battery separator film plant in Debrecen have found manganese concentrations far above Hungary’s drinking water limit, with two wells exceeding the legal threshold by more than ten times. Environmental organisations say the findings warrant further investigation, although they stress that the source of the contamination has not yet been identified.

The results were announced by Greenpeace Hungary and the Mothers for the Environment of Mikepércs Association, which commissioned laboratory tests following growing public concern after an industrial accident at the Semcorp factory earlier this year.

Tests followed February industrial accident

According to 444.hu, the investigation was launched after a February incident at the Semcorp plant raised fears that pollutants could have reached local groundwater. While the latest laboratory analyses did not detect the substances previously linked to the factory accident, all three tested private wells contained manganese concentrations significantly above the drinking water limit.

According to the organisations, the measured concentrations were 790, 520 and 240 micrograms per litre, compared with Hungary’s drinking water limit of 50 micrograms per litre. The sampled wells are used by local residents for everyday purposes, including drinking, cooking, watering livestock and irrigating gardens.

Cause of high manganese levels remains unknown

Despite the elevated readings, Greenpeace and the local environmental group emphasised that the current data do not prove the Semcorp plant is responsible.

They noted that the Debrecen area’s geological conditions mean the elevated manganese could also have a natural geological origin. However, they said the results justify additional hydrogeological and environmental investigations to determine the source of the contamination.

The organisations plan to submit the laboratory findings to the relevant authorities and formally request an official investigation. They are also calling for broader testing of substances associated with battery manufacturing technologies.

If you missed it: Hungary orders complete shutdown of Chinese battery supplier’s Debrecen factory

Semcorp has faced growing scrutiny

The Chinese battery materials manufacturer has come under increasing pressure in recent months. Following the February industrial incident, environmental groups reported finding chemicals associated with the factory’s production processes in nearby wastewater samples, prompting an official investigation.

In late June, environmental authorities suspended operations at the Debrecen facility after groundwater samples reportedly revealed pollution exceeding regulatory limits. Official data later showed aluminium concentrations in groundwater more than 13,000 times above the applicable limit.

Soon afterwards, Debrecen Mayor László Papp publicly described the pollution as “simply unacceptable” and urged authorities to consider revoking the company’s environmental permit if necessary. On 1 July, he went further, calling on Semcorp to leave the city altogether.

The factory was subsequently ordered to halt all operations with immediate effect after fire safety inspectors identified serious violations that endangered people and property. Authorities also imposed a HUF 3 million fire safety fine, while police launched an environmental damage investigation.

Semcorp said at the time that it accepted the authorities’ decisions and had begun an internal investigation under senior management supervision.

World.title: Swimming banned at popular free Balaton beach after water quality concerns
World.content:
Authorities have imposed a temporary swimming ban at Helikon Beach in Keszthely after routine water quality testing found the latest sample did not meet the required standards.

The announcement was made on Wednesday by the Municipality of Keszthely, following a decision by the Public Health Department of the Zala County Government Office. Officials said the temporary restriction was introduced to protect public health after the most recent water sample produced an “unsatisfactory result” during regular monitoring.

Other Keszthely beaches remain safe

The municipality stressed that the issue is limited to Helikon Beach. The city’s other two beaches, Keszthely City Beach and Libás Beach, continue to have excellent water quality, and swimming there remains completely safe.

New water quality tests will be carried out at Helikon Beach in the coming days. The beach will reopen as soon as health authorities confirm that the water once again complies with safety standards.

One of Lake Balaton’s newest free beaches

The temporary closure comes just a few months after Helikon Beach became one of the most notable free-access beaches on Lake Balaton.

Since 1 May, visitors have been able to use the municipally owned beach free of charge after the town removed the fences that had previously enclosed the paid beach. The symbolic dismantling of the barriers was carried out jointly by the mayor and local volunteers.

The current restriction is temporary, and local authorities have thanked visitors for their patience and understanding while waiting for the follow-up laboratory results.

World.title: Hungarian fake Jesus arrested in Italy after fleeing prison sentence for fraud
World.content:
A 73-year-old Hungarian man known in the media as the “Zala county fake Jesus” has been arrested in Italy after fleeing Hungary to avoid serving a prison sentence for defrauding his followers of HUF millions.

The man was detained by Italian police in Macerata on 7 July, a spokesperson for the Zala County Police Headquarters confirmed. Hungarian and Italian authorities have since begun extradition proceedings, although no date has yet been set for fake Jesus’ return to Hungary. His status on the Hungarian police’s wanted persons database has also been updated to “captured”.

Fake Jesus sentenced to four and a half years in prison

The man was the subject of a nationwide arrest warrant after failing to report to prison to begin serving a four-and-a-half-year sentence. According to the Zalaegerszeg Regional Court, he could not be located at his registered address, prompting the court to issue a warrant for his arrest.

He had originally been sentenced in October 2024 to six years’ imprisonment for 23 counts of fraud and one count of disorderly conduct. The court also ordered him to pay a HUF 300,000 fine and nearly HUF 19 million, plus interest, in compensation to his victims. On appeal, the sentence was reduced to four years and six months in November 2025, taking into account his advanced age and previous clean criminal record.

Followers allegedly manipulated for decades

According to the courts, the man claiming to be Jesus’ reincarnation spent decades presenting himself as a spiritual healer, energy therapist and saviour of souls. He organised group sessions and private consultations in several Hungarian cities, including Zalaegerszeg, Nagykanizsa, Pécs, Budapest and Böhönye.

During these gatherings, he reportedly preached about unconditional love, God, the Saviour, modesty, self-sacrifice and rejecting material wealth, while claiming he had little understanding of financial matters.

Investigators found that he portrayed himself as the reincarnation of Jesus, gradually gaining the trust of people seeking healing or spiritual guidance. Prosecutors said he created emotional dependence among his followers and increasingly influenced their personal relationships, career choices and financial decisions.

Millions collected for charitable causes apparently funded luxury lifestyle

The court found that the man persuaded followers to donate money for what he described as charitable or noble causes, including buying homes, supporting people in need and funding children’s camps. Instead, prosecutors said the money was spent financing his own luxurious lifestyle.

The victims were defrauded of nearly HUF 20 million (EUR 55,200) in total. Some followers reportedly continued to believe in his spiritual mission throughout the investigation, while others questioned his activities but felt unable to break free from his influence. According to the court, he warned followers that anyone who “betrayed” him would become seriously ill.

Throughout the legal proceedings, the man denied criminal wrongdoing. While acknowledging that he was not Jesus, he maintained that he nevertheless possessed exceptional spiritual knowledge.

World.title: Hungarian parliamentary committee backs lifting Tisza MP’s immunity over drink-driving case
World.content:
Hungary’s parliamentary Immunity Committee has recommended lifting the parliamentary immunity of Tisza Party MP Lőrinc Varga in connection with a drink-driving offence committed in 2024, before he became a member of parliament.

Committee chair Edit Sasi-Nagy, also a Tisza Party MP, told the Hungarian News Agency (MTI) after Wednesday’s meeting that the proposal will be submitted to Parliament for a vote next Monday.

According to Sasi-Nagy, the offence took place in 2024, when Varga was neither an MP nor a parliamentary candidate. However, because the court proceedings were still ongoing when he was elected to Parliament, the case was suspended, and the court requested that his parliamentary immunity be lifted so the trial could continue.

Committee unanimously supports lifting immunity

Sasi-Nagy explained that the committee follows a long-established practice: in public prosecution cases, it generally recommends suspending parliamentary immunity, while in private prosecution cases, it recommends maintaining it.

On that basis, the committee unanimously voted to recommend lifting Varga’s immunity. Varga, one of the youngest MPs in the Tisza Party parliamentary group, publicly addressed the incident in May.

In a social media post, he acknowledged responsibility, writing that during a routine police check following a gathering with friends, alcohol had been detected in his system the following morning.

“I made a mistake, and I fully accept responsibility,” he said at the time.

Magyar, Toroczkai and Takács retain immunity in defamation cases

The committee also considered several private prosecution cases involving other MPs. It unanimously recommended maintaining the parliamentary immunity of Prime Minister Péter Magyar in a defamation case initiated by a politician.

Similarly, the committee proposed maintaining the immunity of László Toroczkai, leader of the Mi Hazánk (Our Homeland) party, in four separate court proceedings relating to the same alleged act involving defamation and insult.

The committee also unanimously recommended preserving the immunity of Fidesz MP Péter Takács, who is likewise facing private defamation and insult proceedings.

Committee: immunity protects political work, not criminal offences

Summing up the decisions, Sasi-Nagy said the private prosecution cases illustrate the original purpose of parliamentary immunity: ensuring that elected representatives can carry out their political duties without being hindered by private legal disputes.

By contrast, she noted that public prosecution cases—such as Varga’s alleged drink-driving offence—are generally treated differently, which is why the committee recommended allowing the criminal proceedings to continue.

World.title: Report: Orbán government sent EUR 705,000 overseas in 10 months, funding New York office, cemetery restoration
World.content:
The Orbán government’s Bethlen Gábor Fund (BGA) distributed HUF 255.9 million (approximately EUR 705,000) in discretionary grants to Hungarian diaspora organisations outside Europe between July 2025 and the end of April 2026, according to documents obtained through a freedom of information request.

The documents, first reported by Hungarian news outlet 444, show that the Orbán government’s funding reached organisations in the United States, Canada, Uruguay, Argentina, Chile and Japan, supporting both cultural programmes and day-to-day operating costs. Unlike standard grant schemes, the funding was awarded through individual applications rather than open public calls.

Two organisations received around two-thirds of the Orbán government’s funding

According to the documents, 19 individual funding decisions were made by the Orbán government during the ten-month period, with roughly two-thirds of the total allocated to just two organisations. The Hungarian Scout Association in Exteris, based in Morris Plains, New Jersey, received HUF 119 million (EUR 328,000) to operate the Hungarian House and support its Diaspora School Camp programme.

Meanwhile, the Hungarian Human Rights Foundation in New York was awarded HUF 70 million (EUR 193,000) for its Reconnect Hungary initiative, which brings young people of Hungarian descent born in the United States to Hungary to strengthen their ties with the country.

The Orbán government’s funding covered a wide range of expenses, including staff salaries, project management, flights to Hungary, accommodation, meals, admission fees and the operating costs of the organisation’s New York office. According to the report, HUF 35 million (EUR 96,500) of this funding was approved on 9 and 10 April, just days before Hungary’s parliamentary election.

Funding also supported church, cultural and heritage projects

Other grants included HUF 14 million (EUR 38,500) for the Independent Hungarian Reformed Church of Ontario in Canada, HUF 13 million (EUR 35,800) for the Duna Hungarian Arts and Folklore Association in Chile, HUF 10 million for the Pannonia Hungarian Bookstore in Ontario.

One of the more unusual projects was supported in Uruguay, where the Federation of Hungarian Organisations in Latin America received HUF 11.4 million (EUR 31,400) for operational costs and development projects, including the creation of a Hungarian diaspora museum and the renovation of the Hungarian Pantheon, a Hungarian mausoleum located in the Tucumán Cemetery.

Stay up-to-date: Scandal, if true — PM Orbán’s former deputy and opposition KDNP party head Zsolt Semjén accused of raping a minor by victim

Discretionary funding process has drawn criticism

According to the documents, organisations seeking support were required to submit detailed applications explaining their projects, budgets and how the proposed activities would serve the interests of Hungarian communities abroad. Following a professional assessment by the Bethlen Gábor Fund, the final decisions were made by the Prime Minister’s Office, under the supervision of the State Secretary responsible for national policy.

While discretionary grants are a recognised form of public funding in Hungary, the system has faced criticism from transparency advocates because awards are made without open competition and can involve substantial public funds. The latest disclosures follow earlier reports that the Bethlen Gábor Fund allocated HUF billions to Hungarian football academies and organisations outside Hungary during the same period.

World.title: Paks nuclear reactor unit shut down as Danube reaches record-low water levels
World.content:
Hungary has begun shutting down one of the four reactor units at the Paks Nuclear Power Plant after the Danube reached exceptionally low water levels, highlighting the growing impact of the country’s prolonged heatwave and severe drought.

The operator, MVM Paks Nuclear Power Plant Ltd., announced on Wednesday afternoon that the shutdown of Unit 3 began at 3 PM as the Danube continued to fall to record-low levels along several sections of the river.

According to the company, the water level at Paks had dropped to -118 centimetres, prompting the decision to take the reactor offline in line with operational and environmental safety requirements.

Plant operators said they are continuously monitoring river flow and water temperature and will make further operational decisions based on changing conditions. The company stressed that maintaining the plant’s safe operation while complying with environmental regulations remains its top priority.

Emergency measures in place to secure cooling water

Earlier on Wednesday, Environment Minister László Gajdos announced that Hungary’s water management authority had entered a state of heightened readiness to ensure a continuous cooling water supply for the nuclear power station despite the extreme drought.

In a Facebook post, the minister said authorities have already deployed four floating pumping units and two floating cranes on the Danube near Paks. Although pumping is not yet necessary, 55 specialists are working around the clock on standby to respond if conditions deteriorate.

“The protective measures are ongoing. We are safeguarding Hungary’s water resources and national security,” Gajdos wrote.

Output had already been reduced

The shutdown follows several days of gradually reducing the plant’s electricity output as the Danube’s water level continued to decline.

Economy and Energy Minister István Kapitány previously described the power reductions as a planned precautionary measure rather than a technical fault, emphasising that they are carried out under pre-established operational rules.

He also warned that another heatwave is expected to sweep across Europe in the coming days, likely increasing electricity demand while causing the Danube’s water level to fall even further.

Extreme heat and drought continue to affect Hungary

According to MVM, the combination of persistent drought and extreme summer temperatures has significantly reduced the Danube’s flow this year.

Environmental regulations limit the temperature of the cooling water discharged back into the river after passing through the reactors. To remain within these limits, the plant has already had to reduce the output of its reactor units on several occasions during June and July.

Meanwhile, the Danube has reached historic lows in Budapest as well. On Tuesday morning, the river gauge measured just 30 centimetres, before falling even further later in the day, according to Telex.

World.title: Romania’s men’s sabre team to compete for bronze medal at 2026 Senior World Fencing Championships
World.content:
Romania’s men’s sabre team will fight for bronze at the World Championships in Hong Kong after losing against South Korea in the semifinals (44-45).

Comprising Vlad Covaliu, Radu Nițu, Răzvan Ursachi and George Dragomir, Romania’s sabre team defeated Italy in the quarter-finals, with a score of 45-36. Previously, Romania’s team had defeated Great Britain (45-17) and Venezuela (45-30).

The Romanian sabre fencers lost by a decisive touch in the semifinal against South Korea, after being led 35-26 at one point. In the second-to-last bout, however, fencer Vlad Covaliu won 12-5, recovering points for Romania.

In the final bout, Radu Nițu entered at 38-40. The score was tied at 44, but Oh Sanguk scored the final touch.

From the stands, Mihai Covaliu, Olympic champion and former coach of the Romanian team that won the world title, constantly encouraged the young sabre fencers, according to the Romanian Fencing Federation.

The Romanian team will face Hungary in the bronze medal match. In the final, South Korea will face France.

The Hong Kong World Championships 2026 brought together over 1400 athletes from 113 nations, all competing for the top spots. Romania already has a bronze medal, through Radu Nițu in men’s sabre.

World.title: Beko upgrades Romania logistics hub with EUR 1.3 mln investment
World.content:
Beko Romania invested approximately EUR 1.3 million to modernize its spare parts logistics hub in Căteasca, Argeș County, doubling its storage capacity and expanding its role within the company's regional after-sales operations. The facility serves 22 markets in Central and Eastern Europe and also ships spare parts to destinations including the United States, China, Morocco, Israel, and South Africa.

The investment included the expansion of the hub's logistics infrastructure, the implementation of a digital warehouse management system E-WMS, the installation of an automated conveyor system, new picking equipment, and upgrades to its Wi-Fi and security infrastructure.

According to the company, the Căteasca hub manages more than 35,000 stock-keeping units, or SKUs, and over 550,000 spare parts. It also supplies Beko's central warehouse in Italy, which serves Western European markets.

The upgraded facility has enabled the introduction of direct-to-consumer (B2C) deliveries and reduced delivery times to 3-4 days for Eastern European markets, from 7-10 days previously. Delivery times for service teams in Romania have been shortened to around 24 hours.

Beko said more than 90% of deliveries are now completed within seven days, while over 70% arrive within two days. Spare parts availability has increased by more than 15%, exceeding 90%, according to the company.

irina.marica@romania-insider.com

(Photo source: press release)

World.title: Western Romania: Art Encounters Foundation eyes further international collaborations with revamped HQ opening
World.content:
The new Art Encounters Foundation center, set to open in September with the exhibition Picasso en visite, will allow the Timișoara-based institution to expand its international collaborations while continuing to support the new generation of artists and curators.

The center, dedicated to contemporary art, education and public engagement, is housed in the building previously known as Casa ISHO.

It will be the first dedicated contemporary art venue in Timișoara built to international museum standards for climate control, security and the conservation of artworks, Art Encounters said. These facilities make it possible to host exhibitions in partnership with leading international museums and collections, opening a new stage in the foundation's exhibition program.

The exhibition Picasso en visite is organized in a partnership with the Musée Picasso in Antibes.

Alongside the exhibition galleries, the center includes an art library and bookshop designed as spaces for research and dialogue, open to artists, students and the wider public. Its education facilities will host year-round activities including workshops for children and schools, family programs, student workshops, adult courses, lectures, book launches and other events dedicated to learning and public engagement.

The ground floor will also house Focus Art Encounters, the foundation's new platform for experimental artistic and curatorial practices. It will present exhibitions, performances, site-specific interventions and interdisciplinary projects developed with artists, curators and researchers from Romania and abroad. Particular attention will be given to emerging artists and collaborations across art, architecture, design, film, literature and new technologies, the foundation explained.

"The opening of the new Art Encounters space allows us to design the foundation's program as an ecosystem in which exhibitions, research, education and experiment reinforce one another. Alongside expanding our international collaborations, we will continue to support a new generation of artists and curators, while the Focus program will provide a dedicated platform for experimental practices and interdisciplinary dialogue. We want Art Encounters to become an active institution where visitors return not only for a single exhibition, but for an ongoing program of encounters with contemporary art," Diana Marincu, the artistic director of the Art Encounters Foundation, said.

The transformation of the headquarters has been designed by Attila KIM Architects. The development and implementation of the ground-floor interior design have been carried out in collaboration with Andreea Andresoiu. Beyond upgrading the building to international museum standards, the project included the installation of a lift and the reconfiguration of visiting routes, and making the venue fully accessible to visitors with disabilities.

"With its new headquarters, the Art Encounters Foundation is contributing to the development of Timișoara's cultural infrastructure by creating a space dedicated to contemporary art, education, and bringing people together. We envision it as a year-round destination, with a continuous program of exhibitions, educational activities and events for audiences of all ages. At the same time, the new venue provides the conditions needed to collaborate with international museums and cultural institutions, strengthening Timișoara's place on the European contemporary art map," Ovidiu Șandor, the founder and president of the Art Encounters Foundation, said.

The building housing the Art Encounters Foundation's permanent headquarters has been made available by the foundation's founder and his family. The transformation and fit-out of the new venue, representing an investment of several hundred thousand euros, has been financed through private funding and contributions from partner companies.

"For years we have built a community around contemporary art and helped establish Timișoara on Romania's and Europe's cultural map through exhibitions, biennials and large-scale projects. Today we are building its home as well: a place where people come for outstanding exhibitions, cultural education, to browse a book in the Art Encounters library, enjoy a conversation over coffee, or simply spend time in an open and welcoming environment," Georgia Bacinschi, director of the Art Encounters Foundation, said.

(Photos: Art Encounters)

World.title: Romanian MPs extend deadline for home purchases eligible for 9% VAT after cyberattack
World.content:
Romania's Chamber of Deputies approved legislation extending the deadline for completing certain home purchases eligible for the reduced 9% VAT rate until September 30, 2026, Agerpres reported. The measure is intended to protect buyers whose transactions were delayed by the recent cyberattack on the National Agency for Cadastre and Land Registration (ANCPI).

Under the bill, individuals who signed preliminary home purchase agreements by July 31, 2025, will be able to complete the acquisition without being subject to the higher VAT rate, provided they meet the eligibility criteria.

The reduced 9% VAT rate will apply to the purchase of a single home with a usable area of up to 120 square metres and a value of no more than RON 600,000, excluding VAT, including the land on which it is built, according to the project. The property must be delivered by September 30, 2026, and be suitable for occupancy under the legal requirements in force when the advance payment agreement was signed.

To qualify, buyers must not have purchased another home using the reduced VAT rate since January 1, 2023, and must have signed a legally binding advance payment agreement for the property before August 1, 2025.

The legislation had already been approved by the Senate. The Chamber of Deputies, which had the final say on the bill, adopted it on Wednesday, July 29, clearing the way for the measure to become law.

World.title: Cluj airport to introduce Fast Track boarding system
World.content:
Cluj International Airport plans to introduce a Fast Track access and verification system designed to speed up boarding and reduce waiting times for passengers. The airport has launched a tender for the project, estimated at RON 1.87 million, as part of its efforts to modernise passenger services.

The new system will consist of two eGate access gates equipped with integrated electronic document readers capable of scanning boarding pass barcodes, according to an announcement by the Cluj County Council.

The same source said the Fast Track system is already widely used at European airports handling more than 2 million passengers annually and will help streamline passenger flows while improving the overall boarding experience.

Alin Tișe, president of the Cluj County Council, said the investment is intended to keep the airport aligned with passengers' growing expectations and strengthen its position as Romania's leading regional airport.

“The acquisition of this rapid access system will help streamline passenger flows, reduce waiting times, and improve comfort for those using our airport. We want every passenger to enjoy the best possible travel experience while further strengthening Avram Iancu Cluj International Airport's position as the country's leading regional airport and an important gateway to Europe," Tișe said.

The investment is part of the airport's broader strategy to modernise its infrastructure.

World.title: Two languages, more ways to understand the world: The benefits of bilingual education in Kindergarten
World.content:
Partner Content

For many families in Bucharest, choosing a kindergarten is no longer only about location, facilities or the daily schedule. Language has become an equally important consideration.

International and mixed-nationality families may be looking for an environment in which their children can continue learning in English while gradually becoming familiar with Romanian. Romanian families, meanwhile, increasingly want their children to develop genuine confidence in English from an early age, not simply by attending several language classes each week, but by using the language naturally throughout the day.



This is where bilingual and English-immersion education can make a meaningful difference.

Young children learn languages through life, not translation



Preschool children do not learn a new language in the same way adults usually do. They acquire it through relationships, routines, stories, movement, play and repeated meaningful experiences.



A child may first understand the English phrase "Let's wash our hands" because it is heard every day before lunch. Later, the child begins to use the same words independently. During play, expressions such as "Can I have this?", "Let's build a house" or "It's my turn" gradually become part of the child's natural communication.



This type of learning is different from memorising vocabulary lists or translating isolated words. Language is connected to an action, an emotion, an object or a relationship. As a result, children understand not only what a word means, but also when and why it is used.



Exposure to two languages in early childhood does not inherently confuse children. Research shows that young children are able to distinguish between the languages they hear and can learn the sounds and patterns of both. Their vocabulary may sometimes be distributed between the two languages, knowing certain words in one language and others in the second, but their total language knowledge should be considered across both.

Communication before perfection



One of the most valuable outcomes of early bilingual education is not flawless pronunciation or an impressive vocabulary at the age of four. It is the confidence to communicate.



In a well-designed bilingual environment, children are not constantly corrected or placed under pressure to produce the "right" answer. They are encouraged to participate, express a need, share an idea, ask a question and join a game.



At first, a child may respond through gestures, facial expressions or a combination of languages. This is a natural stage of language development. With consistent exposure and sensitive support from teachers, comprehension usually develops before speaking fluency.



Over time, children begin to experiment with the new language. They repeat familiar phrases, combine words, initiate conversations and eventually communicate with increasing independence.



This confidence is particularly important for children growing up in international communities. Language becomes more than an academic skill, it becomes a means of building friendships, adapting to new environments and feeling that they belong.

Bilingual education can encourage flexible thinking



Moving between two languages requires children to notice context: who they are speaking to, which words are appropriate and how the same idea can be expressed differently.



Researchers continue to debate whether bilingualism creates a universal cognitive advantage, and the evidence should not be overstated. Some studies, however, suggest that bilingual experience may support areas such as attentional control, inhibition and cognitive flexibility, particularly when children use both languages regularly and meaningfully. Other reviews have found mixed results, indicating that benefits depend on factors such as proficiency, frequency of use and the child's wider educational environment.



The clearest everyday benefit can often be observed without a test: bilingual children learn that there may be more than one way to name, explain or understand something.



This awareness can help nurture openness, adaptability and curiosity about people whose experiences differ from their own.

The quality of the educational experience still matters most



Simply exposing children to English does not automatically create a strong bilingual programme.



The quality of early education continues to depend on the relationships children build with adults, the relevance of the learning experiences, the teachers' understanding of child development and the emotional safety of the environment.



Young children acquire language most effectively when they feel secure enough to take risks. They need teachers who notice when they are ready to speak, when they need visual support, when they require repetition and when they understand more than they can yet express.



They also need opportunities to use language for a genuine purpose.



At kindergarten, these opportunities arise through role play, stories, music, construction, outdoor exploration, creative projects, scientific investigation and everyday problem-solving. A child who is designing a bridge with classmates has a real reason to discuss size, shape, balance and possible solutions. A child investigating insects in the garden has a reason to observe, describe, compare and ask questions.



Language learning becomes stronger because it is part of a broader learning experience.

Two language pathways at Genesis College



At Genesis College, families can choose between two Early Years pathways, depending on the linguistic environment they want for their child.



The standard bilingual programme is designed for families who value education in both Romanian and English. Children develop their communication skills in the two languages within a learning environment shaped by play, inquiry and meaningful daily interaction.



English is integrated into the children's experience rather than treated only as an isolated subject. At the same time, Romanian remains an important language for communication, relationships and learning. This pathway may be particularly suitable for Romanian families seeking strong, natural exposure to English while maintaining a solid connection to the child's first language, as well as for international families who want their children to gradually become comfortable using Romanian.



As a novelty, beginning with the 2026-2027 school year, Genesis College is introducing the English Immersion Programme, created for families who want their child's entire educational experience to unfold in English.



In this programme, English is the language through which children learn, play, build relationships, investigate ideas and understand the world. It is not simply taught; it is lived throughout the kindergarten day.



The programme follows the International Baccalaureate Primary Years Programme framework and is delivered by a dedicated team of educators with experience in IB PYP implementation and English-language learning environments.



Both pathways share the same educational philosophy. Learning is personalised around each child's interests, developmental stage and individual rhythm. Play is treated as a central form of learning, while care, emotional wellbeing and secure relationships provide the foundation from which children can explore with confidence.

"For us, bilingual education is not about asking children to perform in a second language before they are ready. It is about creating an environment in which language becomes useful, meaningful and connected to real experiences. When children feel safe, cared for and genuinely interested in what they are doing, they begin to communicate naturally. Our responsibility is to offer them both the confidence and the opportunities to do so." said Elena Mănescu, Kindergarten Principal at Genesis College.

Learning beyond the classroom



Drawing on 26 years of educational excellence, Genesis College has carefully designed learning environments that reflect decades of expertise in supporting children's holistic development, ensuring every space is purposefully created to inspire curiosity, exploration and meaningful learning.



The physical environment also plays an important role in the Genesis Early Years experience.



Children have access to a generous 5,000-square-metre outdoor area, offering space for movement, free play, nature exploration and learning outside the classroom. Outdoor experiences provide rich opportunities for language development: children negotiate games, describe discoveries, collaborate on projects and communicate in spontaneous, authentic situations.



The campus also includes the Genesis Discovery Centre, a STEAM learning space created specifically for preschool children.



Its areas, including the Tech & Construction Lab, Nature & Art Studio, Journey of Discovery Hallway and Soft Play Room, invite children to build, experiment, create, collaborate and move. In both the bilingual and English-immersion pathways, these experiences create natural contexts in which children use language to develop ideas rather than merely demonstrate vocabulary.

Which programme is right for each family?



There is no single language pathway that suits every child.



A bilingual programme may be the right choice for families who want children to develop naturally in both Romanian and English and to feel equally connected to the local and international dimensions of their community.



An English-immersion programme may better suit international families, children preparing for an English-language school pathway or Romanian families seeking an educational environment conducted entirely in English.



Parents should consider the languages already used at home, the child's previous exposure, the family's longer-term educational plans and, importantly, the type of environment in which the child feels most secure.



Whichever pathway they choose, the goal should extend beyond producing children who can speak another language. High-quality early bilingual education can help children become confident communicators, attentive listeners and curious learners, children who understand from an early age that the world can be described in more than one language and viewed from more than one perspective.

World.title: Over 88,000 students from 150 countries apply for study scholarships in Romania in 2026
World.content:
Over 88,000 young people from more than 150 countries and five continents applied this year for a study scholarship in Romania, according to an announcement made by interim foreign minister Oana Țoiu on Wednesday, July 29.

The number of applications is more than 19 times higher than four years ago and represents a record.

“I looked twice. 88,795 applications, from five continents. Young people from distant places chose to submit their applications to study here, with us,” the minister said on Facebook.

Most foreign applicants are from Pakistan (14,515), Afghanistan (8,956), Bangladesh (8,916), Nigeria (4,524), Siria (3,257), Palestina (2,677), Ciad (2,488), Indonesia (2,417), Ethiopia (2,408), and Somalia (2,108).

“What do these young people see in Romania? Beyond a country that deserves to be known, they see universities that train engineers, doctors, lawyers, IT professionals and artists, but also a chance to build their future starting from here. They most likely also see our progress over the last 30 years and, certainly, our membership in the European Union,” Țoiu emphasized.

The official said that after all stages of interinstitutional validation of the selection carried out by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs are completed, the final results will reach all candidates, and those selected will study, based on the Romanian Government scholarship, in university centers across the country.

“In a few years, many of them will return home with a Romanian diploma and with a lifelong connection to our country, while others will remain bridges between Romania and the places they came from. With these scholarships, we open new doors, connect people and build trust in Romania. And a scholarship for a young person thousands of kilometers away is one of the best investments we can make,” she concluded.

World.title: Ukraine’s Biofarma reportedly doubles investment in Romanian plants at EUR 85 mln
World.content:
Ukrainian plasma-derived drugs producer Biofarma has doubled its planned investment in a pharmaceutical plant in Oradea, western Romania, with the first stage of the project now valued at EUR 85 million, Bihoreanul reported, cited by Economedia.ro.

The investment is EUR 48 million above the minimum amount announced in 2024, when the construction of the pharmaceutical factory was presented as the largest investment of that year in the industrial parks managed by the Oradea Local Development Agency.

The Oradea project is planned in four stages, according to Biofarma representatives cited by Interfax-Ukraine. The company has not disclosed the total value of the investment, providing only the cost of bringing the first stage into operation.

"We have already completed the construction of the building, and by September 1 we will finish connecting the entire engineering infrastructure. We have already ordered the filling line," Biofarma Plasma President Kostiantyn Yefymenko told Ukrainian media.

The first stage will involve putting the production line into operation. The facility is planned to have the capacity to process up to 1.2 million litres of frozen human plasma a year.

Biofarma was founded in 1965 and initially focused on developing technologies for the production of plasma-derived medicines. The company describes itself as operating one of the largest plasma fractionation facilities in Eastern Europe.

The Oradea plant forms part of Biofarma’s expansion outside Ukraine, with the investment adding pharmaceutical production capacity in Romania.
