World.title: Before China’s First Emperor: Unearthing the Long Rise of the Qin
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018803/Before China’s First Emperor: Unearthing the Long Rise of the Qin
World.content:
Wang Hui still remembers everything about the sensational tomb-robbing scandal that launched his career.

It was the early 1990s, barely a decade into China’s transition from planned to market economy, and grave robbing had become a lucrative cottage industry in the Chinese countryside — a rare way for villagers to get rich. So when a local farmer in northwestern China’s Gansu province uncovered bronzes while digging for oracle bones, it kicked off a feeding frenzy.

The looters who descended on the site — now known as Dabuzi — were embedded in a highly specialized chain covering target scouting, excavation, transportation, trafficking, and smuggling. At its peak, there were reportedly tens of thousands of grave robbers and dealers in Dabuzi and the surrounding Lixian County. Their numbers were so great that they generated entire side businesses, with people setting up camp near the tombs to sell them water, food, and cigarettes.

Finally, in 1993, the problem became too big to ignore. After the influential China Youth Daily published a shocking expose on the extent of the problem — priceless artifacts being sold off for pennies on the dollar and entire tomb complexes stripped bare — the Gansu provincial government dispatched an archaeological team to the area to crack down on looting and salvage what they could.

“When we arrived, the entire area looked like a battlefield, full of massive pits,” recalls Wang, a member of the archaeological rescue team and now a professor at Shanghai’s Fudan University. “As we dug, we used the cigarette boxes we found inside the tombs to guess who had been there. Expensive ‘Hongtashan’ and ‘Ashima’ brand cigarettes — those were probably smoked by antiquities dealers. ‘Benma’ and ‘Fenghu’ were for the local villagers, while cheap brands from elsewhere meant laborers from across China.”

The looting of Dabuzi was catastrophic: It scattered countless artifacts across the world and triggered nearly two decades of repatriation work by Chinese authorities. But northern China is filled with ancient burial sites, and there was little reason at first to think the tombs themselves were of any special importance.

It was only after the team started digging that they realized the robbers had stumbled onto one of the most important Chinese archaeological discoveries of the past century: the Xichui necropolis, the first royal burial ground of the Qin people.

Although famous for unifying China after the chaos of the Warring States period (475–221 BC), very little is known about the Qin’s early history. Originating in a remote backwater far from China’s ancient heartland, the Central Plains, they appear only rarely in surviving histories from the period.

That left historians and archaeologists to piece together fragmentary evidence from oracle bones and bronze inscriptions. In this context, the discovery of Xichui changed everything, bringing new attention — and new resources — to a millennia-old mystery: Why was it the Qin, and not any of their rivals, that unified China?

Holes in the history books

In 230 BC, a Qin army swept out of the Hangu Pass and into the Central Plains, the heartland of Chinese civilization.

Over the next nine years, the other six of China’s seven remaining Warring States fell, one by one. By 221 BC, only Qin remained. With China unified for the first time in centuries, the Qin king proclaimed a new dynasty — and gave himself the title of Qinshihuang, or the Qin’s “first emperor.”

Qinshihuang’s empire would outlive him by only four years, collapsing in 206 BC before being replaced by the longer-lived Han dynasty (206 BC–AD 220). But the title — and the scope of his conquests, which stretched from Liaoning in the northeast to the coast of the Gulf of Tonkin in the south — would largely endure for the next two millennia.

The speed of the Qin’s rise was extraordinary, and the reasons for it have been the subject of intense debate among generations of Chinese scholars.

But due to a lack of textual sources from the Qin itself, the terms of this debate were largely set by later histories — most notably Sima Qian’s monumental “Records of the Grand Historian” and Jia Yi’s celebrated essay “On the Faults of Qin,” both written during the ensuing Han.

These accounts, composed well after the fact, generally attribute the Qin’s success to the “Shang Yang reforms”: a series of institutional and economic policies promoted by the fourth-century BC Legalist philosopher Shang Yang. Together, they are credited with growing the Qin’s population, strengthening its military, and making the Qin the most powerful of the Warring States.

If that narrative seems too tidy — a single set of reforms magically transforming a poor state into the most powerful war machine in Asia — many historians would agree. The Qin’s rise from a marginal tribal polity to the state that unified China took more than eight centuries. By the time of Shang Yang’s reforms, Qin was already a major player in Warring States-era politics.

Nor was Shang Yang the only reformer of the Warring States era. But his reforms took root in a way few others did. Why? What was Qin like before he came on the scene? And how was it, unlike the other states, able to break the stalemate and impose its will across China?

The lack of reliable sources hasn’t stopped modern scholars from trying to reconstruct early Qin history. As early as a century ago, the great historian Wang Guowei attempted to apply his famous “dual evidence method” — corroborating transmitted texts with newly unearthed materials such as oracle bone and bronze inscriptions — to trace how the Qin people gradually expanded eastward.

Yet, with little archaeological evidence to go on, research into Qin’s early and middle periods remained stalled for decades — until the tomb-robbing incident at Dabuzi.

It took nearly a decade to confirm the site as the Qin royal tombs, but with Xichui as a starting point, Chinese archaeologists could finally begin systematically tracing Qin history.

Progress was fast. In 2004, shortly after returning to China from doctoral studies in Japan, Wang — then deputy director of the Gansu Provincial Institute of Cultural Relics and Archaeology — formally launched the “Early Qin Culture Archaeological Survey, Excavation, and Research Project.” In the decades since, archaeologists have made rapid progress: uncovering the earliest known Qin remains, pinpointing the first county ever established by the Qin, and identifying most of the nine capitals founded by the Qin as they pushed eastward from the western frontier into the Central Plains.

And the more Qin relics they uncover, the more archaeologists and historians have come to question the picture painted by Sima Qian and Jia Yi.

“Tigers and wolves”

For most Chinese people, the phrase that comes to mind when speaking of the Qin is “a state of tigers and wolves.”

Sima Qian was the first to use the term in relation to the Qin. In his “Records of the Grand Historian,” the phrase appears twice. The first time, it’s attributed to the great poet Qu Yuan, then serving as a minister to a rival state, who uses it to try to dissuade his king from making an official visit to Qin. Later, Su Qin, a Warring States strategist, invokes the same label to rally the other six states into a last-ditch alliance against the Qin’s overwhelming power.

But how did Qin become such a formidable opponent?

Historical texts provide only a sketchy account. Sima Qian, for instance, describes the Qin’s origins as follows: The distant ancestors of the Qin people were descended from Zhuanxu, grandson of the Yellow Emperor and one of China’s legendary Five Emperors. They had once been a major tribe under the Shang (c. 1600–1046 BC) kings before being relocated to the western frontier after the rise of the Western Zhou dynasty (c. 1046–771 BC).

During this period, a chieftain of this tribe, Feizi, was granted the fief of Qin in recognition of his skill in horse breeding. After the Western Zhou fell, Duke Xiang of Qin escorted the Zhou king to the new capital and was enfeoffed as a feudal lord, officially making Qin one of the states of the Eastern Zhou (c. 770–256 BC).

The archaeological record backs up some of these details. To start, early Qin material culture shows clear links to the Shang and Zhou. The layout of Qin ancestral temples, the style of its palace architecture, and the types of bronze ritual vessels used all follow Zhou tradition, while its large burial pits — including dog sacrifices, chariot-and-horse pits, and even human sacrifices — reflect Shang practice.

But archaeologists have found something else: evidence that the Qin people intermingled closely with the various non-Chinese tribes known as the “Western Rong.”

“Rong” was a broad term used by people of the Central Plains to describe various non-Zhou groups, many of which were quite different from each other.

One of the most important of these was the Bronze Age Siwa culture, centered in what is today southern Gansu.

Current archaeological evidence suggests that, after the Qin moved west, they developed a close but complicated relationship with the Siwa and other tribes inhabiting the region, one that gradually evolved from coexistence to conflict and finally to Qin domination.

When the Qin first moved westward, they initially settled in the Liya site in present-day Qingshui County, Gansu. It was at Liya — currently the earliest identified Qin cultural site — that Liang Yun, a professor at Northwest University and a key member of the Early Qin Culture Project, unearthed a paired burial containing the bodies of a man and a woman.

The woman’s grave contained Qin-style pottery, while the man’s contained Siwa-style artifacts — an arrangement that Liang believes points to intermarriage between Qin and Siwa peoples.

“When the Qin first arrived (in Gansu), they had little foundation there and could only survive in regions where indigenous power was relatively weak,” he says. “This burial indicates that relations between the Qin and Siwa populations were relatively harmonious at the time — or at the very least, there was intermarriage.”

But circumstances changed after the Qin expanded further into nearby Lixian. Unlike Qingshui, Lixian was densely populated by Siwa communities and rich in resources such as salt, gold, and copper. Competition over land and mineral wealth between Qin and Siwa led to repeated clashes and eventually resulted in the extermination of the Qin branch living in Lixian, Liang says.

Fortunately for the Qin, another Qin group had remained in Qingshui. Their leader secured military support from the Zhou, then led the Qin back into Lixian, where he avenged their defeat and established a new capital.

From that point onward, Qin gradually subdued the Siwa, either destroying them outright or incorporating them into Qin rule.

Liang argues that this experience — and later, frequent warfare against nomadic peoples looking to expand from the Eurasian steppe — left Qin fundamentally different from the more established states of the Central Plains.

The Qin’s rise was extraordinarily difficult; its territory had to be seized bit by bit from western tribes, and several Qin rulers died in battle. “The Qin were deeply committed to militarism and expansion,” Liang says. “If you compare a state to a person, then the Qin’s interactions with the Western Rong were its childhood experiences — they shaped its ‘cultural genes.’”

In other words, Qin had already developed a strongly militarized culture more than four centuries before Shang Yang’s reforms.

“Many people see Shang Yang’s reforms as the cause of the Qin’s rise,” Liang adds. “In reality, they were the result. Why did (the Qin leaders) embrace Shang Yang? Why were these reforms successful in Qin? Because the conditions were already there. Qin’s political culture was inherently suited to strengthening centralized authority and military power.”

From west to east

The Qin were certainly adept at warfare, but wanting to unify the realm was one thing — actually achieving it was another. So how did Qin pull off the impossible: vanquishing multiple entrenched rivals in a series of devastating campaigns, all in just a decade?

Once again, the answer may lie in the soil of China’s northwest.

Among the major Warring States, the Qin are often portrayed as the most geographically marginalized. Although Qin’s rivals recognized its military strength, the elites of China’s Central Plains regarded it as uncivilized and culturally backward — a belief that persisted even as the Qin expanded inexorably eastward.

But this belief, dutifully recorded and largely accepted as true by later historians, is being overturned by recent archaeological discoveries. What the Central Plains states saw as “uncultured” may in fact have been the fruit of Qin cultural and technological exchanges with Eurasian steppe cultures.

Long before the Han dynasty envoy Zhang Qian opened formal diplomatic contact with Central Asia in the second century BC — generally viewed as the beginning of the Silk Road and China’s integration into Eurasian trade networks — early Chinese states had begun developing commercial and cultural ties with the steppe.

And the Qin stood at a pivotal node on this East-West corridor. What eastern elites considered the periphery may have actually been a central location in an emerging cross-continent exchange of technologies and ideas.

For example, archaeological evidence shows that, while the Central Plains states remained fixated on traditional materials like bronze and jade, the Qin had developed a taste for the gold artifacts popular on the Eurasian steppe.

Likewise, Qin animal motifs tended toward naturalism, in stark contrast to the abstract, stylized animal decoration found on Central Plains ritual vessels of the same era. In the sacrificial pits at the Emperor Qinshihuang’s Mausoleum Site Museum, archaeologists have found 46 examples of bronze waterfowl — swans, geese, and cranes — each life‑size, posed differently, and strikingly realistic. Even more remarkable is a solid gold camel figurine, so finely wrought that even its toenails are perfectly realized.

The influence of steppe cultures wasn’t limited to art. The Qin’s position also gave them a crucial technological edge.

Take metallurgy, for example. The Qin were early adopters of multiple important metalworking techniques. For centuries, the Central Plains region had favored the “lost-wax casting method” for casting ceremonial and military objects: melting metal, pouring it into a mold, and allowing it to cool and solidify. But gold pieces unearthed from Dabuzi demonstrate Qin mastery of a different process: the repoussé technique, in which gold is heated until soft and repeatedly hammered to stretch it into thin sheets or into the desired shape.

Breakthroughs in one area spawned others. Beyond metallurgy, the Qin built large-scale water conservancy projects such as the Zhengguo Canal and Dujiangyan — still functional today — which dramatically boosted agricultural yields. They invented the two-shaft chariot and introduced the “exotic livestock” of the northwest — donkeys and mules — as pack animals, improving carrying capacity and efficiency. Their craftspeople also invented new materials, including “Chinese purple,” a synthetic pigment that requires precise control of firing temperature and proportions of raw material to produce.

According to research by Wang Zijin of Northwest University, by the late Warring States era, Qin held a leading position over the other six states in multiple technological fields, including water conservation, transportation, and machinery.

They also had a highly advanced state system that enabled the deployment of these technologies at scale.

Archaeologists have found evidence of an early quality-control process known as wu le qi ming, in which artisans were required to carve their names on the objects they produced so their supervisors could trace each item back to its creator.

Perhaps the best-known example is the “Lü Buwei Halberd,” forged in the second half of the first millennium BC. Its inscription identifies four individuals involved in the weapon’s manufacture: the highest supervising official, the workshop master, the workshop assistant, and the individual craftsman who produced it, suggesting that Qin weapons production operated under a highly structured chain of accountability.

Excavations at the Emperor Qinshihuang’s Mausoleum Site have likewise shown that Qin bronze trigger mechanisms were produced to tight specifications. Components made by the same workshop group were interchangeable, while different types of crossbows were distributed systematically across different sections of the battle formation. This suggests that Qin had achieved standardized, interchangeable, large-scale weapons production — a factor now regarded as a key military advantage in Qin’s wars of unification.

“In my view, Qin’s greatest technological advantage over the six states was not any single invention, but the establishment of a large-scale standardized production system,” says Qian Wei, Dean of the Institute for Cultural Heritage and History of Science & Technology at the University of Science and Technology Beijing. “That organizational innovation was the decisive factor behind Qin’s victory.”

Systemic change

The Qin’s moment of glory lasted less than a quarter-century: a decade to conquer the six Warring States, then 15 years for it to all fall apart.

Yet the Qin’s legacy has endured — its achievements and failings remembered, debated, and ceaselessly revisited.

That’s not just because it was the first empire to unify much of what is today China, or because of its standardization of writing, currency, and weights and measures. Much of its importance stems from its political system, which centralized imperial authority through a commandery-county administrative structure — a governing logic that would shape China for more than two millennia.

Unlike the nobility-based system of the earlier Zhou dynasty, which was based on blood ties, the commandery‑county system was centrally administered. Officials at all levels were directly appointed, evaluated, and transferred by the central government. That allowed central power to reach down through the bureaucratic apparatus, from prefecture to county to township to village, and from there to every household in China.

The question of how this system evolved has long puzzled scholars, with some arguing it wasn’t an indigenous invention at all, but another technology the Qin borrowed from the Western regions — specifically the Achaemenid Persian Empire.

This seemingly far-fetched idea has a certain logic. If the Qin interacted extensively with the Western Rong and other steppe nomads during its rise, then it may also have encountered — directly or indirectly — civilizations further west.

The late Sinologist Jao Tsung-I was one of the first to suggest there may have been some connection between Qin and the Achaemenids. As evidence, he pointed to a linguistic coincidence. After unifying China, Qin referred to commoners as qianshou (“black-headed people”), a phrase previously unseen in Chinese sources. In the Cyrus Cylinder, created in the 6th century BC in honor of the Persian conquest of Babylon, Persian subjects are likewise referred to as “black-headed people.”

Does that mean the Qin had been influenced by Persian norms? Jao chose his words carefully, merely expressing “some suspicion” of a link between the two, without reaching a firm conclusion.

Another scholar, the late Duan Qingbo — former director of the excavation team at the Emperor Qinshihuang’s Mausoleum Site Museum — was bolder. He repeatedly proposed that the political civilization of the Persian Empire may have influenced the Qin’s imperial institutions. In his view, Qin policies such as the commandery-county system, codified laws, imperial roads and relay stations, the standardization of weights and measures, script unification, the use of grandiose imperial titles, and the implementation of large-scale construction projects all bore striking similarities to the policies of the Persian king Darius I (c. 550–486 BC).

But Duan’s views have gained little support from other scholars.

According to Wang, the founder of the Early Qin Culture Project, similarities between the two empires merely reflect the comparable challenges they faced. Both Qinshihuang and Darius I ruled vast territories populated by diverse peoples and cultures. Given the circumstances, centralization was a natural choice, as were standardization, road construction, legal codes, and other forms of administrative integration.

“Look at the roads, for example,” Wang says. “The Roman Empire also built extensive road systems. Does that mean Rome copied Persia?”

Wang adds that many core features of Qin political culture took shape in the state’s early developmental stages. Take its approach to ethnic conflict: Through centuries of exchange and warfare with the Western Rong, the Qin developed a sophisticated approach to managing conquered populations. What began as military conquest and forced relocation gradually expanded to include conciliation, trade, and reward systems. Administratively, the Qin governed tribes through specialized structures, including subordinate states and frontier districts known as dao.

“This approach was later used extensively during Qin’s unification of China,” Wang notes.

Northwest University’s Liang acknowledges that the Qin likely did have some exchanges with Central and Western Asia. At Yuandingshan cemetery in Lixian, for example, archaeologists unearthed a bronze model chariot with wheels that suggest it was Central or Western Asian in origin.

“But that’s it,” Liang says. “Aside from a few luxury items, there is no evidence that the Qin Empire was influenced by Persia.”

More evidence can be found in the Qin’s burial customs. Funerary rituals often reflect core aspects of a people’s identity. “The state religion of Persia was Zoroastrianism, which holds that burying corpses pollutes the earth,” Liang says. “That is why Persian royal tombs are cut into rock. In stark contrast, Qin tombs were dug deep into the earth — the deeper, the better. The two worldviews are polar opposites.”

As for the commandery-county system, Liang has no doubt it was a Qin invention. In fact, he led the archaeological team that identified the first-ever county established by the Qin. “That was more than 2,700 years ago,” he notes. “More than a century before Darius I.”

Liang is more interested in other questions, such as where the Qin originally lived and how they served the Shang. And while scholars now have a relatively clear picture of the Qin’s repeated capital relocations during its eastward expansion, the locations of one or two capitals remain debated.

These questions have been unresolved for centuries, but new archaeological discoveries are finally putting them within reach.

“Don’t be impatient,” Liang says. “Remember, the Early Qin Culture project has only been going on for a little over two decades — that is far too short by archaeological standards. The Qin people walked a path of more than 800 years.”

Visuals: Ding Yining and Fu Xiaofan.

(Header image: Visuals from the Shanghai Museum, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.title: Who comes after MVP? Pangilinan has successors in mind.
World.content:
The 80-year-old tycoon says the next crop of leaders will be in their 30s or early 40s, adding that they can't be 'the run-of-the-mill legacy guys majored in HRM or home economics'

Manuel V. Pangilinan has spent decades assembling one of the country’s most diversified business groups.

Now, the time to pass the reins on to the next generation is nearing. And he already has a list of names.

“I just spoke to the HR people this morning. I said, we need to identify the first ones down. And name them,” he said in a mix of English and Filipino as reporters huddled around him. “And then the second down from my level, we will name them. I have a few names already, younger people.”

His remarks came during a Meralco briefing on Wednesday, July 29, but the succession question extends far beyond the distribution giant because Pangilinan continues to hold top positions across the wider MVP group.

Unlike the family empires of the Sys, Gokongweis, or Aboitizes, the MVP group is not housed under a single listed conglomerate. It’s a web of companies anchored on telecommunications giants PLDT and Smart, Meralco, and its power generation arm MGen, and Metro Pacific Investments Corporation’s interests in toll roads, Maynilad, hospitals, property, and agriculture.

Pangilinan also chairs Philex Mining and PXP Energy. His media interests, meanwhile, run through MediaQuest Holdings, whose portfolio includes TV5, Cignal, The Philippine Star, BusinessWorld, Radyo5, One News, and One Sports.

To put it in terms familiar to the basketball-loving Pangilinan, succession may be less about singing out one MVP and more about assembling an all-star team to lead his companies across vastly different boards, shareholders, and industries.

The 80-year old tycoon already had some difficulty leaving his biggest posts in the past. He stepped down as PLDT president and chief executive officer in 2021, only to return in 2024 after his successor, Al Panlilio, resigned for health reasons. (READ: Wanted: Manny Pangilinan’s replacement)

But the veteran businessman already has a profile in mind.

“Probably in their 30s and early 40s. And they have to be IT-oriented, right?” he said. “They can’t be the run-of-the-mill legacy guys majored in HRM or home economics.”

The jab at “legacy” managers and non-technology degree programs was blunt. The next crop of leaders will be young and digitally fluent. After all, the group is going big into cutting-edge technologies — everything from AI-ready data centers, large-scale renewable energy projects, and electric vehicle charging networks. (READ: [Finterest] Want to invest in data centers? Watch out for PLDT’s VITRO REIT)

Meralco: Solar roofs, EV chargers

In the meantime, MVP is still getting busy. He’s already charted out where Meralco’s growth in the next few years could come from.

Pangilinan said the “intrusion of solar power” partly explained tepid electricity-volume growth in the first half. Rooftop systems allow homes and businesses to draw less electricity from the grid, slowly chipping away at the utility’s conventional market.

But instead of resisting that shift, Pangilinan wants Meralco to lean into it. “It’s important that Meralco gets into solarization rooftops in a big way because you don’t need a franchise to solarize Cebu City, Davao City, wherever,” he said.

Rooftop solar would also let Meralco expand outside the geographic boundaries of its distribution franchise. The commercial and industrial market would be the easier first target: there are fewer customers, but each consumes significantly more power. Households offer the larger mass market, although Pangilinan acknowledged that serving them would be operationally harder because of installations and varying local permit requirements.

The other big bet is electric vehicles.

“The company that is best able to build a network of charging stations is Meralco, right? Not only in its franchise area but elsewhere,” Pangilinan said, adding that a separate unit had been created for the business.

Meralco plans to initially pursue companies with large fleets of cars, taxis, buses, or jeepneys. A single customer operating hundreds or thousands of vehicles could create far more electricity demand than scattered individual motorists, making fleet charging a quicker route to scale.

A battle between two jumbo listings

Pangilinan is also standing his ground on VITRO REIT, PLDT’s proposed data center real estate investment trust, even as it risks competing for investor funds with the much larger GCash offering.

VITRO REIT is seeking to raise up to P24.2 billion from an initial portfolio of eight income-generating data centers. The listing would make it the country’s first digital infrastructure REIT.

GCash parent Mynt, meanwhile, is preparing a share sale of as much as P92.3 billion, potentially the largest initial public offering in Philippine history.

The timing has prompted questions over whether the local market has enough liquidity to absorb both within a tight window.

Asked whether PLDT would consider giving way to the GCash listing, Pangilinan pointed to VITRO’s position in the queue. “Nauna kami. (We were first.) I understand we will be first,” he said. “So far as we’re concerned, we’re pushing the REIT.”

In other matters, Pangilinan may soon have one fewer billionaires in his orbit.

Batangas Representative Leandro Leviste founded SP New Energy Corporation and built a fortune by selling down his holdings to the Meralco group. Meralco now controls the listed solar company and its flagship MTerra Solar project, while Leviste remains a minority shareholder.

It has not been an entirely trouble-free partnership. Leviste’s broader Solar Philippines group was slapped with around P24 billion in penalties after the Department of Energy canceled several contracts over projects it failed to deliver. The Ombudsman has also investigated allegations that a congressional franchise was effectively transferred to the Pangilinan group without congressional approval. Leviste has denied selling an active franchise, arguing that the company holding it had already ceased operations.

Now, Leviste’s remaining financial link to the MVP group could be loosened.

“He’s still there, but I understand he’s talking to several people about disposing his shares — some or all of his shares,” Pangilinan said, keeping his remarks brief. “We’re not party to that discussion.” – Rappler.com

World.title: Japan quake survivors battle thirst, heat as death toll rises to 25
World.content:
KEEPING SAFE. Hirosuke Shimada (46), his wife Yuka (45) and their daughters Tsugumi (3), Nana (14) and Mizuki (16) have lunch inside a tent in front of their house as they are concerned about aftershocks after a magnitude 7.1 earthquake struck Japan's southern Kumamoto prefecture, amid water outages in the area during a heatwave, in Yatsushiro, Japan, July 30, 2026.

Many of the port city's roughly 58,000 households are still without running water or power

YATSUSHIRO, Japan – The magnitude 7.1 earthquake that struck southern Japan toppled houses and split open streets in the small city of Yatsushiro, but there was mounting concern about invisible threats from the lack of water and power amid the punishing summer heat.

Many of the port city’s roughly 58,000 households were still without running water or power on Thursday, July 30, two days since the quake hit Kumamoto prefecture killing at least 25 people.

Akio Matsushita, a local officialhelping lead relief efforts, said he had no idea whether it would take days, weeks or months to repair the badly damaged water mains.

“Because of the summer heat, the lack of water is especially difficult,” he said in the city hall.

With the city hall’s toilets out of order, officials erected emergency toilets over sewer manholes outside the building, in temperatures of around 35 degrees Celsius (95 degrees Fahrenheit) and stifling humidity.

“It will require painstaking work, and there is currently no timetable,” Matsushita added.

A Kyushu Electric Power representative said the utility was aiming to restore power by Friday evening.

Death toll climbs

The Kumamoto prefectural government said the death toll from the earthquake was now at 25 — the majority of them at Nippon Paper Industries’ paper mill, which suffered major structural damage, and at Aeon’s shopping mall, where a possible gas explosion occurred.

Nine other deaths in the prefecture were being investigated to ascertain if they were linked to the quake, it said.

One of the victims of the quake was a newlywed Vietnamese factory worker, survived by his wife and seven-month-old baby, according to Vietnamese news site Kenh14.

In an interview with the news site, Vu Thi Thuy recalled her last conversation with her husband the night before the tremor struck.

“Every time we video-called, my son never wanted to look at his dad but that night, for some reason, he stayed glued to the screen, wanting to be with his dad,” she said. “It was after 11 p.m. when I finally told him, ‘Let’s hang up so dad can get some sleep. He has to work tomorrow.’ I never imagined that would be our last call.”

Authorities warn of heat stroke

While rescue and relief efforts continue, a Kumamoto official warned of the risk of heat stroke with temperatures that were forecast to reach close to 40 degrees Celsius at the weekend. The Self-Defense Forces (SDF) — Japan’s military — is installing about 300 air-conditioning units in evacuation centers and other key sites around Kumamoto.

Immediately after the quake, SDF trucks towed water tanks to community centres and schools across Yatsushiro city, returning to city hall to refill from emergency tanks beneath the building. Residents were limited to 5 liters each.

Among them was Masahiro Miyamoto, who had been helping clear rubble from a temple gate that had toppled.

He returned home after the late-afternoon quake to find his house still standing beside the collapsed remains of his neighbour’s home. But with no running water, he was forced to rely on military water tankers.

The few shops still open were packed with people searching for supplies, he said, while cars formed long queues at petrol stations.

“It would be better if disasters did not happen, but this is Japan, so perhaps it is something we simply have to live with,” Miyamoto said.

Production halt hits major manufacturers

Japan sits on the Pacific “Ring of Fire,” an arc of volcanoes and ocean trenches that account for about one-fifth of the world’s large earthquakes. Strict building standards and regular disaster drills reduce casualties, but powerful tremors can still cripple the regions in which they occur.

Kumamoto and other parts of the Kyushu region have increasingly become key production sites for automobiles and semiconductors, raising concerns over a possible hit to the economy.

Tuesday’s quake has forced manufacturers such as Toyota, Honda, Nissan, Aisin, and Sony to halt some production and prompted Taiwan’s TSMC to evacuate workers and briefly suspend operations to assess any damage.

Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said it was difficult to estimate the impact on the economy now.

“Our immediate priority is to restore and repair infrastructure, including ports and other key facilities. We will also closely monitor the impact on economic activity, particularly supply chains in sectors such as semiconductors and automobiles,” he told reporters.

Miyamoto and many residents of Yatsushiro and nearby Kumamoto city have endured major earthquakes before. Two powerful quakes in April 2016 killed more than 260 people and destroyed thousands of homes.

But Tuesday’s shaking, which toppled shelves and hurled computers to the floor, was worse in Yatsushiro than anything Matsushita experienced a decade ago.

“I had never experienced the world moving like that before. It felt as though my body became weightless and was thrown through the air,” Miyamoto said. – Rappler.com

World.title: 10 years after Arbitral Award, marine scientists still await programmed funding
World.content:
CELEBRATE. Fisherfolk on their boats form the colors of the Philippine flag as they kick off the commemoration of the 10th anniversary of the Philippines’ landmark 2016 Arbitral Ruling, in Zambales on July 5, 2026.

Is the President’s passion for the West Philippine Sea cause commensurate to the support Filipino marine scientists are getting?

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. ended his State of the Nation Address with an impassioned vow to “do all that is necessary” to uphold the 2016 Arbitral Tribunal Award, proof of the Philippines’ victory against China’s claims in the South China Sea.

Marcos thanked the Armed Forces, the Coast Guard, and the small fisherfolk who “patrol and ply our seas in the face of great risks.”

A day after Marcos gave his speech at the Batasan, Filipino marine scientists gathered in Quezon City to celebrate the 10th anniversary of the Arbitral Award. Science has helped the Philippine case by establishing the environmental damage caused by China’s extensive reclamation activities in the area.

A decade later, scientists are still asking for programmed funds to support marine scientific research in the West Philippine Sea. Programmed funds can help scientists plan long-term, eliminate the constraints imposed by the uncertainty of where to get the next tranche of funds.

“Is the support commensurate?” Fernando Siringan, professor at the University of the Philippines Marine Science Institute, asked on Tuesday, July 28. “First, we thank the national government for all the support that we have received thus far. But that support is not sufficient. There needs to be a continuing support and a programmatic support.”

Siringan had first-hand experience of harassment from Chinese maritime forces in 2024, when he led researchers for an acoustic and coral assessment survey at Escoda Shoal.

“We’re only making do with the opportunities available,” said Siringan. “But it’s better to have a program that one can follow through time.”

Marine scientists operate on a grants-based approach. They pitch, get funding if approved, and try to finish the work on time amid bureaucratic barriers and the uncertain, fluid circumstances of scientific research. One thing I was told in a recent visit to the Marine Science Institute in the University of the Philippines is that laboratories are accumulated equipment from various grants.

“To go at sea is not cheap,” said Siringan. Crude oil, crew to man the ship — we’re talking about millions already, the expert said. And there is much of the Philippine seas that should be covered. Big funds are needed to go where the scientists need to go. On top of that, much is yet to be done in deep sea research. Many of the studies on the West Philippine Sea that the scientists presented are all done on shallow waters (18 meters and shallower).

What is the magnitude of the West Philippine Sea beyond the depth of 18 meters? Much life in our own waters are yet to be known.

As the Arbitral Award has shown, scientific research in the contested waters serves the Philippines’ sovereign rights and national security. And work at sea is not easy, Siringan said. It is physically demanding to the crew. Waters can be unforgiving to equipment.

For Mariglo Laririt, assistant director of the Biodiversity Management Bureau (BMB), the budget for marine scientific research is “the carriage, not the horse.”

“Meaning the budget will come if it becomes clear which is the lead agency for ocean governance,” Laririt told Rappler during a phone call.

“So for DENR’s part, specifically for BMB, we’re contributing by working towards a national ocean environments policy in the hopes that this will help — this will aid decision makers to determine where best to lodge ocean governance as a lead agency.”

The environment department has a budget for management and rehabilitation of coastal and marine resources.

“But [ocean] governance, obviously, is another thing because it requires so many things,” said Laririt. “It requires integration of all efforts.”

In the name of conservation and the Arbitral Award, there is a popular push among experts and government officials to campaign for a declaration of marine protected areas in the West Philippine Sea.

A basic requirement for proposed marine protected areas is baseline ecological data. What is in the waters that ought to be protected? That would require time at sea, the right tools for sound analysis, and dedicated, hard-working scientists.

Will Marcos match his zeal, lauded in the international community, with the institutional support scientists need? The President should, unless he wants to be accused of being all bark, no bite.

– Rappler.com

Quotes are translated to English for brevity.

World.title: Why didn’t banks flag large check encashments by Sara Duterte staff?
World.content:
Former Landbank manager Violeta TESTIMONY. Constantino testifies during the 10th day of Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial on July 29, 2026.

The 10th day of Vice President Sara Duterte’s trial on Wednesday, July 29, saw two former bank officials describe the encashment of large funds by her staff as “unusual,” but not necessarily “suspicious.”

Violeta Constantino, former Land Bank of the Philippines (LBP) Shaw Boulevard branch manager, said it was the first time in her 32-year career to oversee the conversion into cash of a P125-million check. Retired LBP Department of Education branch manager Nenita Camposano also testified that DepEd had never withdrawn a check as large as P37.5 million before.

“In our personal opinion at the bank, of course we wondered: What is all this cash going to be used for?” Constantino said in Filipino.

“‘Unusual’ just means the transaction was different from what we normally saw,” Camposano added.

Play Video

As pointed out by Senator Ping Lacson, there is no middle ground such as “doubtful” transactions under Philippine banking guidelines.

The Anti-Money Laundering Council, based on its Guidelines on Transaction Reporting and Compliance Submissions, requires banks to submit mainly two types of reports to them: covered transaction reports (CTRs), and suspicious transaction reports (STRs).

CTRs are submitted automatically by banks every time there is standard cash or equivalent monetary instrument transaction exceeding the P500,000 legal threshold within a single day. When AMLC’s report released to the House justice committee in April revealed that the bank accounts of Duterte and her husband Mans Carpio were the subject of 630 CTRs from 2006 to 2025, these were generated without human intervention.

STRs are different. AMLC guidelines, as contained in Regulatory Issuance No. 2 Series of 2024, dictate that suspicious transactions are reported by banks regardless of the amount when a “suspicious circumstance” exists based on reasonable grounds.

These include transactions with no underlying legal or trade obligation or economic justification, clients who are not properly identified, amounts not commensurate to the client’s financial capacity, structured transactions designed to avoid reporting, or links to money laundering.

The graphic below contains various reasons that prompt a bank to file an STR.

For the OVP, the LBP Shaw Boulevard branch processed four checks worth P125 million each on December 20, 2022, January 31, 2023, April 18, 2023, and July 13, 2023.

For DepEd, LBP DepEd branch encashed three checks worth P37.5 million each on February 20, 2023, April 19, 2023, and July 11, 2023.

In total, the P612.5 million is believed to be Duterte’s confidential fund allocation as OVP head and DepEd secretary. They have been the subject of various COA notices of disallowance, and at the center of the prosecution’s impeachment case against the Vice President.

For the record, the two bank officials declined to confirm whether the encashments were reported to AMLC due to confidentiality laws.

But they said themselves that they didn’t find the transactions suspicious because the withdrawals underwent the standard process — Duterte’s staff in the OVP and DepEd advised the banks prior to the encashment, the checks were released by the Department of Budget and Management, and authorized signatories were involved.

“For this particular (transaction), we didn’t have doubts because we knew the transaction was legitimate,” Constantino said.

Duterte’s legal team did not cross-examine Constantino and asked Camposano only one question. Defense lawyer Michael Poa downplayed the witnesses’ description of the transactions as “unusual,” saying it was just the bank managers’ opinion.

The prosecution, for its part, said it is not concerned that the transactions didn’t ring alarm bells for the witnesses they presented.

“If we listen to the purpose of these witnesses’ testimonies, Congressman Joel Chua never mentioned anything about suspicious or covered transactions. I think it’s clear that the sole purpose of their testimony is to establish that the funds came from the National Treasury, were downloaded to two agencies, and were eventually encashed by these payees, who apparently represented those agencies,” lead prosecutor Jinky Luistro said. – Rappler.com

World.title: Big fishers win as Supreme Court declares tracking at sea unconstitutional
World.content:
The Supreme Court directs the Department of Agriculture and the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources to immediately 'rectify deficiencies' in Fisheries Administrative Order No. 266

MANILA, Philippines – The Supreme Court (SC) struck down as unconstitutional the government policy that mandated a vessel monitoring system in commercial vessels, citing violations of commercial fishing operators’ constitutional rights against unreasonable searches and seizures, due process, and equal protection of law.

The decision, promulgated on January 21 and which Rappler obtained a copy of on Thursday, July 30, affirmed the 2021 decision of Malabon Regional Trial Court Branch 170 that declared Fisheries Administrative Order (FAO) No. 266 unconstitutional.

FAO 266, issued by the Department of Agriculture in 2020, set the guidelines for vessel monitoring measures and an electronic reporting system for commercial Philippine-flagged fishing vessels. The policy was part of the government’s efforts to curb illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing. These measures record data such as vessel position, volume of fish catch, and port of origin and arrival.

The High Court, voting 13-2, said the government failed to show that the vessel monitoring system is effective in detecting IUU fishing violations. Detecting IUU fishing through the vessel monitoring system is one of the main arguments the government used to justify the need to track fishing vessels at sea through the vessel monitoring system.

“The availability of other means, which are less intrusive and even more effective in preventing and detecting IUUF, makes the 24/7 monitoring required by FAO No. 266 unduly restrictive,” read the decision penned by Supreme Court Justice Maria Filomena Singh. “VMS cannot even detect overfishing or unreported fishing.”

Moreover, the court said the policy exceeded parameters in monitoring and surveillance of commercial fishing vessels and “permits unreasonable searches and seizures.” Commercial fishing operators were singled out in FAO 266, said the court, when vessel monitoring also includes municipal and distant water fishers, thus violating the equal protection clause of the Constitution.

There was “palpable violation,” as well, of the commercial operators’ right to due process, as the government already acquired VMS transceivers before the conduct of public consultations. Royale Fishing and others “had no real opportunity to be heard and to give their comments on the proposed regulations.”

Additionally, the court said no proof was presented to show that Philippine relations with the European Union and other countries suffered because of the injunction against the vessel monitoring system. In 2014, the EU issued a yellow card (a threat of a fish export ban) against the Philippines if it would not carry out reforms to combat illegal fishing. The following year, the ban was lifted when the Philippines amended its Fisheries Code.

A case from 2021

This case involves government agencies the Department of Agriculture (DA), the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR), and the National Telecommunications Commission.

Big fishers involved in the case are Royale Fishing Corporation, Bonanza Fishing and Market Resources Inc, and RBL Fishing Corporation. The case started when these fishing operators sought declaratory relief from the Malabon regional trial court.

The Supreme Court has directed the DA, through the (BFAR), to immediately “rectify deficiencies” in FAO 266 and report action taken.

Environmental groups following the resolution of the case have been concerned about the implementation of the amended Fisheries Code, the fight against illegal fishing, and commercial operators’ encroachment within municipal waters.

The resolution in a related case that revolves around Malabon Regional Trial Court Branch 170’s decision to allow a commercial operator to fish within municipal waters is still pending.

In the final note of the decision, the court said there was “no doubt” that the government policy was “driven with noble intentions.” But its implementation has violated fundamental rights.

“In every instance, when the Court is confronted with the need to weigh a state interest against the sacrosanct rights of its people, the scales must always tip in favor of the protection of the latter if the state interest can be preserved through lawful and less restrictive means,” Singh wrote. – Rappler.com

World.title: Low-key Regina Jurado finding her voice as UST’s new leader
World.content:
HIGH FIVE. Regina Jurado (2nd left, 18) in action for the UST Golden Tigresses in the UAAP Season 88 women's volleyball tournament.

Now the UST Golden Tigresses' new captain, the usually reserved Regina Jurado is determined to step out of her comfort zone and let her voice be heard

MANILA, Philippines – In her four years playing for the UST Golden Tigresses, Regina Jurado played a supporting role behind vocal leaders Eya Laure and Detdet Pepito.

Now the Tigresses’ new captain, the usually reserved Jurado is determined to step out of her comfort zone and let her voice be heard.

“Actually, [being the shy type] is one of my worries as captain, because, as I’ve seen from [Pepito], she was very vocal, and that’s what I need to work on,” Jurado said in Filipino after helping UST win the Shakey’s Super League National Invitational on Sunday, July 26.

“It’s still a work in progress, but for now, I’ll try to lead in my own way, with my own style.”

Jurado let her game do the talking in the championship game against NCAA powerhouse College of St. Benilde, pouring in a game-high 21 points in the 22-25, 25-8, 25-12, 25-22 triumph.

Angge Poyos added 20 markers en route to MVP honors, while rookie Kim Rubin supplied 12. Middle blocker Blessing Unekwe recorded 7 blocks.

The win sealed the program’s first major preseason title under Shaq delos Santos, the last coach to guide the Tigresses to a UAAP championship in 2010.

“So this is how it feels. I forgot the feeling of being champion already,” said Delos Santos in Filipino.

“This is big for us, it’s a big help, it gives us huge impact, and we will be inspired to work harder for the next tournaments,” he added, saying that the team will play in the Collegiate V-League and the main Shakey’s Super League tournament.

Like Jurado, Poyos prefers to let her game speak for itself, but she knows the team needs leadership from the veterans as only five seniors remain.

UST captured the title despite missing setter Cassie Carballo, who continues to recover from a leg injury, and UAAP Season 88 girls’ MVP Diza Marie Berayo, who is working her way back from a tweaked ankle. – Rappler.com

World.title: FACT CHECK: Lordan Suan quote criticizing VP Sara’s hospital visit is fake
World.content:
A staff member from the Cagayan de Oro lawmaker's office debunked the claim; the fake quote was previously falsely attributed to Palace press officer Claire Castro, too

Claim: Cagayan de Oro 1st District Representative Lordan Suan criticized Vice President Sara Duterte for making a hospital visit, saying that doing so should be the job of the President.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: The claim was posted by Facebook user Dan Cartagena on July 21. As of writing, it has reached more than 2,100 reactions and 400 comments.

The post shows photos of Duterte visiting patients at a hospital, alongside a photo of Suan and his supposed quote: “Wala akong problema sa pagtulong mo, pero kaunting respeto naman Sara. Gawain yan ng pangulo, wag mo sanang pangunahan.”

(I have no problem with you helping, but show a little respect, Sara. That is the President’s job; please don’t preempt him.)

Social media users were quick to accept the false claim as true, questioning whether the lawmaker from Cagayan de Oro was jealous of Duterte.

Some asked why all of the Vice President’s recent moves were being questioned rather than commended.

The graphic was also reposted by various social media platforms.

The facts: Suan did not make any statement about Duterte’s hospital visit, as confirmed by his office to Rappler.

In a message, Political Affairs Officer 6 Joel Torres said, “Hindi po kailanman nagsabi o naglabas ng anumang pahayag na katulad nito si Cong Suan. Hinihikayat po namin ang lahat to verify information first before believing or sharing it.”

(Cong. Suan has never said or issued any statement like this. We urge everyone to verify information first before believing or sharing it.)

The post’s false claim mirrors a recently-debunked fake quote attributed to Presidential Communications Office Undersecretary Claire Castro.

Duterte’s field hospital visit: The photo used in the false claim’s graphics came from the Vice President’s visit to a field hospital in June 2026 in Sarangani.

Duterte visited the Philippine Emergency Medical Assistance Team Field Hospital at the Glan School of Arts and Trades, where she checked on the conditions and medical needs of residents affected by the earthquake that struck Mindanao on June 26.

Suan and Duterte’s impeachment: Suan is among 11 House prosecutors in the impeachment trial of Duterte, the first public official to be impeached twice by the lower chamber.

Duterte’s trial is currently in its fourth week.

She is accused of several alleged offenses based on four grounds:

Culpable violation of the Constitution, graft and corruption, and betrayal of public trust, related to her alleged misuse of public funds

Culpable violation of the Constitution and betrayal of public trust, related to her supposed unexplained wealth, stemming from discrepancies in her Statements of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN)

Bribery, graft and corruption, culpable violation of the Constitution, and betrayal of public trust, related to her alleged monetary gifts to education department officials

Culpable violation of the Constitution, high crimes, and betrayal of public trust, related to her alleged death threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta Marcos, and former House speaker Martin Romualdez

– Lourence Angelo Marcellana/Rappler.com

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.
