World.title: Prominent Darwin doctor allegedly caught with up to 1m child abuse files
World.content:
A prominent Darwin doctor charged with possessing up to a million child sexual abuse images and videos could be released from custody within a fortnight after appealing a decision refusing him bail.

The doctor, who cannot be identified for legal reasons, is facing a dozen charges related to accessing and possessing child abuse material.

The Australian Federal Police began investigating the man after the United States's National Center for Missing and Exploited Children raised the alarm over an internet user in Australia accessing files containing the material.

The doctor was arrested last week after police searched his Darwin home and seized mobile phones, tablets, hard drives, USB sticks and laptops, all allegedly containing explicit child abuse images and video files.

The man's lawyer proposed a series of conditions she said would reduce any risk to the community. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

The man appeared from custody in the Northern Territory Supreme Court today after being denied bail by Local Court Judge Alan Woodcock earlier this week, in an attempt to have the initial decision overturned.

Defence lawyer Brooke Houen told the court the application for bail was not an attempt to "sidestep" the seriousness of the allegations, saying there were "strong reasons" for her client to be released.

Ms Houen said the main risk to the community was her client's access to the internet and proposed strict bail conditions, which she likened to home detention.

Those conditions included her client being unable to access the internet unless in the presence of his lawyers, wearing an electronic monitoring device, avoiding childcare centres and surrendering his passport.

Brooke Houen says the case will require "significant" legal advice given the volume of files seized by police. (ABC News: Olivana Lathouris)

"There's no allegation of inappropriate in-person behaviour and there's also no allegation of chat rooms, procuring, producing, or anything of that nature," Ms Houen said.

" It's limited entirely to possession. "

Ms Houen also said her client would need to seek "significant" legal advice and the case was unlikely to be finalised this year given the volume of material and images which needed to be analysed.

More than a million files seized

Prosecutor Euan Malcolm opposed the bail application, arguing the Crown's case against the doctor was "extremely strong".

Mr Malcolm told the court that of the more than 1 million files which had been retrieved from the man's devices, the "majority comprised child abuse material".

He said the man was "somewhat forthcoming to police" about his "voyeuristic addiction" and had made admissions to police about his "habitual viewing" of child abuse material, allegedly spanning more than a decade.

Justice Meredith Huntingford agreed to order a bail assessment report before ruling on the application later this month. (ABC News: Tristan Hooft)

"At the same time, the applicant says that he did not think what he was doing was illegal as the material was obtained from the internet," he said.

Mr Malcolm said the man's alleged behaviour was indicative of "some lack of impulse control" and without "intensive intervention" there was a "high risk" to community safety.

Justice Meredith Huntingford agreed to order a bail assessment report but told Ms Houen not to "read into" that decision.

The case will return to court on August 10 for a final decision on whether the man will be released.

World.title: Hopes for renewed Australian helium production after SA extraction
World.content:
Three years after Australia stopped producing its own helium, the rare gas that hospitals rely on has been extracted from South Australia's Yorke Peninsula.

Gold Hydrogen carried out testing at its Ramsay 1 site, just outside Port Vincent, and managed to extract the gas over the weekend.

It is the first helium capture in Australia since the closure of Darwin's production plant in 2023, the only one in the Southern Hemisphere.

At the time, there was little concern about a shortage of the gas.

But since then there has been a global shortage after about a third of the world's helium supply was taken out by Iranian missile strikes on Qatar's Ras Laffan gas plant in March.

Gold Hydrogen's Ramsay 1 site, just outside Port Vincent, has produced helium gas. (ABC Rural: Isabella Kelly)

Gold Hydrogen chief executive Neil McDonald said people underestimated the role helium played in their day-to-day lives.

"It's not just party balloons and squeaky voices. People touch things that have needed helium every day of their life," he said.

"MRIs cannot operate unless there's helium. And there's a shortage of helium around the world and Australia.

"Helium is required to help make mobile phones; helium has helped make a lot of electronics, computers.

"When it comes to defence, you cannot do submarines without requiring helium."

Helium is the second-lightest gas in the world, and this low weight means when it is extracted from underground, it floats up into the atmosphere, never to be recovered, making it a finite resource.

"Some countries have actually stopped exporting, so there's a world shortage of helium with a growing demand," Mr McDonald said.

"It's the best cooling agent possible … and you can't man-make helium."

Santos's Darwin LNG plant exhausted its feedstock in 2023, bringing an end to Australian helium production, but Gold Hydrogen aims to have a supply commercially available within 18 months.

The next stage of testing on site is now underway on the Yorke Peninsula, where gas volume and extraction ease will be assessed, with results used in developing any potential commercial pilot projects.

Helium project a 'good thing for Australia'

Gold Hydrogen's exploratory Ramsay Project covers a 75,000-square-kilometre tenement on the Yorke Peninsula, where natural hydrogen was first discovered in the 1920s and 1930s.

In 2023, Gold Hydrogen reported it had found natural hydrogen and helium on the site.

The drilling process involves an almost 900-metre-deep hole in the ground, with equipment initially set up on a "soccer field"-sized area.

Local landholder Brendan Moloney, who believes there is further helium on his land near Maitland, has welcomed the project.

Brendan Moloney believes there is more helium on his land near Maitland. (ABC Rural: Isabella Kelly)

"It's a good thing for Australia," he said.

A farmer himself, Mr Moloney was not concerned the project would impact land use.

"It's only a small area [of land] … it's just all underground.

"I think as long as there's no fracking involved … it's a good thing. It creates more employment, and it'll take us off the grid. It's just a win-win."

World.title: Businesses back engineering works to protect Lismore from devastating floods
World.content:
A group of business leaders in northern NSW has backed engineering work to reduce flooding following a landmark study.

The CSIRO report found strategically placed water retention basins could significantly reduce flooding and protect homes and businesses in the Richmond River catchment.

The devastating Lismore floods in 2022 were estimated to cost close to $1 billion to rebuild the community, including more than $350 million in damage to council assets.

Lismore Alliance, which represents 6,000 members, said at a press conference on Thursday the measures could be "the difference between a region with an economic future and one without".

"Flood risk is not just a community safety issue — it is the single biggest constraint on the economic future of this region," said alliance chair and head of the Casino Food Co-op, Simon Stahl.

" It would just give so much confidence to this region, knowing there is something being done about the height of the floods. "

"The first thing you look at when investing [in a region] is the risk to property, assets and workforce."

Lismore Alliance chair Simon Stahl says the feasibility of the CSIRO modelling needs to be explored (ABC North Coast: Hannah Ross)

He said a lot of important considerations had become "lost in the noise" of the public meetings, including the question of compensation for landholders whose properties could be inundated by detention basins.

"If the feasibility does go that far, we are fully supportive of that because people's lives are going to be affected," he said.

Heated debate

More than a thousand people attended a series of information sessions hosted by the CSIRO last week to explain the science behind its flood mitigation modelling.

The meetings became heated at times, with many people frustrated that issues like property inundation and nature-based solutions were not addressed.

Meetings across the Northern Rivers became heated. (ABC North Coast: Hannah Ross)

The national science agency has tested how flooding could be reduced across the catchment if engineering solutions were built, including up to 10 detention basins and a secondary outlet for the river to flow out to sea.

Under February 2022 flood conditions, these measures would reduce flooding in Lismore by 2.07 metres.

That record-breaking flood saw water overtop the Lismore levee at 10.2 metres and reach a height in the CBD of 14.37 metres.

The NSW and federal governments have committed $3 million to now assess the technical, environmental, economic and social feasibility of the mitigation measures.

Business confidence

Lismore business owner Felicity Hyde had to cease trading for three months after flooding inundated her shop in 2022, and lay off four employees.

She said so many businesses had rebuilt after the floods, trusting that no level of government had made a decision to relocate the city's central business district.

Lismore ice cream shop owner Felicity Hyde has rebuilt her business since the 2022 floods. (ABC North Coast: Hannah Ross)

"If the government had the idea that Lismore needs to move, they would have suggested that early on, or at some stage," she said.

Former Summerland Bank chief executive John Williams said the bank's repair bill after the 2022 floods was $4 million, which was only partially covered by insurance, and it can no longer get coverage for its branch in the Lismore CBD.

Mr Williams said he saw first-hand the social impact of the disaster on people trying to pay mortgages on houses destroyed or damaged by flooding.

John Williams says mitigation will attract insurers and investment. (ABC North Coast: Hannah Ross)

He said reducing flood heights by 2 metres would help businesses get insurance.

"What we need to do is reduce the risk to bring insurers back to the market," he said.

"It will still be expensive but it will definitely be worthwhile to encourage investment back into Lismore."

The National Emergency Management Agency is expected to release maps in early August showing which properties around the detention basins would be inundated in times of flood.

Farmers are demanding information about how much of their pasture would be underwater, and for how long.

The largest detention basin would hold 94 gigalitres. (Supplied: CSIRO)

Communities in the upper catchment have also raised concerns about how the detention basins could affect road access and other services.

The NSW Reconstruction Authority will be co-ordinating feasibility assessments of the CSIRO modelling.

World.title: Obama lawyer slammed for claiming Epstein victim’s allegations ‘lacked credibility’
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaEpstein fallout Obama lawyer slammed for claiming Epstein victim’s allegations ‘lacked credibility’ Poppy Wood July 30, 2026 — 7:38pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Virginia Giuffre’s family has hit out at a prominent US Democratic lawyer after she claimed the Jeffrey Epstein victim “lacked inherent credibility”. Kathryn Ruemmler, who served as White House counsel to former US president Barack Obama, testified to Congress that she thought Giuffre’s sex-trafficking allegations lacked sufficient detail. In closed-door testimony delivered earlier this month and published on Wednesday (Washington time), Ruemmler said: “There were allegations that she made that were, I believed, based on my experience as a former prosecutor and as a defence counsel, that were of such a nature that they were – they lacked inherent credibility. Virginia Giuffre triggered a royal crisis in 2015 after she accused Jeffrey Epstein and his accomplice Ghislaine Maxwell of trafficking her to London in 2001 to have sex with then-prince Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor. Netflix “Typically, when someone says, I was sex trafficked to someone, they say who, when, where, not multiple world leaders, multiple foreign presidents.”



Giuffre’s family reacted furiously to the remarks, saying Ruemmler was “the only person who lacks credibility”. Related Article Investigation

Good Weekend Isolated, scared, forlorn: The heartbreaking final months of Virginia Giuffre’s life Sky Roberts, the brother of Giuffre, who took her own life last year, and his wife Amanda Roberts, accused the Goldman Sachs lawyer of “trying to get people to believe she didn’t know Jeffrey Epstein was actively engaged in sex trafficking”. “To attempt to cast doubt on Virginia, whose bravery was the reason so many other survivors stepped forward, resulting in more than 50 people having to step down from their positions of power, is reprehensible. She should be ashamed of herself,” they said in a statement. “Kathy Ruemmler enriched herself while girls and young women suffered and had their lives destroyed because she enabled their abuser. Shame on Goldman Sachs for keeping her in its employ.”



Giuffre triggered a royal crisis in 2015 after she accused Epstein and his accomplice Ghislaine Maxwell of trafficking her to London in 2001 to have sex with then-prince Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor. She alleged in her memoir, Nobody’s Girl, which was published posthumously last October, that she had sex with Mountbatten-Windsor on three occasions when she was 17. The former prince vehemently denies the claims. Goldman Sachs general counsel Kathy Ruemmler previously played down her relationship with Epstein. Getty Images Giuffre also accused Epstein of subjecting her to years of physical and sexual abuse after Maxwell recruited her in 2000, when she was 16 and working at Mar-a-Lago, Donald Trump’s Florida resort. She claimed Epstein also shopped her around to have sex with his high-flying friends, naming, among others, Jean-Luc Brunel, the French model scout who died in his cell while awaiting sex-trafficking charges in 2022.



Ruemmler told Congress’ House Oversight Committee that she never saw “any evidence suggesting that [Epstein] was abusing women or girls”, but that she had later come to realise he “was a masterful liar”. Related Article Visual story

Domestic violence ‘Mommy pls call’: The secret ‘scrapbook’ of Virginia Giuffre She also acknowledged in testimony made public on Wednesday that she had accepted gifts from Epstein during their six-year friendship and “sometimes irreverently” exchanged emails with him. The lawyer resigned as Goldman Sachs’ chief legal officer last month, where she was paid $US25 million a year, after details of her relationship with the sex offender came to light. She remains at the investment bank as a temporary adviser. Ruemmler is one of several high-profile figures to have voluntarily testified to Congress in recent months as part of its investigation into Epstein, including Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates, and most recently Jes Staley, the former chief executive of Barclays.



The House Oversight Committee is seeking testimony from Todd Blanche, whose nomination to become US attorney-general has garnered fierce backlash from Epstein victims. They claim that he mishandled the release of the Epstein files through poor redactions of names and contact details – a task he was delegated as US deputy attorney-general – and by failing to publish the full stash of documents. Blanche also conducted an interview last northern summer with Maxwell, who was convicted of sex-trafficking charges in relation to Epstein in 2021 and sentenced to 20 years in jail. She was moved from a federal prison in Florida to a minimum-security camp in Texas a week after her meeting with Blanche.



It has prompted concerns among victims that Maxwell could eventually be handed a presidential pardon. The US Senate voted unanimously on Wednesday to declare its opposition to any such move. Introduced by Democratic senator Jacky Rosen, from Nevada, the resolution stated that Maxwell “should not be granted a presidential pardon or any form of clemency for her crimes with Jeffrey Epstein relating to the sexual exploitation and abuse of minors”. The resolution added: “The Senate stands with the victims of sexual exploitation and trafficking and affirms its commitment to justice, accountability, and the protection of children.” Republicans refused to object to the move, which is non-binding and largely symbolic, meaning they effectively allowed it to pass.



A spokesman for Ruemmler told London’s Telegraph: “As Ms Ruemmler told the committee, she had no knowledge of any ongoing criminal activity by Epstein and there is not a shred of evidence to suggest otherwise. “Ms Ruemmler would never turn a blind eye to any criminal activity, and if she had seen or heard anything to suggest that Epstein was harming women or girls, she would have taken action to stop it.” If you or anyone you know needs support, you can contact the National Sexual Assault, Domestic and Family Violence Counselling Service on 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732), Lifeline 131 114, or Beyond Blue 1300 224 636. World.title: ‘What she’s doing is unbelievable’: How Nelly Korda is taking women’s golf to new heights
World.content:
SportGolfWorld golf ‘What she’s doing is unbelievable’: How Nelly Korda is taking women’s golf to new heights Evin Priest July 30, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Lytham St Annes: Nelly Korda is instantly recognisable, even from a distance across the windswept dunes at England’s Royal Lytham course. As fans filed in ahead of the Women’s British Open, the final major of the year, most searched for the world No.1. Nelly Korda in action during the Pro-Am on Wednesday before the Women’s Open at Royal Lytham. R&A via Getty Images It didn’t take long to locate the tall, athletic frame of the American, not least for the fact her outfits alone have Nike X-factor compared to the rest of the field: baggy, camouflage pants, and a cropped, luxe sweater. Then there’s the balance and power of the 28-year-old’s golf swing – equal parts natural talent, which she shares with a family of tennis and golf stars, and more than two decades of hard work advancing from Florida’s ultra-competitive junior golf scene to the LPGA Tour.



Korda isn’t just the biggest drawcard in women’s golf; she’s among the biggest women’s sports stars in the world. Worthy of a mention alongside basketballer Caitlin Clark, gymnast Simone Biles and tennis player Coco Gauff. But Korda is a reluctant star; one who concedes she was unprepared when her profile soared in 2024. Nelly Korda tees off. Getty Images That year, she became a multiple major winner with her second trophy, won seven LPGA Tour titles including a record-equalling five in a row, returned to the Olympic stage in Paris as the gold medal winner from the previous games in Tokyo and became the first golfer since Tiger Woods to appear at the Met Gala in New York. A year later, she was featured in Sports Illustrated’s Swimsuit Issue.



“I have had to learn that,” Korda said at Royal Lytham about dealing with her heightened fame. “It’s not something that just like came with it. In 2024, it was a lot at once, and I had to go through last year to even embrace it.” The 19-time LPGA Tour winner can at times be coy with the media, appearing to draw a line between the public and private versions of herself. But, in 2026, Korda’s celebrity and results have taken off. She won the first two majors of the year, including an epic battle with England star Charley Hull at the US Women’s Open at Riviera Country Club in Los Angeles. She’s searching for a maiden Women’s British Open title after finishing tied second with Yin Ruoning and Lilia Vu at St Andrews to Lydia Ko in 2024. It’s all been a learning curve. “I think if you asked me two years ago, I maybe would’ve lied up here and said I’m fine with it [all],” Korda said candidly. “But I think that I’m at a stage in my career where I’m just going to be myself. If people don’t like it, that’s fine. If that inspires the next generation, that’s great; that’s what I would like.



“I had to learn that I’m going to go the direction I want and be very authentic. I feel like when I’m not, it drains my battery a lot.” Korda at least has a family of athletes to lean on. Her father, Petr Korda, was ranked world No.2 in tennis and the Czech star won the 1998 Australian Open. Her mother, Regina Rajchrtová, played tennis and competed at the 1988 Olympics. Sister Jess Korda, who chose golf, won six LPGA Tour titles including the Women’s Australian Open, while brother Sebastian Korda pursued tennis and has four ATP wins. A young Korda with father Petr, a former tennis major winner, and brother Sebastian at the US Open. Instagram “My family, I think they always make sure that my batteries are always recharged,” Korda said. New Zealand star Ko, a former world No.1 and the most recent LPGA Hall of Fame inductee, has been blown away by Korda’s past three seasons.



“She’s had an incredible year, and to kind of have that twice in the span of three years, is really unbelievable,” Ko said on Wednesday. “She’s proven herself to everyone [that] she’s one of the best players in the United States and one of the best female athletes.” Korda’s sustained success hasn’t just benefited herself. Interest has never been higher in women’s golf. KPMG, the title sponsor of the Women’s PGA Championship, has bumped its prize purse up to a record $US13 million ($18.7m), while this week’s presenting partner, AIG, has also moved the Women’s British Open purse up to $US10 million. Only 11 years ago, the Masters, the biggest tournament in men’s golf, had its prize pool increased to $US10 million. “Listen, what Nelly is doing for the game of golf is unbelievable and so good to watch, and she’s a nice girl as well,” Hull said at Royal Lytham. Hull is regarded as the biggest women’s star behind Korda, for her aggressive, exciting brand of golf and her dry, British sense of humour.



Related Article World golf Even greats like Minjee Lee have form slumps. The battle to end it has started Fans are yearning for Hull, who has three LPGA wins, to challenge Korda on a more regular basis and

have that rivalry take women’s golf to new heights. Hull, 30, did so at the recent US Women’s Open where she took it to Korda and finished tied second. “I don’t really see it as a rivalry at the minute because – no offence – Nelly has got [four] majors and I’ve got none. I’ve got five second-places,” Hull said bluntly. “So let me get my major in first and then that’s something we can think about in the future. I just want to get over the line and win my first major. Five second-place finishes in majors kind of hurts.



“I remember looking at the faces walking in on the first day from last year and I was like, ‘Oh, I wish that was me.’” At Royal Lytham, perhaps it could become an official rivalry if local favourite Hull was to win, and better yet while fending off Korda. Perhaps both would be then on equal footing. But for now, Korda is the golfer every fan wants a glimpse of. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport are sent every Monday.

World.title: The ghost of Bob Hawke supports Pauline Hanson? I saw first-hand how wrong that notion is
World.content:
PoliticsFederalIndigenous Opinion The ghost of Bob Hawke supports Pauline Hanson? I saw first-hand how wrong that notion is Tony Wright Associate editor and special writer July 30, 2026 — 7:30pm

July 30, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

On the night of June 12, 1988, Bob Hawke sat by a campfire in the Northern Territory scrub about 80 kilometres north of Katherine and accepted from a gathering of painted Aboriginal elders a declaration on bark calling for a treaty between white and Indigenous Australia. Hawke, much moved, made a promise. Prime minister Bob Hawke accepts the Barunga Statement from Galarrwuy Yunupingu in 1988, and promises a treaty. Fairfax Archives He’d do all in his power to deliver such a treaty within two years. Three and a half years later, Hawke was defeated as prime minister, the promised treaty undelivered.



Expressing remorse that no treaty had been completed, Hawke’s last action in the minutes before Paul Keating was sworn in as prime minister was to enshrine that bark request, known as the Barunga Statement, on the wall of Parliament House. He insisted it remind successors of unfinished business that must not be ignored. Related Article Vale A gathering of tribes - how Bob Hawke would have loved it It happened that I was around that campfire at Barunga in 1988 when Hawke promised to work towards a treaty. I also reported first-hand Hawke’s emotional last minutes as PM as he hoisted the Barunga statement and expressed personal regret that his promise was not fulfilled. “The important thing is what’s in our minds and in our hearts,” he said. All these years later, Hawke dead since May 2019, the Institute of Public Affairs, a conservative “think tank”, purports to know what was in Bob Hawke’s mind and heart in relation to Aboriginal identity and tradition.



Ludicrously, the institute’s deputy executive director, Daniel Wild, claimed Hawke would have supported Pauline Hanson’s call for a ban on Welcome to Country and Acknowledgment of Country ceremonies. “There is no doubt Labor’s greatest political figure, Bob Hawke, would have supported Senator Hanson’s call for racial equality through the termination of Welcome to Country and acknowledgment of country ceremonies,” Wild said in a statement issued this week. His evidence? It was a fragment of Hawke’s speech on Australia Day in 1988 – Australia’s Bicentenary – in which Hawke, attempting to define modern Australia’s identity, declared “in Australia there is no hierarchy of descent: there must be no privilege of origin. The commitment is all.” Precisely how this might translate to Aboriginal Welcome to Country ceremonies is to draw the longest bow beyond breaking point.



Wild and Hanson might feverishly fantasise that such ceremonies equate to some form of inverted racial privilege or “hierarchy of descent” favouring Aboriginal people. But the fragment of the speech ignores that Hawke was speaking to those who had immigrated to Australia in the 200 years since the First Fleet sailed in. He said it out loud immediately before Wild’s artfully chosen tract, declaring he was referring to “that common commitment which binds the Australian-born of the seventh or eighth generation and all those of their fellow Australians born in any of the 130 countries from which our people are drawn”. Hawke at the National Press Club in January 1988 – a speech that Tony Wright witnessed first hand. Richard Briggs Four days previously, at the National Press Club, Hawke made clear he accepted that Aboriginal people had rights separate to immigrants. They had a special relationship to the land, which they had always owned, he declared, and said his government’s policy, “Foundations for the Future”, was a landmark of “tremendous significance”. And he framed it as an Acknowledgment of Country.



“It acknowledges the descendants of the Aboriginal people of Australia as the prior occupiers and original owners of this land; it acknowledges the dispossession of their land by subsequent European occupation; it acknowledges that the dispossession occurred without compensation and with no serious attempt to reach agreement with the Aboriginal people on the use of their land,” Hawke said. “It acknowledges the deep disadvantages and deprivations the Aboriginals have thereby suffered and continue to suffer. “And it pledges the Australian Government and the Australian people to an earnest and continuing effort of rectification and reconciliation.” Wild might, almost, be forgiven for distorting Hawke’s words and misrepresenting his stance on Australian Aboriginals, as it was so many years ago. I reported first-hand on Hawke over many years, travelling Australia and the world with him and listening to him, and it was never difficult to discern what was in his heart and mind concerning Australia’s original inhabitants.



A lifetime of opposing racism in Australia and abroad built in him a deep disdain for those who denied that Australia’s Aboriginal people had a right to their own identity and traditions. He reserved, in his years beyond politics, a special contempt for Pauline Hanson’s views. In 1998, when Hanson’s influence was rising for the first brief time, Hawke, Keating and fellow former prime ministers Gough Whitlam and Malcolm Fraser issued a joint statement aimed primarily at her approach and by implication that of John Howard, who was avoiding direct condemnation of Hanson. Former prime ministers Bob Hawke, Gough Whitlam, Malcolm Fraser, Paul Keating and Kevin Rudd after Rudd’s apology to Indigenous Australia, specifically the Stolen Generations. Andrew Taylor “Racism,” Hawke and his fellow signatories declared, “is an unmitigated evil, it is immoral, it does Australia significant harm through Asia and the wider world, it destroys our self-esteem and self-respect. In Australia, it would pit Australian against Australian. It would be destructive of our society.”



It was a follow-up to a scathing statement organised by Hawke and signed by Keating and Whitlam the previous year, directed straight at Hanson. They described her views as “bigoted, uninformed, simplistic and subversive nonsense”. And now Hawke is being accused of supporting Hanson and her mean-minded jihad against Aboriginal people extending a Welcome to Country and others acknowledging their respect for traditional owners and their ongoing connection to the land? On behalf of Bob Hawke, who has been gone these seven years, may I offer a response? Bloody preposterous. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: NRL LIVE updates: Roosters’ winning streak on the line against in-form Cowboys
World.content:
Winger Daniel Tupou is leaning towards playing one more year with the Sydney Roosters, but should the Bondi club not accommodate him, he is prepared to pursue a two-year deal in the Super League.

Daniel Tupou celebrates a try against Parramatta. NRL Photos

Sydney Roosters coach Trent Robinson on Tuesday confirmed Tupou would return for the NRL finals after dislocating his shoulder last Friday night against the Knights – but no call had been made about next year.

Tupou’s preference would be to play a 16th season in the red, white and blue. But the 35-year-old met his manager Sam Ayoub on Monday who informed him several English Super League clubs had expressed interest in him.

The chance to sign a two-year deal has appeal, while Tupou also knows the Super League would be less physically demanding.

Disturbing footage has emerged of a racially fuelled attack on three Chinese international students who were allegedly confronted by two women after a night out in the Sydney CBD. Lenny Tai, 29, and his two friends were waiting near Central Station for a DiDi ride-share trip home in the early hours of last Saturday when the women began taunting them from the opposite side of the road. Loading “Do you want Pokemon cards?” they allegedly yelled repeatedly at the students. After a few minutes, the women crossed the street and approached the group, swearing and jeering at them. Tai and Zhao alleged they also directed racist and sexually explicit abuse at the trio. In Australia? … You will never be let back in our country”, before she begins shoving and grabbing the men. Tai said he was grabbed by the neck, choked and scratched on the face by one of the women. Lenny Tai’s alleged scratches after the incident. Lenny Tai Zhan and Tai reported the incident to the police that day.



NSW Police have begun an investigation into the incident on the corner of Pitt Street and Hay Street in Haymarket. “The man was allegedly assaulted by two women who were unknown to him,” a spokesperson told the Herald. “The man sustained a scratch to his chin during the alleged assault.” Tai, who has lived in Sydney for five years, said he has not left his home since the alleged attack took place five days ago. Families of three people killed in a triple-fatal highway crash might have to wait another year for an alleged murderer’s trial. Rafferty Raymond Rolfe was charged with three counts of domestic violence-related murder after emerging as the sole survivor of a multi-vehicle collision on a major Queensland highway. Rafferty Rolfe is due to face court after the Bruce Highway crash. Nine News The Yandina man is accused of following and attempting to ram a ute driven by a good Samaritan who had picked up Rolfe’s girlfriend as a passenger. The ute was allegedly hit and veered onto the wrong side of the Bruce Highway at Federal, near the Sunshine Coast, and into the path of an oncoming ute on June 21, 2023.



Rolfe, who is in custody, was not required to appear on Thursday for a pre-trial review in Brisbane Supreme Court. The case had a provisional listing for a trial lasting up to four weeks to start on February 1 next year, Justice Lincoln Crowley heard. “The matter won’t be confirmed until the court calendar for the first half of 2027 is finalised,” Crowley said. Crowley was told the prosecutor who was due to handle the trial had taken leave for unexpected health issues and the trial plan had not been finalised. Rolfe’s barrister Gregory McGuire said his instructing solicitor had been told the trial prosecutor would not be back at work before August 28.



“The prosecution has yet to settle on a list of witnesses to be called at trial and provide that list to the defence,” McGuire said. Crowley said the provision trial date was now facing difficulty. “I expect the court calendar will need to be finalised before September 10, so if nothing can happen to progress soon then the provision trial listing would be lost,” Crowley said. “If the [trial prosecutor] is going to be on leave for any significant further period, someone else is going to have to take over.” Finch said he would raise the issue with a senior prosecutor immediately.



Retiree Terry Bishop, 65, was driving with Rolfe’s girlfriend – 25-year-old Gypsy Satterley – when his dual-cab ute was allegedly rammed. They died in the crash along with the driver of the other ute, 38-year-old Jessica Townley. Rolfe has been accused of stealing an SUV in Gympie’s main street 12 hours before the fatal crash, after threatening a mother and three children at knifepoint. Police allege Satterley travelled with Rolfe in the stolen car before fleeing and being rescued by Bishop, who has been described by police as a good Samaritan and a tragic victim of circumstance. The matter will return to court for another review next Thursday. AAP

World.title: Obama lawyer slammed for claiming Epstein victim’s allegations ‘lacked credibility’
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaEpstein fallout Obama lawyer slammed for claiming Epstein victim’s allegations ‘lacked credibility’ Poppy Wood July 30, 2026 — 7:38pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Virginia Giuffre’s family has hit out at a prominent US Democratic lawyer after she claimed the Jeffrey Epstein victim “lacked inherent credibility”. Kathryn Ruemmler, who served as White House counsel to former US president Barack Obama, testified to Congress that she thought Giuffre’s sex-trafficking allegations lacked sufficient detail. In closed-door testimony delivered earlier this month and published on Wednesday (Washington time), Ruemmler said: “There were allegations that she made that were, I believed, based on my experience as a former prosecutor and as a defence counsel, that were of such a nature that they were – they lacked inherent credibility. Virginia Giuffre triggered a royal crisis in 2015 after she accused Jeffrey Epstein and his accomplice Ghislaine Maxwell of trafficking her to London in 2001 to have sex with then-prince Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor. Netflix “Typically, when someone says, I was sex trafficked to someone, they say who, when, where, not multiple world leaders, multiple foreign presidents.”



Giuffre’s family reacted furiously to the remarks, saying Ruemmler was “the only person who lacks credibility”. Related Article Investigation

Good Weekend Isolated, scared, forlorn: The heartbreaking final months of Virginia Giuffre’s life Sky Roberts, the brother of Giuffre, who took her own life last year, and his wife Amanda Roberts, accused the Goldman Sachs lawyer of “trying to get people to believe she didn’t know Jeffrey Epstein was actively engaged in sex trafficking”. “To attempt to cast doubt on Virginia, whose bravery was the reason so many other survivors stepped forward, resulting in more than 50 people having to step down from their positions of power, is reprehensible. She should be ashamed of herself,” they said in a statement. “Kathy Ruemmler enriched herself while girls and young women suffered and had their lives destroyed because she enabled their abuser. Shame on Goldman Sachs for keeping her in its employ.”



Giuffre triggered a royal crisis in 2015 after she accused Epstein and his accomplice Ghislaine Maxwell of trafficking her to London in 2001 to have sex with then-prince Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor. She alleged in her memoir, Nobody’s Girl, which was published posthumously last October, that she had sex with Mountbatten-Windsor on three occasions when she was 17. The former prince vehemently denies the claims. Goldman Sachs general counsel Kathy Ruemmler previously played down her relationship with Epstein. Getty Images Giuffre also accused Epstein of subjecting her to years of physical and sexual abuse after Maxwell recruited her in 2000, when she was 16 and working at Mar-a-Lago, Donald Trump’s Florida resort. She claimed Epstein also shopped her around to have sex with his high-flying friends, naming, among others, Jean-Luc Brunel, the French model scout who died in his cell while awaiting sex-trafficking charges in 2022.



Ruemmler told Congress’ House Oversight Committee that she never saw “any evidence suggesting that [Epstein] was abusing women or girls”, but that she had later come to realise he “was a masterful liar”. Related Article Visual story

Domestic violence ‘Mommy pls call’: The secret ‘scrapbook’ of Virginia Giuffre She also acknowledged in testimony made public on Wednesday that she had accepted gifts from Epstein during their six-year friendship and “sometimes irreverently” exchanged emails with him. The lawyer resigned as Goldman Sachs’ chief legal officer last month, where she was paid $US25 million a year, after details of her relationship with the sex offender came to light. She remains at the investment bank as a temporary adviser. Ruemmler is one of several high-profile figures to have voluntarily testified to Congress in recent months as part of its investigation into Epstein, including Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates, and most recently Jes Staley, the former chief executive of Barclays.



The House Oversight Committee is seeking testimony from Todd Blanche, whose nomination to become US attorney-general has garnered fierce backlash from Epstein victims. They claim that he mishandled the release of the Epstein files through poor redactions of names and contact details – a task he was delegated as US deputy attorney-general – and by failing to publish the full stash of documents. Blanche also conducted an interview last northern summer with Maxwell, who was convicted of sex-trafficking charges in relation to Epstein in 2021 and sentenced to 20 years in jail. She was moved from a federal prison in Florida to a minimum-security camp in Texas a week after her meeting with Blanche.



It has prompted concerns among victims that Maxwell could eventually be handed a presidential pardon. The US Senate voted unanimously on Wednesday to declare its opposition to any such move. Introduced by Democratic senator Jacky Rosen, from Nevada, the resolution stated that Maxwell “should not be granted a presidential pardon or any form of clemency for her crimes with Jeffrey Epstein relating to the sexual exploitation and abuse of minors”. The resolution added: “The Senate stands with the victims of sexual exploitation and trafficking and affirms its commitment to justice, accountability, and the protection of children.” Republicans refused to object to the move, which is non-binding and largely symbolic, meaning they effectively allowed it to pass.



A spokesman for Ruemmler told London’s Telegraph: “As Ms Ruemmler told the committee, she had no knowledge of any ongoing criminal activity by Epstein and there is not a shred of evidence to suggest otherwise. “Ms Ruemmler would never turn a blind eye to any criminal activity, and if she had seen or heard anything to suggest that Epstein was harming women or girls, she would have taken action to stop it.” If you or anyone you know needs support, you can contact the National Sexual Assault, Domestic and Family Violence Counselling Service on 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732), Lifeline 131 114, or Beyond Blue 1300 224 636. World.title: ‘What she’s doing is unbelievable’: How Nelly Korda is taking women’s golf to new heights
World.content:
SportGolfWorld golf ‘What she’s doing is unbelievable’: How Nelly Korda is taking women’s golf to new heights Evin Priest July 30, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Lytham St Annes: Nelly Korda is instantly recognisable, even from a distance across the windswept dunes at England’s Royal Lytham course. As fans filed in ahead of the Women’s British Open, the final major of the year, most searched for the world No.1. Nelly Korda in action during the Pro-Am on Wednesday before the Women’s Open at Royal Lytham. R&A via Getty Images It didn’t take long to locate the tall, athletic frame of the American, not least for the fact her outfits alone have Nike X-factor compared to the rest of the field: baggy, camouflage pants, and a cropped, luxe sweater. Then there’s the balance and power of the 28-year-old’s golf swing – equal parts natural talent, which she shares with a family of tennis and golf stars, and more than two decades of hard work advancing from Florida’s ultra-competitive junior golf scene to the LPGA Tour.



Korda isn’t just the biggest drawcard in women’s golf; she’s among the biggest women’s sports stars in the world. Worthy of a mention alongside basketballer Caitlin Clark, gymnast Simone Biles and tennis player Coco Gauff. But Korda is a reluctant star; one who concedes she was unprepared when her profile soared in 2024. Nelly Korda tees off. Getty Images That year, she became a multiple major winner with her second trophy, won seven LPGA Tour titles including a record-equalling five in a row, returned to the Olympic stage in Paris as the gold medal winner from the previous games in Tokyo and became the first golfer since Tiger Woods to appear at the Met Gala in New York. A year later, she was featured in Sports Illustrated’s Swimsuit Issue.



“I have had to learn that,” Korda said at Royal Lytham about dealing with her heightened fame. “It’s not something that just like came with it. In 2024, it was a lot at once, and I had to go through last year to even embrace it.” The 19-time LPGA Tour winner can at times be coy with the media, appearing to draw a line between the public and private versions of herself. But, in 2026, Korda’s celebrity and results have taken off. She won the first two majors of the year, including an epic battle with England star Charley Hull at the US Women’s Open at Riviera Country Club in Los Angeles. She’s searching for a maiden Women’s British Open title after finishing tied second with Yin Ruoning and Lilia Vu at St Andrews to Lydia Ko in 2024. It’s all been a learning curve. “I think if you asked me two years ago, I maybe would’ve lied up here and said I’m fine with it [all],” Korda said candidly. “But I think that I’m at a stage in my career where I’m just going to be myself. If people don’t like it, that’s fine. If that inspires the next generation, that’s great; that’s what I would like.



“I had to learn that I’m going to go the direction I want and be very authentic. I feel like when I’m not, it drains my battery a lot.” Korda at least has a family of athletes to lean on. Her father, Petr Korda, was ranked world No.2 in tennis and the Czech star won the 1998 Australian Open. Her mother, Regina Rajchrtová, played tennis and competed at the 1988 Olympics. Sister Jess Korda, who chose golf, won six LPGA Tour titles including the Women’s Australian Open, while brother Sebastian Korda pursued tennis and has four ATP wins. A young Korda with father Petr, a former tennis major winner, and brother Sebastian at the US Open. Instagram “My family, I think they always make sure that my batteries are always recharged,” Korda said. New Zealand star Ko, a former world No.1 and the most recent LPGA Hall of Fame inductee, has been blown away by Korda’s past three seasons.



“She’s had an incredible year, and to kind of have that twice in the span of three years, is really unbelievable,” Ko said on Wednesday. “She’s proven herself to everyone [that] she’s one of the best players in the United States and one of the best female athletes.” Korda’s sustained success hasn’t just benefited herself. Interest has never been higher in women’s golf. KPMG, the title sponsor of the Women’s PGA Championship, has bumped its prize purse up to a record $US13 million ($18.7m), while this week’s presenting partner, AIG, has also moved the Women’s British Open purse up to $US10 million. Only 11 years ago, the Masters, the biggest tournament in men’s golf, had its prize pool increased to $US10 million. “Listen, what Nelly is doing for the game of golf is unbelievable and so good to watch, and she’s a nice girl as well,” Hull said at Royal Lytham. Hull is regarded as the biggest women’s star behind Korda, for her aggressive, exciting brand of golf and her dry, British sense of humour.



Related Article World golf Even greats like Minjee Lee have form slumps. The battle to end it has started Fans are yearning for Hull, who has three LPGA wins, to challenge Korda on a more regular basis and

have that rivalry take women’s golf to new heights. Hull, 30, did so at the recent US Women’s Open where she took it to Korda and finished tied second. “I don’t really see it as a rivalry at the minute because – no offence – Nelly has got [four] majors and I’ve got none. I’ve got five second-places,” Hull said bluntly. “So let me get my major in first and then that’s something we can think about in the future. I just want to get over the line and win my first major. Five second-place finishes in majors kind of hurts.



“I remember looking at the faces walking in on the first day from last year and I was like, ‘Oh, I wish that was me.’” At Royal Lytham, perhaps it could become an official rivalry if local favourite Hull was to win, and better yet while fending off Korda. Perhaps both would be then on equal footing. But for now, Korda is the golfer every fan wants a glimpse of. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport are sent every Monday.

World.title: The ghost of Bob Hawke supports Pauline Hanson? I saw first-hand how wrong that notion is
World.content:
PoliticsFederalIndigenous Opinion The ghost of Bob Hawke supports Pauline Hanson? I saw first-hand how wrong that notion is Tony Wright Associate editor and special writer July 30, 2026 — 7:30pm

July 30, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

On the night of June 12, 1988, Bob Hawke sat by a campfire in the Northern Territory scrub about 80 kilometres north of Katherine and accepted from a gathering of painted Aboriginal elders a declaration on bark calling for a treaty between white and Indigenous Australia. Hawke, much moved, made a promise. Prime minister Bob Hawke accepts the Barunga Statement from Galarrwuy Yunupingu in 1988, and promises a treaty. Fairfax Archives He’d do all in his power to deliver such a treaty within two years. Three and a half years later, Hawke was defeated as prime minister, the promised treaty undelivered.



Expressing remorse that no treaty had been completed, Hawke’s last action in the minutes before Paul Keating was sworn in as prime minister was to enshrine that bark request, known as the Barunga Statement, on the wall of Parliament House. He insisted it remind successors of unfinished business that must not be ignored. Related Article Vale A gathering of tribes - how Bob Hawke would have loved it It happened that I was around that campfire at Barunga in 1988 when Hawke promised to work towards a treaty. I also reported first-hand Hawke’s emotional last minutes as PM as he hoisted the Barunga statement and expressed personal regret that his promise was not fulfilled. “The important thing is what’s in our minds and in our hearts,” he said. All these years later, Hawke dead since May 2019, the Institute of Public Affairs, a conservative “think tank”, purports to know what was in Bob Hawke’s mind and heart in relation to Aboriginal identity and tradition.



Ludicrously, the institute’s deputy executive director, Daniel Wild, claimed Hawke would have supported Pauline Hanson’s call for a ban on Welcome to Country and Acknowledgment of Country ceremonies. “There is no doubt Labor’s greatest political figure, Bob Hawke, would have supported Senator Hanson’s call for racial equality through the termination of Welcome to Country and acknowledgment of country ceremonies,” Wild said in a statement issued this week. His evidence? It was a fragment of Hawke’s speech on Australia Day in 1988 – Australia’s Bicentenary – in which Hawke, attempting to define modern Australia’s identity, declared “in Australia there is no hierarchy of descent: there must be no privilege of origin. The commitment is all.” Precisely how this might translate to Aboriginal Welcome to Country ceremonies is to draw the longest bow beyond breaking point.



Wild and Hanson might feverishly fantasise that such ceremonies equate to some form of inverted racial privilege or “hierarchy of descent” favouring Aboriginal people. But the fragment of the speech ignores that Hawke was speaking to those who had immigrated to Australia in the 200 years since the First Fleet sailed in. He said it out loud immediately before Wild’s artfully chosen tract, declaring he was referring to “that common commitment which binds the Australian-born of the seventh or eighth generation and all those of their fellow Australians born in any of the 130 countries from which our people are drawn”. Hawke at the National Press Club in January 1988 – a speech that Tony Wright witnessed first hand. Richard Briggs Four days previously, at the National Press Club, Hawke made clear he accepted that Aboriginal people had rights separate to immigrants. They had a special relationship to the land, which they had always owned, he declared, and said his government’s policy, “Foundations for the Future”, was a landmark of “tremendous significance”. And he framed it as an Acknowledgment of Country.



“It acknowledges the descendants of the Aboriginal people of Australia as the prior occupiers and original owners of this land; it acknowledges the dispossession of their land by subsequent European occupation; it acknowledges that the dispossession occurred without compensation and with no serious attempt to reach agreement with the Aboriginal people on the use of their land,” Hawke said. “It acknowledges the deep disadvantages and deprivations the Aboriginals have thereby suffered and continue to suffer. “And it pledges the Australian Government and the Australian people to an earnest and continuing effort of rectification and reconciliation.” Wild might, almost, be forgiven for distorting Hawke’s words and misrepresenting his stance on Australian Aboriginals, as it was so many years ago. I reported first-hand on Hawke over many years, travelling Australia and the world with him and listening to him, and it was never difficult to discern what was in his heart and mind concerning Australia’s original inhabitants.



A lifetime of opposing racism in Australia and abroad built in him a deep disdain for those who denied that Australia’s Aboriginal people had a right to their own identity and traditions. He reserved, in his years beyond politics, a special contempt for Pauline Hanson’s views. In 1998, when Hanson’s influence was rising for the first brief time, Hawke, Keating and fellow former prime ministers Gough Whitlam and Malcolm Fraser issued a joint statement aimed primarily at her approach and by implication that of John Howard, who was avoiding direct condemnation of Hanson. Former prime ministers Bob Hawke, Gough Whitlam, Malcolm Fraser, Paul Keating and Kevin Rudd after Rudd’s apology to Indigenous Australia, specifically the Stolen Generations. Andrew Taylor “Racism,” Hawke and his fellow signatories declared, “is an unmitigated evil, it is immoral, it does Australia significant harm through Asia and the wider world, it destroys our self-esteem and self-respect. In Australia, it would pit Australian against Australian. It would be destructive of our society.”



It was a follow-up to a scathing statement organised by Hawke and signed by Keating and Whitlam the previous year, directed straight at Hanson. They described her views as “bigoted, uninformed, simplistic and subversive nonsense”. And now Hawke is being accused of supporting Hanson and her mean-minded jihad against Aboriginal people extending a Welcome to Country and others acknowledging their respect for traditional owners and their ongoing connection to the land? On behalf of Bob Hawke, who has been gone these seven years, may I offer a response? Bloody preposterous. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Retiree Terry Bishop, 65, was driving with Rolfe’s girlfriend – 25-year-old Gypsy Satterley – when his dual-cab ute was allegedly rammed. They died in the crash along with the driver of the other ute, 38-year-old Jessica Townley. Rolfe has been accused of stealing an SUV in Gympie’s main street 12 hours before the fatal crash, after threatening a mother and three children at knifepoint. Police allege Satterley travelled with Rolfe in the stolen car before fleeing and being rescued by Bishop, who has been described by police as a good Samaritan and a tragic victim of circumstance. The matter will return to court for another review next Thursday. AAP

World.title: New $2 million blood bank opens in Wellington, major upgrade on old facilities
World.content:
The New Zealand Blood Service says the capital's new blood bank - officially opened by the Health Minister on Wednesday - couldn't come soon enough.

The service at Wellington Regional Hospital plays a critical role in delivering life-saving donor blood to patients and according to staff, the new facility is a major upgrade.

NZ Blood Service chief executive Sam Cliffe said the almost 50-year-old former laboratory was "hopelessly not fit-for-purpose".

"The light fittings were so old we couldn't get new bulbs ... it was virtually impossible to clean. The staff did an amazing job of continuing to operate a very safe and reliable service."

She said the new space had been a long time coming and a couple of years ago things reached a crisis point.

"It could have been quite a dangerous situation in that we could have had our accreditation removed and we wouldn't have been able to provide a full service blood bank," she said.

That didn't happen. Health New Zealand found a solution, Cliffe said and the team was "utterly delighted" with it.

She said the facility was built for under $2 million "on time and on budget".

Sam Cliffe says the old laboratory was old and not fit for purpose. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Wellington blood bank team leader Dan Gyles said he felt a mixture of relief and excitement at Wednesday's opening after pushing for a new lab for close to 16 years.

"It means everything. We now have space to do the job that we should have been doing all along. We have, despite the previous conditions, managed to maintain a safe service, but that was all it was."

He said they now had the space to implement laboratory practices around wearing gowns and protective gear, where required. "Rather than having tea breaks on our knees in the corner."

The laboratory, which includes pneumatic tubes that send and receive blood to and from the wards, multiple blood fridges, freezers storing plasma at minus 35 degrees, and room-temperature storage cabinets that keep platelets "jiggling," is three times the size of the old lab - built to meet expected future demand.

The new Wellington blood bank offices was built for $2 million and came in on time and one budget. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Gyles said the extra space also meant a second blood grouping and screening machine, which was a game changer for the dozen staff that keep the service running around the clock.

Mel Homer received multiple blood transfusions during treatment for blood cancer. Supplied

"These do our grunt work, so this is where the patient samples are loaded up and we determine their blood group ... and then we do a red cell antibody screen."

The process ensured the blood was compatible with the patient who received it, he said.

Gyles said the blood bank was the behind-the-scenes critical step between people donating blood and patients receiving a transfusion - the majority of which were cancer patients, like Mel Homer.

Homer has received multiple blood transfusions over the past year while undergoing treatment for acute myeloid leukaemia, a blood cancer.

"They basically nuke your whole system, it's like scorched earth and you have no immune system and the idea is that they also kill off the cancer cells, and hopefully they don't grow back."

She said the treatment saw her haemoglobin and white blood cell count drop and her platelets - the clotting component - tank.

"You can't function properly so you need blood transfusions to top you up to a level so you can start healing."

In addition to red blood transfusions, Homer also needed platelets to reduce the risk of brain bleeds - but there were only two donors whose platelets were compatible, she said.

"It was life-saving." She said every time she used it - which was multiple times - she would think, "I'm so grateful".

The frozen blood product has to be thawed before it can be used. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

The blood bank also had to be ready for emergencies, Gyles said. Plasma was most often used for bleeding patients, patients in theatre, or trauma patients, he said.

It took about 15 minutes for the frozen blood product to thaw in a jiggling bath at 37C, he said.

"A bleeding patient - they need it quickly. So we've got some pre-thawed ahead of time."

Megan Piercy required an emergency blood transfusion after suffering from a post-partum haemorrhage. Supplied

Two years ago, Megan Piercy became a bleeding patient when she suffered a post-partum haemorrhage following the birth of her son.

"It was all kinds of bells and whistles from there. I had lost ... just over two litres at once."

She said given the emergency situation, she received blood from the universal donor type, however, samples of her blood were also sent off for testing in case she needed something more specific.

Piercy said the transfusion was crucial.

As a passionate blood donor herself, she knew the importance of it, she said. "I just never expected to be on the receiving end of it."

Michelle Sutherland, interim group director of operations for Capital, Coast and Hutt Valley, said the new blood bank was an important investment in the region's health services.

"Having this purpose-built facility on site strengthens our ability to deliver timely, safe and high-quality care for patients who need blood transfusions and other specialist services," she said.

Cliffe said patients, however, shouldn't notice the difference between Wellington's new blood bank and its predecessor.

"We've continued to maintain the same level of service delivery under incredibly trying conditions. [For] the people of Wellington this should be seamless."

Health Minister Simeon Brown cutting the ribbon to open the new Wellington Blood Bank. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

She said the new facility - in addition to future-proofing the service - provided the space for it to resume practical laboratory training for pathology professionals in the Pacific.

World.title: Defence Force training infrastructure in 'World War II era', new documents reveal
World.content:
The Defence Force is on its biggest push ever to get more combat ready and lethal at the same time its training infrastructure is in "World War II era", according to newly released documents.

Proactively released Cabinet papers from April and May outline the big deficit.

"The infrastructure to support training of recruits, in particular, is not in a position to meet existing ... demand in an effective way," said one 12-page paper that asked for, and got, a start to planning for an upgrade to how recruits are trained.

"Much of the infrastructure required to train NZDF personnel, like classrooms or rifle ranges, is World War II era, and is increasingly ineffective, and creating a potential for unsafe training environments.

"Investment is needed to avoid future failure."

The paper asked Cabinet to back a business case for fixing this, and Budget 2026 put in $23m.

However, this only funds a design phase out to 2029-30.

That means an actual fix of systems and infrastructure together appears at least three years away.

Defence Minister Chris Penk said there have been many years of under-investment into the Defence Force and this government is working to fix the consequences.

"We've begun the process of doing so to ensure training can be delivered safely, effectively and at the scale required into the future."

The Defence Capability Plan suggested investments over the next 15 years including into recruitment, retention and training, he said in a statement.

The paper said one upgraded rifle range would be added meantime, but one or two other short-term moves "to add resilience to a significantly degraded capability" were blanked out.

'Failing condition makes it difficult to train'

The deficiencies are a big hurdle to Defence's must-have in its new workforce strategy "to grow more soldiers, sailors and aviators, with urgency" and more tech-savvy ones as drone, cyber and electronic warfare take over.

Instead, "poor infrastructure in failing condition makes it difficult to train and retain people."

An example is old manual target practice ranges not suitable for modern weapons. Two other examples were blanked out.

The wider context is grim:

The state of bases and facilities was a key reason given at scrutiny week in June for the land combat readiness falling to 45 percent at the end of 2025.

Defence has admitted its training systems are degraded too much to rapidly boost battlefield adaptability and agility.

NZDF's ways of managing its existing assets do not meet Treasury standards, and it is slow to get contracts for projects signed up.

Eroded by old gear and slow take-up of new tech, 60 percent of the army's land training system had got to the end of its life, said the May Cabinet paper.

Recruits 'most pressing'

The whole system relied in the first place on recruit training but this was significantly degraded and the "most pressing" thing needing fixing.

That fix would focus on Waiouru camp and line up with Australia, which was putting almost a billion dollars into recruit training, as well as looking to the US, UK and Singapore.

The paper that Penk lodged with Cabinet showed the ministers - Judith Collins was Defence Minister at the time - walking a line between "capability and affordability", even after Defence got a $9 billion fillip in new spending over four years from 2025.

So they narrowed in on a new recruit training system and curriculum which was the "minimum viable capability needed in the short term", and would need to integrate with Australia, other partners and other government services.

"Australian designs will be used where possible" in the detailed business case that is now being worked on.

'Future growth' option not chosen

A third more ambitious option that catered for "future growth and the introduction of new and emerging ... capabilities" did not make the cut.

Budget 2026 also had funding for an undisclosed amount for a new 'virtual training' facility at Linton camp near Palmerston North.

Defence has a huge estate, huge budgets and a chequered track record running it all.

The latest available Treasury report on how NZDF was doing with its big capital investments said it was no longer reporting a significant underspend (which can indicate projects hitting delays). Its actual spend on projects at $406m, and its spending on repairs and maintenance at $193m, at that stage were only a bit behind forecast.

However, Defence spending on specialist equipment and on data/digital was running well behind forecast.

The report for the September-December 2025 quarter showed it took about a year for procurement processes to get to the point of signing contracts, among the slower on the major public agencies covered by the Treasury investment reports.

Its asset registers and asset management plans were not up to scratch according to the latest gauge in June 2025. An update for 2026 won't be publicly available for months.

Labour's defence spokesperson Damien O'Connor said it supported the direction of the Defence Capability Plan.

"Personnel is the most acute issue facing NZDF. Labour sees this as a priority and will get advice on ensuring training capacity is built when in government," he said.

World.title: Rush to desex pigs rehomed after alleged murder as boars break in
World.content:
An animal rescue charity is rushing to desex 42 female pigs due to frisky wild boars breaking through electric fencing and into their enclosure.

The 70 or so pigs were previously cared for by Coromandel farmer Stuart Edmonson, who has been charged with murdering a pig hunter and attempting to murder another in December 2024.

His pigs were taken into the care of charitable trust HUHA, whose chief executive Carolyn Press-McKenzie said the break-ins mean they're scrambling to desex 42 females at their Wellington sanctuary.

"We were never quite sure how they were getting in, we can't find any holes in the fencing, but they're very determined so they're either throwing themselves over the fencing or they're wiggling under the fencing."

Supplied/HUHA

The male pigs were desexed soon after coming into HUHA's care, so they thought they wouldn't need to do the same for the females in order to prevent any unwanted litters.

"One day we saw a skinny, wily-looking chap wandering around. It was definitely a wild boar," Press-Mckenzie said.

"We'd been really responsible desexing our boys but we hadn't factored the food and the environment attracting wild boars down."

They de-sexed the "wily-looking chap", but he was followed by two more wild boars.

"Our ones don't get out - they all stay-put because they've got everything they need. They've got like a little village, there's a lovely little stream, they have this beautiful forest with natives and some pine trees," Press-Mckenzie said.

The 70 or so pigs had gone into the care of HUHA Supplied/HUHA

"They don't really want for anything. But of course the wild boars on the outside looking in, they're desperate, they need food and they need care."

HUHA staff were able to catch and castrate two of the three wild boars.

"They're now living as part of the community so they've achieved the dream life they were after."

Stuart Edmonson, who was known internationally for the wild pigs he kept as pets, is due to stand trial next year charged with the murder of 41-year-old father-of-five Kevin Mabbott and attempting to murder another man.

Mabbott, 41, was a father-of-five and was described by his loved ones as a "loveable ratbag".

The 70 or so pigs had gone into the care of HUHA Supplied/HUHA

Carolyn Press-McKenzie said HUHA staff have managed to desex most of the female pigs with just a few more to go.

"We shouldn't be having any more piglets, and that's forever, so that's really exciting."

She said the pigs are doing very well, and are enjoying meals including malt donated by Panhead Brewery and vegetables by Pak'nSave.

World.title: Chinese Embassy in New Zealand voices concerns to MFAT over Winston Peters comments
World.content:
China has expressed its concerns to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade over comments Winston Peters made to Green MP Lawrence Xu-Nan.

The Chinese Embassy in New Zealand said it had lodged "solemn representations" with MFAT over the "negative China-related remarks made by a certain politician in the New Zealand Parliament."

That certain politician, Peters, told the Chinese-born MP to "go back to your own country" during a debate in Parliament on Wednesday.

"That's where they lie like a flatfish, but they don't lie like that here, all right?" Peters said.

"This is called a democracy, unlike what you're used to."

China's ambassador Wang Xiaolong had earlier posted on social media that New Zealand's domestic politics were not China's concern, but "sometimes, a statement says more about the person that makes it than anything or anybody else."

RNZ

Now, China has escalated the matter, with the Embassy saying it had urged the New Zealand side to "value the equal and mutually beneficial relationship between China and New Zealand and to do more things conducive to bilateral relations rather than the other way around."

The Embassy's statement called on the New Zealand side to respect and safeguard the Chinese community in New Zealand's legitimate rights and interests "and to create an open, inclusive and non-discriminatory environment for them to study, live and work in New Zealand."

Peters had earlier double-down in response to Wang, saying he was "defending New Zealand's democracy."

He continues to stand by his comments.

On Thursday night, a spokesperson for the minister said he had been briefed on an MFAT official's conversation with the Chinese Embassy that afternoon.

"He stands by his comments over the last couple of days, which have been aimed at defending New Zealand's democracy," the spokesperson said.

"The Minister is a long-standing custodian of the New Zealand-China relationship, having made seven official visits to China - most recently in late 2025."

World.title: English to become official language of NZ alongside Te Reo Māori and sign language
World.content:
English will join Te Reo Māori and sign language as an official language of New Zealand, after the English Language Bill passed its third and final reading at Parliament.

The bill, in the name of Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith, is just two pages long, and states English "has long been a de facto official language in New Zealand, that is, widely used and accepted as an official language, but its official language status is not set out in legislation".

Once again, Goldsmith did not contribute to the debate. He has previously said the bill was not a priority, but was a coalition commitment.

New Zealand First got the bill into the coalition agreement, and speaking at the third reading, MP Casey Costello said the bill was important to the "hard-working Kiwi battlers" her party represented, and denied it was a waste of time.

"It is not trivial, unnecessary, or a distraction to this House in a democracy to deliver for those who elected us to this House," she said.

Costello said the bill provided clarity and certainty in legislation, and changed none of the existing legal protections afforded to Te Reo Māori or New Zealand sign language.

Her contribution was significantly less combative than New Zealand First leader Winston Peters' call at the first reading of the legislation in February.

NZ First MP Casey Costello. VNP / Louis Collins

Back then, Peters said the purpose of the bill was to help solve a "virtue signalling narrative," and that New Zealand should be using English as the primary and language.

Now, his colleague Costello said the purpose of the bill was providing clarity in law.

"This is a practical measure. It aligns the statute book with long-standing practice, and provides a clear statement about the status of English within New Zealand's official framework."

'Snowflake government' - opposition questions the bill's purpose

Opposition parties have questioned the government's priorities, given most laws are already written in English.

Green MP Tamatha Paul said the bill's proponents were "bunch of snowflakes that hear the word Aotearoa and cry themselves to sleep," and noted English was also not an official language of England.

"Let me tell you why Te Reo Māori has a protected language status, because it was beaten out of Māori systematically. We had to march our arses to Parliament, demanding that the indigenous first language of this country be recognised and not beaten out of the mouth of its native speakers."

Green MP Tamatha Paul. VNP / Phil Smith

Paul has recently returned from a cross-party visit to the Welsh Senedd.

"They've got their their beautiful indigenous language, Cymraeg, everywhere before English. And guess what? The world didn't fall over, and the world didn't end. People still knew where they were going. In fact, people saw it and thought, 'wow, we're in a country that values their indigenous language and identity,' unlike our snowflake government that cannot handle Te Reo Māori."

Her colleague Lawrence Xu-Nan, who on Wednesday had been told by Peters to "go back to your own country," asked what the House was protecting the English language from.

"What is an example where English has not been otherwise provided for? There is no response to that. Because there is no instance that a minister can think of that will make this bill fulfil any requirement of why we need to legislate or give a legislative recognition of an official language status to English."

Speaking in Te Reo Māori, Te Pāti Māori MP Oriini Kaipara spoke of the "pain Māori has taken to establish its space in this country," while English had not followed the same path.

"What benefit will come from this kaupapa, from this event? Why are these hours and the time of all of these Members being used up in this way? Why are we spending all this time on this bill, when we know that English is already the main language of New Zealand?"

Te Pāti Māori MP Oriini Kaipara. Parliament TV

Despite being opposed to the legislation philosophically, Labour voted it through the House.

Labour MP Duncan Webb said the bill was "silly" and "meaningless", while his colleague Camilla Belich said New Zealand First was attempting to politicise what was already a self-evident truth.

"I wondered if they might want to legislate for the changing of the seasons? Or for the fact that there are sometimes four seasons in one day in Auckland, or whether they should legislate for the southerly winds to blow through Wellington?"

ACT's Simon Court said his party supported the bill because many New Zealanders had been asking for it.

"When we go to a hospital, for example, and we want to find our way to the ward, find our way to an appointment, of course, the English language is important. Same if you're an air traffic controller. Better make sure you're using English so the pilots understand how to land, where to land the plane."

In a sign the bill was not really a National Party priority, National MPs' contributions were short.

Carl Bates and Paulo Garcia said little more than their commending the bill to the House, Greg Fleming delivered his contribution mostly in Te Reo Māori, and Vanessa Weenink said sometimes the best medical intervention one could do was as much of nothing as possible.

World.title: Call for more solar installation training if subsidies implemented
World.content:
Solar installers are warning of a looming worker shortage, if low-cost loans or subsidies are brought in without any support or training for the wider electrical industry.

Many political parties have announced policies to boost rooftop solar uptake ahead of this year's election, and the Ministry for Regulation today recommended streamling the regulatory process for installing solar.

Some installers have seen demand explode this year already and said the industry was now near capacity, even without additional incentives.

New Plymouth electrician Brad Lynch has run solar installation company Solar One for the last seven years, starting out as one man and a van.

That had rapidly changed in the last two years, he said.

"Last year we were three to four staff and we've scaled up to seven staff this year and we're hiring again to keep up with demand."

Interest had surged after the current Middle East conflict began, he said.

"Everyone wanted electric vehicles, gas prices went up and solar was the talk of the town. We saw a 300 percent increase in inquiries overnight with that war kicking off."

With some form of financial support or incentive for households looking inevitable post-election, he was anticipating yet another jump in demand.

"We're planning for about a 40 to 50 percent increase in work as these subsidies roll out, so we're looking to scale to between 10 and 15 people over the next 12 months to make sure that we're set up for these schemes to roll out," Lynch said.

Each new staff member was already a qualified electrician, but still took about six months to get up to speed with solar, he said.

Workforce needs to double - at least

Solar Energy Association of New Zealand spokesperson Gareth Williams agreed that interest had "really just taken off quite suddenly" after the Middle East conflict began.

"Even though that doesn't directly relate to solar, it's got people thinking about their costs, and then there was another round of quite significant electricity price increases in April."

Many of the organisation's members had reported similar increases in business to Brad Lynch, which was putting pressure on their turnaround times, Williams said.

"In some cases, there are several weeks' lead time before they can even go and visit the site to look at the job to give the customer a quote."

Supplied

SEANZ estimated there were between 1500 and 1800 solar installers working in New Zealand.
